padding: 0 2px; }\n  .flow .stage.main { border-color: var(--accent); box-shadow: 0 0 0 3px var(--accent-soft); }\n\n  dl.glossary dt { font-weight: 600; margin-top: 12px; }\n  dl.glossary dd { margin: 2px 0 0 0; }\n  ul.tight li, ol.tight li { margin: 4px 0; }\n  .pill {\n    display: inline-block; font-size: 12px; font-weight: 600; border-radius: 999px;\n    padding: 1px 10px; border: 1px solid var(--line); background: #f0f3f8; color: #3c4a5d;\n  }\n  footer.docinfo {\n    margin-top: 50px; padding-top: 14px; border-top: 1px solid var(--line);\n    color: var(--muted); font-size: 13.5px;\n  }\n  @media (max-width: 720px) {\n    nav.toc ol { columns: 1; }\n    header.hero { padding: 24px 22px; }\n  }\n</style>\n</head>\n<body>\n<div class=\"wrap\">\n\n<header class=\"hero\">\n  <span class=\"kicker\">Visual C · Backend documentation</span>\n  <h1>The Trace Engine: how Visual C records a running C&nbsp;program</h1>\n  <p>\n    The <strong>trace engine</strong> (<code>c-trace-engine</code>) is the part of Visual C\n    that actually <em>runs</em> a student's C program and turns what happens into one\n    detailed, replayable file — the <strong>trace</strong>. Everything the future Visual C\n    interface shows (the C view, the assembly view, memory, pointers, the heap, crashes)\n    is read back from that file. This page explains what the engine does and what the\n    trace contains, in plain language.\n  </p>\n</header>\n\n<nav class=\"toc\">\n  <strong>On this page</strong>\n  <ol>\n    <li><a href=\"#overview\">What the trace engine is</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#pipeline\">The big picture</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#steps\">What happens, step by step</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#trace-tour\">A guided tour of the trace file</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#sync\">How the C view and assembly view stay in sync</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#honesty\">What is exact, and what is not</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#limits\">Safety limits, timeouts, partial traces</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#memory-errors\">Crashes and memory errors</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#performance\">Performance at a glance</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#run-it\">Running it yourself</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#limitations\">Known limitations</a></li>\n    <li><a href=\"#glossary\">Glossary</a></li>\n  </ol>\n</nav>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"overview\">1. What the trace engine is</h2>\n\n<p>\n  Visual C is an <strong>offline-first</strong> learning tool: a student writes a small C\n  program, and Visual C shows them how it really executed — statement by statement,\n  instruction by instruction, allocation by allocation. The trace engine is the\n  command-line component that makes this possible.\n</p>\n\n<p>Its job in one sentence:</p>\n\n<div class=\"callout\">\n  <p>\n    <strong>Compile the program, run it once under a debugger, and record\n    everything observable about that single run into a versioned JSON\n    file — the trace.</strong>\n  </p>\n</div>\n\n<p>Three principles guide every design decision:</p>\n<ul class=\"tight\">\n  <li><strong>Real execution only.</strong> The engine never simulates loops or invents\n      instruction events. If something is not in the trace, it was not observed.</li>\n  <li><strong>One timeline.</strong> The C-level view and the machine-instruction view come\n      from the <em>same</em> debugger run, so they can never disagree about what happened.</li>\n  <li><strong>Honesty about gaps.</strong> Whenever data could not be observed (timeout,\n      limit, unreadable memory, optimized-out variable), the trace says so explicitly\n      instead of guessing.</li>\n</ul>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"pipeline\">2. The big picture</h2>\n\n<div class=\"flow\">\n  <div class=\"stage\"><b>Your C sources</b><span class=\"small\">one or more <code>.c</code> files, plus build settings</span></div>\n  <div class=\"arrow\">→</div>\n  <div class=\"stage\"><b>Compiler stage</b><span class=\"small\">GCC builds a debug binary; a second sanitizer binary is built for crash diagnosis</span></div>\n  <div class=\"arrow\">→</div>\n  <div class=\"stage main\"><b>Debug run</b><span class=\"small\">the program runs once under GDB; the engine single-steps user code and records stops</span></div>\n  <div class=\"arrow\">→</div>\n  <div class=\"stage\"><b>Analysis stages</b><span class=\"small\">Valgrind re-runs the program; the sanitizer pass runs when triggered; caller locations resolved</span></div>\n  <div class=\"arrow\">→</div>\n  <div class=\"stage\"><b>The trace (JSON)</b><span class=\"small\">one file describing the whole run</span></div>\n</div>\n\n<p class=\"small muted\">\n  The compiler, debugger and analyses are real external tools (GCC, GDB, Valgrind,\n  addr2line). The engine drives them, enforces time and memory budgets, and stitches\n  their outputs into one coherent document.\n</p>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"steps\">3. What happens, step by step</h2>\n\n<ol class=\"tight\">\n  <li><strong>Compile.</strong> Every translation unit is compiled with debug info\n      (<code>-g -O0</code>). Compiler errors are captured in a machine-readable form and\n      end up in the trace, so even a failed build produces a useful partial trace.\n      A small runtime is linked in that records every <code>malloc</code>/<code>calloc</code>/\n      <code>realloc</code>/<code>free</code> the program makes to a side file.</li>\n  <li><strong>Run under GDB.</strong> The engine launches GDB in its machine-facing mode\n      (MI2), breaks at <code>main</code>, and steps through the student's code —\n      instruction by instruction in dual mode, or line by line in the cheaper\n      source-only mode. Program output is captured through a separate channel so it\n      never mixes with debugger chatter.</li>\n  <li><strong>Record at every stop.</strong> Each time the program pauses, the engine\n      records where it stopped (file, line, function, call stack), every visible\n      variable (name, type, value, its own address, and for pointers the address it\n      points to), the live contents of heap blocks, and the program's output so far.\n      In dual mode each attempted machine instruction is recorded too: its address,\n      the address of the <em>next</em> instruction, what happened (completed, faulted,\n      interrupted), and selected memory reads.</li>\n  <li><strong>Analyze independently.</strong> Valgrind re-runs the program on its own to\n      hunt for memory errors with a second opinion. When triggered — a crash, or\n      Valgrind findings — the sanitizer-built binary also runs once as a diagnostic\n      pass. Allocation callers are resolved to <code>file:line</code> in one batched\n      <code>addr2line</code> call.</li>\n  <li><strong>Assemble the trace.</strong> Everything is written as one JSON document\n      with a schema version, per-stage health reports, resource usage, and honest\n      notes about anything that was skipped or degraded.</li>\n</ol>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"trace-tour\">4. A guided tour of the trace file</h2>\n\n<p>\n  A trace is a single JSON object. These are its main sections, grouped by what a\n  reader (and later the Visual C interface) uses them for. A full real example lives\n  at <a href=\"../examples/v21_dual.json\"><code>examples/v21_dual.json</code></a>.\n</p>\n\n<table>\n  <tr><th>Section</th><th>What it contains</th><th>Think of it as…</th></tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>snapshots</code></td>\n    <td>One record per stop in the student's code: source file/line/function, the call\n        stack, all visible variables with addresses and raw bytes, live heap-block\n        contents, and program output so far.</td>\n    <td>\"A photo of the program's state\" at each C statement</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>instruction_events</code><br><code>disassembly_table</code></td>\n    <td>Every <em>attempted</em> machine instruction in order (address, next address,\n        outcome, source line it belongs to), plus a de-duplicated table of instruction\n        definitions (text, bytes, function) referenced by ID.</td>\n    <td>\"The assembly view\" — what the CPU really did</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>heap_events</code><br><code>heap_state</code><br><code>allocation_lifetimes</code></td>\n    <td>The full allocation story: every <code>allocated</code>/<code>reallocated</code>/\n        <code>freed</code> event, the final state of every block (live or freed, with\n        contents), and each block's lifetime boundaries with stable IDs.</td>\n    <td>\"The memory view\" — the heap's biography</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>crash_report</code></td>\n    <td>For a crash: the signal (e.g. <code>SIGSEGV</code>), the exact source line and\n        faulting instruction address, and a backtrace.</td>\n    <td>\"Why did it die?\"</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>valgrind_report</code><br><code>sanitizer_report</code></td>\n    <td>The independent memory analyses: Valgrind errors (with stacks and leak\n        classification) and the sanitizer reproduction attempt, each with its own\n        completeness flags.</td>\n    <td>\"Second opinions\" from other tools</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>execution</code>, <code>execution_status</code></td>\n    <td>The overall outcome: completed, crashed, timed out, hit a limit, failed to\n        compile, and so on — with exit code and signal.</td>\n    <td>\"How did the run end?\"</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>stage_results</code></td>\n    <td>Health report per stage (compiler, debugger, Valgrind, sanitizer, allocation\n        tracker): status, duration, and a reason whenever something did not complete.</td>\n    <td>\"Did each part finish, and if not, why?\"</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>coverage</code>, <code>trace_gaps</code></td>\n    <td>Which parts of execution were observed (<code>user_code</code> scope) and which\n        intervals were not (program startup, skipped library code), with explicit gap\n        records — never guessed counts.</td>\n    <td>\"What did we NOT see?\"</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>resource_usage</code>, <code>profiling</code></td>\n    <td>Measured consumption: wall time, number of debugger commands issued, snapshot\n        count, which limits fired, timing breakdowns.</td>\n    <td>\"What did the recording cost?\"</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>analysis_notes</code>, <code>session_meta</code>,\n        <code>execution_limits</code>, <code>tracing_configuration</code>,\n        <code>compile_errors</code>, <code>storage</code></td>\n    <td>Everything else a careful reader needs: warnings and degradations, tool\n        versions, the effective limits, the configuration used, compiler diagnostics,\n        and storage/bookkeeping details.</td>\n    <td>\"The fine print, in the document itself\"</td>\n  </tr>\n</table>\n\n<h3>A single instruction event, annotated</h3>\n\n<pre><code>{\n  <span class=\"k\">\"event_id\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">4</span>,              <span class=\"cm\">// ordered, zero-based: this is the 5th attempt</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"address\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"0x0000000000401106\"</span>,   <span class=\"cm\">// the instruction that was ABOUT to run</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"next_address\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"0x0000000000401109\"</span>, <span class=\"cm\">// actually observed next stop — never guessed</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"instruction_id\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">0</span>,         <span class=\"cm\">// index into disassembly_table (no repeated text)</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"source\"</span>: { <span class=\"k\">\"line\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">22</span>, <span class=\"k\">\"func\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"sum_of_three\"</span> },\n  <span class=\"k\">\"outcome\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"completed\"</span>,      <span class=\"cm\">// completed | faulted | interrupted | unknown</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"stopped_reason\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"end-stepping-range\"</span>,\n  <span class=\"k\">\"memory\"</span>: [ { <span class=\"k\">\"expression\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"&amp;x\"</span>, <span class=\"k\">\"raw_bytes_hex\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"0a000000\"</span>,\n               <span class=\"k\">\"status\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"valid\"</span> } ],\n  <span class=\"k\">\"checkpoint_id\"</span>: <span class=\"hl\">12</span>          <span class=\"cm\">// links to the nearest snapshot (the C-level state)</span>\n  <span class=\"cm\">// note: no \"registers\" key — see the performance section</span>\n}</code></pre>\n\n<h3>A single variable record, annotated</h3>\n\n<pre><code>{\n  <span class=\"k\">\"name\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"heap\"</span>, <span class=\"k\">\"c_type\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"int *\"</span>,\n  <span class=\"k\">\"value\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"0x705010\"</span>,            <span class=\"cm\">// what the pointer CONTAINS</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"address\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"0x7fffffffd8f0\"</span>,   <span class=\"cm\">// where the pointer variable itself lives</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"points_to\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"0x705010\"</span>,\n  <span class=\"k\">\"target\"</span>: { <span class=\"k\">\"kind\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"heap\"</span>, <span class=\"k\">\"allocation_id\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">1</span>,\n              <span class=\"k\">\"base_address\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"0x705010\"</span>, <span class=\"k\">\"offset_bytes\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">0</span> },\n  <span class=\"k\">\"raw_bytes_hex\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"10500700…\"</span>,  <span class=\"cm\">// the pointer's own bytes, as observed</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"read_status\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"valid\"</span>\n}</code></pre>\n\n<p class=\"small muted\">\n  Pointer targets are classified as <code>stack</code>, <code>heap</code> (with the\n  allocation ID it belongs to), <code>global</code>, <code>code</code>,\n  <code>null</code>, <code>unmapped</code> or <code>unknown</code> — so the interface\n  can draw \"this pointer goes to that heap block\" without guessing.\n</p>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"sync\">5. How the C view and assembly view stay in sync</h2>\n\n<p>\n  Both views come from <strong>one run of the program under one GDB session</strong>.\n  Every event in the assembly view carries a <code>stop_id</code> pair and optionally a\n  <code>checkpoint_id</code> pointing into the source view's snapshots. Concretely:\n</p>\n<ul class=\"tight\">\n  <li>Each recorded instruction event names the source file, line and function it was\n      paused in — that is the link from assembly back to the C statement.</li>\n  <li>Snapshots (the C-level state photos) record how many instruction attempts had\n      happened before them, so either timeline can be navigated from the other.</li>\n  <li>Instruction addresses are taken from the debugger's own stop reports. The\n      <em>next</em> address is always the actually observed next stop — crucial,\n      because machine code frequently does <em>not</em> run sequentially (branches,\n      calls, returns, faults).</li>\n</ul>\n\n<div class=\"callout\">\n  <p><strong>Why this matters for Visual C:</strong> the interface can highlight a C\n  statement, show the exact machine instructions that executed for it, and step\n  through them — all from one file, with no risk of the two views disagreeing.</p>\n</div>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"honesty\">6. What is exact, and what is not</h2>\n\n<p>\n  A learning tool must never show invented data as if it were real. The trace follows\n  a strict honesty policy:\n</p>\n<ul class=\"tight\">\n  <li><strong>Values are exact only at their recorded stop.</strong> A snapshot shows the\n      program's state at that moment; nothing claims to know intermediate values\n      between stops.</li>\n  <li><strong>Nothing is fabricated.</strong> Unobservable data is <code>null</code>,\n      with a machine-readable <em>why</em>: validity flags such as\n      <code>valid</code>, <code>unavailable</code>, <code>unreadable</code>,\n      <code>optimized_out</code>, <code>truncated</code>, <code>not_captured</code>.</li>\n  <li><strong>Gaps are explicit.</strong> Startup before <code>main</code>, and code the\n      engine deliberately steps over (library internals), appear as\n      <code>trace_gaps</code> with observed boundary addresses — the number of unseen\n      instructions is never invented.</li>\n  <li><strong>Partial beats silent.</strong> A timeout, a limit or a crash still yields\n      a trace containing everything captured up to that point, clearly marked as\n      incomplete.</li>\n  <li><strong>A freed block's bytes are the last bytes seen while it was alive.</strong>\n      Memory is not read after the block was freed — the trace says so rather than\n      implying the bytes are current.</li>\n</ul>\n\n<div class=\"callout warn\">\n  <p><strong>Rule for the interface:</strong> never present a memory value as\n  \"current\" unless its record says it was observed at the displayed stop. The\n  trace gives you the status flags to enforce this.</p>\n</div>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"limits\">7. Safety limits, timeouts, partial traces</h2>\n\n<p>\n  The engine wraps everything in budgets so a runaway student program cannot hang the\n  session. Limits are configurable on the command line or in a JSON config file;\n  hitting one terminates collection <em>gracefully</em> and keeps the partial trace.\n</p>\n\n<table>\n  <tr><th>Limit (flag)</th><th>Default</th><th>What it bounds</th></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--timeout</code></td><td>10 s</td><td>The whole session: compile + run + analyses</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-steps</code></td><td>1,000</td><td>Debugger stepping commands</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-memory-mb</code></td><td>256 MB</td><td>Address space of the program being traced</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-output-bytes</code></td><td>1 MiB</td><td>Captured program output (ends the run as <code>output_limit_reached</code>)</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-heap-allocations</code></td><td>10,000</td><td>Tracked allocation records</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-snapshots</code></td><td>1,000</td><td>State photos</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-snapshot-memory-bytes</code></td><td>1 MiB</td><td>Variable + heap bytes read per snapshot</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-memory-read-bytes</code></td><td>4 KiB</td><td>A single memory read</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-instruction-events</code></td><td>100,000</td><td>Recorded instruction attempts</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-gdb-commands</code></td><td>1,000,000</td><td>Total debugger traffic</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-processes</code></td><td>16</td><td>Child processes (when cgroups are available)</td></tr>\n</table>\n\n<div class=\"callout warn\">\n  <p><strong>These are not a security sandbox.</strong> They protect the session from\n  runaway programs, not the machine from malicious ones. Real isolation needs a\n  container or VM.</p>\n</div>\n\n<p>\n  Every limit that fires is recorded in <code>resource_usage.limits_triggered</code>\n  (each limit appears at most once), and the overall outcome reflects the\n  <em>real</em> cause — e.g. ending because the output cap was hit is reported as\n  <code>output_limit_reached</code>, not disguised as a step limit.\n</p>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"memory-errors\">8. Crashes and memory errors</h2>\n\n<p>Three independent sources of truth, kept strictly separate:</p>\n\n<ol class=\"tight\">\n  <li><strong>The debugger observes the crash itself.</strong> The trace keeps the\n      signal, the exact faulting instruction (its address matches the last assembly\n      event, marked <code>faulted</code>) and the source line. No events are invented\n      after the crash.</li>\n  <li><strong>Valgrind is the second opinion.</strong> The program runs a second time\n      under Valgrind's memcheck, which can catch errors that did not crash —\n      use-after-free, out-of-bounds accesses, leaks — and reports them with stacks\n      and source locations. Findings are correlated with the heap timeline by\n      file and line.</li>\n  <li><strong>The sanitizer pass is the reproduction attempt.</strong> A second binary\n      built with AddressSanitizer (plus UBSan when installed) runs on its own. What\n      it found, and whether it truly <em>reproduced</em> the recorded crash, is kept\n      separate from the debugger's observations — an ASan finding that does not\n      match the crash is labeled <code>diagnostic_observed</code>, never forced into\n      agreement.</li>\n</ol>\n\n<h3>When does the sanitizer pass run?</h3>\n<p>Configurable with <code>--sanitizer-trigger</code>:</p>\n<table>\n  <tr><th>Mode</th><th>Meaning</th></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>never</code></td><td>Skip the pass entirely.</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>on_crash</code></td><td>Run only when the traced run crashed (the V2 behavior).</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>on_crash_or_valgrind_error</code></td><td><span class=\"pill\">default</span> Run on a crash, <em>or</em> when Valgrind found memory errors even though the program exited cleanly.</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>always</code></td><td>Run for every successful build, budget permitting.</td></tr>\n</table>\n\n<p class=\"small muted\">\n  Valgrind and the sanitizer never run in the same process, global time budgets are\n  always respected, and a skipped pass records the reason in\n  <code>stage_results.sanitizer</code>.\n</p>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"performance\">9. Performance at a glance</h2>\n\n<p>\n  The engine was profiled with a formal audit. The original design polled the CPU\n  registers after every single instruction — useful for a register panel, but it\n  consumed about <strong>90&nbsp;% of all debugger time</strong>. Visual C will not show\n  register panels, so version&nbsp;2.1 removed that collection entirely.\n</p>\n\n<p>Result on the audit benchmark suite (median of 3 runs, same machine):</p>\n\n<table>\n  <tr><th>Workload</th><th>Before</th><th>After</th><th>Speed-up</th></tr>\n  <tr><td>Finite loop (1,012 instructions)</td><td>19.1 s</td><td>6.1 s</td><td>3.1×</td></tr>\n  <tr><td>Function calls (1,413)</td><td>28.5 s</td><td>8.9 s</td><td>3.2×</td></tr>\n  <tr><td>Heap churn (1,363)</td><td>31.1 s</td><td>12.3 s</td><td>2.5×</td></tr>\n  <tr><td>Nested loops (1,352)</td><td>29.9 s</td><td>13.3 s</td><td>2.2×</td></tr>\n  <tr><td>Recursion (671)</td><td>20.0 s</td><td>10.1 s</td><td>2.0×</td></tr>\n  <tr><td>Simple arithmetic (18)</td><td>3.6 s</td><td>3.8 s</td><td>— (fixed startup cost dominates)</td></tr>\n</table>\n\n<p class=\"small muted\">\n  Instruction addresses were never taken from registers — they come from the\n  debugger's stop reports — so nothing about the recorded execution changed. The\n  same audit also confirmed that the remaining big cost is capturing the C-level\n  state photos, which is the core educational feature and stays.\n</p>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"run-it\">10. Running it yourself</h2>\n\n<pre><code><span class=\"cm\"># the basics: compile, run, write trace.json, print the trace to stdout</span>\ncargo run -- sample.c\n\n<span class=\"cm\"># save to a file; give the program some arguments</span>\ncargo run -- sample.c --output trace.json --  --verbose 42\n\n<span class=\"cm\"># common knobs</span>\ncargo run -- sample.c --timeout 3 --max-steps 200\ncargo run -- sample.c --trace-mode source          <span class=\"cm\"># cheaper, C-level only</span>\ncargo run -- sample.c --sanitizer-trigger always\ncargo run -- sample.c --gdb-path /usr/bin/gdb-14   <span class=\"cm\"># override tool discovery</span>\n\n<span class=\"cm\"># a failed build still produces a trace with the compiler diagnostics</span>\ncargo run -- broken.c</code></pre>\n\n<table>\n  <tr><th>Exit code</th><th>Meaning</th></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>0</code></td><td>A trace was produced (completed, crashed, timed out, or hit a limit are all \"success\" for the recorder).</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>2</code></td><td>Compilation failed; a partial trace with the diagnostics is still emitted.</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>1</code></td><td>Operational error (bad arguments, missing source, missing required tool). No trace.</td></tr>\n</table>\n\n<h3>The optional journal</h3>\n<p>\n  With <code>--journal run.jsonl</code> the engine additionally streams every record\n  (configuration, disassembly entries, instruction events, checkpoints, gaps, …) to a\n  line-oriented log as execution proceeds, and finalizes it with a footer record.\n  This is what allows very long runs to keep a complete, durable record even when the\n  JSON is instructed to keep only a bounded index in memory\n  (<code>--journal-only</code>).\n</p>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"limitations\">11. Known limitations</h2>\n\n<ul class=\"tight\">\n  <li>Instruction coverage is <strong>user code only</strong>: program startup and\n      excluded library internals appear as explicit gaps, not recordings.</li>\n  <li>In multi-threaded programs the engine records the <strong>selected\n      thread's</strong> steps; a complete interleaving of all threads is out of scope\n      (the trace marks coverage incomplete and explains why).</li>\n  <li>Children created by <code>fork</code> are not instruction-traced (their\n      allocations may still be recorded).</li>\n  <li>Self-modifying / JIT code is unsupported; the disassembly cache assumes code\n      does not change under the engine.</li>\n  <li>The allocator wrapper sees the program's own allocation calls; memory allocated\n      <em>inside</em> libc or other libraries is invisible to the heap timeline\n      (Valgrind still sees all of it).</li>\n  <li>Per-instruction <strong>CPU register values are not collected</strong> (removed\n      in V2.1 with the feature they served). Old traces that contain them still load.</li>\n  <li>The trace is produced by a development machine, not a security sandbox —\n      see the limits section.</li>\n</ul>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"glossary\">12. Glossary</h2>\n\n<dl class=\"glossary\">\n  <dt>Trace</dt><dd>The versioned JSON document this engine produces — the complete, replayable record of one program run. Schema version 2.</dd>\n  <dt>Snapshot / checkpoint</dt><dd>A \"state photo\": the source location, call stack, variables, heap contents and output captured at one debugger stop in user code.</dd>\n  <dt>Instruction event</dt><dd>One attempted machine instruction: where it was, where execution went next, and what happened. Attempts are recorded even when they fault.</dd>\n  <dt>Disassembly table</dt><dd>A de-duplicated catalog of instruction definitions (text, bytes, function). Events reference it by ID instead of repeating assembly text.</dd>\n  <dt>GDB / MI2</dt><dd>The GNU debugger, and its machine-oriented command interface (\"MI\") that the engine uses to drive it reliably.</dd>\n  <dt>Inferior</dt><dd>Debugger jargon for the program being debugged.</dd>\n  <dt>Valgrind / memcheck</dt><dd>An independent analysis tool that re-runs the program and detects memory errors and leaks without a crash.</dd>\n  <dt>Sanitizer (ASan/UBSan)</dt><dd>Compiler-instrumented error detection linked into a second build of the program; used here as a reproduction pass.</dd>\n  <dt>DWARF</dt><dd>The debug information format GCC embeds in the binary; it is how addresses map back to source lines, variables and types.</dd>\n  <dt>Heap timeline</dt><dd>The ordered story of <code>allocated</code> / <code>reallocated</code> / <code>freed</code> events reconstructed from the program's own allocator calls.</dd>\n  <dt>Trace gap</dt><dd>An explicit record of an interval that was deliberately or necessarily not observed (startup, skipped library code), with observed boundary addresses.</dd>\n  <dt>Stage result</dt><dd>Per-stage health report (compiler, debugger, Valgrind, sanitizer, allocation tracker): completed, failed, timed out, skipped or cancelled — with a reason.</dd>\n  <dt>Journal</dt><dd>The optional line-by-line log the engine writes while running; enables durable recording and memory-bounded operation.</dd>\n</dl>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<footer class=\"docinfo\">\n  <p>\n    <strong>Document info.</strong> Trace engine version: V2.1 (schema version 2),\n    November 2026. This page is the conceptual, reader-friendly layer of the Visual C\n    documentation; the technical contract lives in\n    <a href=\"v2.md\"><code>docs/v2.md</code></a> (schema and semantics) and the focused\n    update reports in <a href=\"v2.1/summary.md\"><code>docs/v2.1/</code></a>\n    (register-capture removal, fixes F-01…F-06, benchmarks, tests). Real example\n    traces: <a href=\"../examples/v21_manifest.json\"><code>examples/v21_manifest.json</code></a>.\n  </p>\n</footer>\n\n</div>\n</body>\n</html>\n",

## Assistant

Done. Created **`docs/trace-engine.html`** — a standalone, plain-language introduction to the trace engine, designed to slot into the full Visual C documentation later.

## What's on the page

Twelve sections, each with a stable anchor (`#overview`, `#pipeline`, `#trace-tour`, …) so other docs or the app can deep-link to them:

1. **What the trace engine is** — one-sentence job description, three guiding principles (real execution only, one timeline, honest gaps)
2. **The big picture** — a visual pipeline diagram: C sources → compiler → debug run under GDB → analyses → trace JSON
3. **Step by step** — the five phases in plain language
4. **Guided tour of the trace file** — every major section explained as "think of it as…", plus two **annotated real-value snippets** taken from `examples/v21_dual.json` (one instruction event, one pointer variable with its `heap` target classification)
5. **Source/assembly sync** — how the two views share one timeline and what that means for the future UI
6. **What is exact, and what is not** — the honesty policy, with an explicit rule box for the interface ("never show a value as current unless its record says so")
7. **Safety limits** — the defaults table, `output_limit_reached`, and the not-a-sandbox warning
8. **Crashes and memory errors** — the three independent sources of truth, plus the sanitizer trigger modes table with the default marked
9. **Performance at a glance** — the register-removal story and the before/after table, simplified
10. **Running it yourself** — quickstart commands, exit codes, the journal
11. **Known limitations** — plain list (user-code scope, selected-thread, no fork tracing, no registers since V2.1, …)
12. **Glossary** — trace, snapshot, MI2, inferior, Valgrind, DWARF, trace gap, stage result…

## Built for future integration

- **Fully self-contained**: no JavaScript, no external assets — one `<style>` block, system fonts, semantic HTML
- **Easy re-theming**: colors and typography all in CSS variables at the top
- **Validated**: tag balance, all 12 TOC anchors, and all relative links (`../examples/…`, `v2.md`, `v2.1/summary.md`) verified to resolve
- **Fact-checked against the repo**: pointer kinds (`stack/heap/global/code/null/unmapped/unknown`), validity flags, heap event types, sanitizer modes, exit codes, and the code snippets all come from real traces — I corrected the `memory` field example mid-way when I found the real value is `[]` unless watch regions are configured
- Cross-referenced with the deep technical docs (`docs/v2.md`, `docs/v2.1/`), and linked from the README intro as the recommended starting point

}\n    pre, table th, table td, .admonition { border-color: #bbb; }\n    pre { background: #f5f5f5; color: #111; }\n    pre .cm { color: #666; }\n  }\n</style>\n</head>\n<body>\n\n<div class=\"topbar\">\n  <span class=\"brand\">Visual C</span>\n  <span class=\"crumb\">Documentation / Engine / <b>The Trace Engine</b></span>\n  <span class=\"version\">engine <b>V2.1</b> · schema <b>2</b></span>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"layout\">\n\n<!-- ================================================================== -->\n<nav class=\"sidebar\">\n  <div class=\"navgroup\">\n    <div class=\"navtitle\">The engine</div>\n    <a class=\"current\" href=\"#\">The Trace Engine</a>\n    <a href=\"architecture.md\">Engine architecture</a>\n    <a href=\"engine-internals.md\">Engine internals</a>\n  </div>\n  <div class=\"navgroup\">\n    <div class=\"navtitle\">Reference</div>\n    <a href=\"v2.md\">V2 schema &amp; semantics</a>\n    <a href=\"build-config.md\">Build configuration</a>\n    <a href=\"v2.1/summary.md\">V2.1 update reports</a>\n  </div>\n  <div class=\"navgroup\">\n    <div class=\"navtitle\">On this page</div>\n    <a href=\"#overview\"><span class=\"num\">1.</span> What the trace engine is</a>\n    <a href=\"#pipeline\"><span class=\"num\">2.</span> The big picture</a>\n    <a href=\"#steps\"><span class=\"num\">3.</span> What happens, step by step</a>\n    <a href=\"#trace-tour\"><span class=\"num\">4.</span> A tour of the trace file</a>\n    <a href=\"#sync\"><span class=\"num\">5.</span> Keeping the views in sync</a>\n    <a href=\"#honesty\"><span class=\"num\">6.</span> What is exact, what is not</a>\n    <a href=\"#limits\"><span class=\"num\">7.</span> Limits, timeouts, partial traces</a>\n    <a href=\"#memory-errors\"><span class=\"num\">8.</span> Crashes and memory errors</a>\n    <a href=\"#performance\"><span class=\"num\">9.</span> Performance at a glance</a>\n    <a href=\"#run-it\"><span class=\"num\">10.</span> Running it yourself</a>\n    <a href=\"#limitations\"><span class=\"num\">11.</span> Known limitations</a>\n    <a href=\"#glossary\"><span class=\"num\">12.</span> Glossary</a>\n  </div>\n  <div class=\"navgroup\">\n    <div class=\"navtitle\">Examples</div>\n    <a href=\"../examples/v21_manifest.json\">Trace manifest</a>\n    <a href=\"../examples/v21_dual.json\">Example dual trace</a>\n  </div>\n</nav>\n\n<!-- ================================================================== -->\n<main class=\"main\">\n\n<h1>The Trace Engine: how Visual C records a running C&nbsp;program</h1>\n\n<p class=\"lede\">\n  The <strong>trace engine</strong> (<code>c-trace-engine</code>) is the part of Visual C\n  that actually <em>runs</em> a student's C program and turns what happens into one\n  detailed, replayable file — the <strong>trace</strong>. Everything the future Visual C\n  interface shows (the C view, the assembly view, memory, pointers, the heap, crashes)\n  is read back from that file. This page explains what the engine does and what the\n  trace contains, in plain language.\n</p>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"overview\">1. What the trace engine is<a class=\"pilcrow\" href=\"#overview\">¶</a></h2>\n\n<p>\n  Visual C is an <strong>offline-first</strong> learning tool: a student writes a small C\n  program, and Visual C shows them how it really executed — statement by statement,\n  instruction by instruction, allocation by allocation. The trace engine is the\n  command-line component that makes this possible.\n</p>\n\n<div class=\"admonition note\">\n  <span class=\"title\">In one sentence</span>\n  <p><strong>Compile the program, run it once under a debugger, and record\n  everything observable about that single run into a versioned JSON\n  file — the trace.</strong></p>\n</div>\n\n<p>Three principles guide every design decision:</p>\n<ul class=\"tight\">\n  <li><strong>Real execution only.</strong> The engine never simulates loops or invents\n      instruction events. If something is not in the trace, it was not observed.</li>\n  <li><strong>One timeline.</strong> The C-level view and the machine-instruction view come\n      from the <em>same</em> debugger run, so they can never disagree about what happened.</li>\n  <li><strong>Honesty about gaps.</strong> Whenever data could not be observed (timeout,\n      limit, unreadable memory, optimized-out variable), the trace says so explicitly\n      instead of guessing.</li>\n</ul>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"pipeline\">2. The big picture<a class=\"pilcrow\" href=\"#pipeline\">¶</a></h2>\n\n<div class=\"flow\">\n  <div class=\"stage\"><b>Your C sources</b><span class=\"small\">one or more <code>.c</code> files, plus build settings</span></div>\n  <div class=\"arrow\">→</div>\n  <div class=\"stage\"><b>Compiler stage</b><span class=\"small\">GCC builds a debug binary; a second sanitizer binary is built for crash diagnosis</span></div>\n  <div class=\"arrow\">→</div>\n  <div class=\"stage main\"><b>Debug run</b><span class=\"small\">the program runs once under GDB; the engine single-steps user code and records stops</span></div>\n  <div class=\"arrow\">→</div>\n  <div class=\"stage\"><b>Analysis stages</b><span class=\"small\">Valgrind re-runs the program; the sanitizer pass runs when triggered; caller locations resolved</span></div>\n  <div class=\"arrow\">→</div>\n  <div class=\"stage\"><b>The trace (JSON)</b><span class=\"small\">one file describing the whole run</span></div>\n</div>\n\n<p class=\"small muted\">\n  The compiler, debugger and analyses are real external tools (GCC, GDB, Valgrind,\n  addr2line). The engine drives them, enforces time and memory budgets, and stitches\n  their outputs into one coherent document.\n</p>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"steps\">3. What happens, step by step<a class=\"pilcrow\" href=\"#steps\">¶</a></h2>\n\n<ol class=\"tight\">\n  <li><strong>Compile.</strong> Every translation unit is compiled with debug info\n      (<code>-g -O0</code>). Compiler errors are captured in a machine-readable form and\n      end up in the trace, so even a failed build produces a useful partial trace.\n      A small runtime is linked in that records every <code>malloc</code>/<code>calloc</code>/\n      <code>realloc</code>/<code>free</code> the program makes to a side file.</li>\n  <li><strong>Run under GDB.</strong> The engine launches GDB in its machine-facing mode\n      (MI2), breaks at <code>main</code>, and steps through the student's code —\n      instruction by instruction in dual mode, or line by line in the cheaper\n      source-only mode. Program output is captured through a separate channel so it\n      never mixes with debugger chatter.</li>\n  <li><strong>Record at every stop.</strong> Each time the program pauses, the engine\n      records where it stopped (file, line, function, call stack), every visible\n      variable (name, type, value, its own address, and for pointers the address it\n      points to), the live contents of heap blocks, and the program's output so far.\n      In dual mode each attempted machine instruction is recorded too: its address,\n      the address of the <em>next</em> instruction, what happened (completed, faulted,\n      interrupted), and selected memory reads.</li>\n  <li><strong>Analyze independently.</strong> Valgrind re-runs the program on its own to\n      hunt for memory errors with a second opinion. When triggered — a crash, or\n      Valgrind findings — the sanitizer-built binary also runs once as a diagnostic\n      pass. Allocation callers are resolved to <code>file:line</code> in one batched\n      <code>addr2line</code> call.</li>\n  <li><strong>Assemble the trace.</strong> Everything is written as one JSON document\n      with a schema version, per-stage health reports, resource usage, and honest\n      notes about anything that was skipped or degraded.</li>\n</ol>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"trace-tour\">4. A guided tour of the trace file<a class=\"pilcrow\" href=\"#trace-tour\">¶</a></h2>\n\n<p>\n  A trace is a single JSON object. These are its main sections, grouped by what a\n  reader (and later the Visual C interface) uses them for. A full real example lives\n  at <a href=\"../examples/v21_dual.json\"><code>examples/v21_dual.json</code></a>.\n</p>\n\n<table>\n  <tr><th>Section</th><th>What it contains</th><th>Think of it as…</th></tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>snapshots</code></td>\n    <td>One record per stop in the student's code: source file/line/function, the call\n        stack, all visible variables with addresses and raw bytes, live heap-block\n        contents, and program output so far.</td>\n    <td>\"A photo of the program's state\" at each C statement</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>instruction_events</code><br><code>disassembly_table</code></td>\n    <td>Every <em>attempted</em> machine instruction in order (address, next address,\n        outcome, source line it belongs to), plus a de-duplicated table of instruction\n        definitions (text, bytes, function) referenced by ID.</td>\n    <td>\"The assembly view\" — what the CPU really did</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>heap_events</code><br><code>heap_state</code><br><code>allocation_lifetimes</code></td>\n    <td>The full allocation story: every <code>allocated</code>/<code>reallocated</code>/\n        <code>freed</code> event, the final state of every block (live or freed, with\n        contents), and each block's lifetime boundaries with stable IDs.</td>\n    <td>\"The memory view\" — the heap's biography</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>crash_report</code></td>\n    <td>For a crash: the signal (e.g. <code>SIGSEGV</code>), the exact source line and\n        faulting instruction address, and a backtrace.</td>\n    <td>\"Why did it die?\"</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>valgrind_report</code><br><code>sanitizer_report</code></td>\n    <td>The independent memory analyses: Valgrind errors (with stacks and leak\n        classification) and the sanitizer reproduction attempt, each with its own\n        completeness flags.</td>\n    <td>\"Second opinions\" from other tools</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>execution</code>, <code>execution_status</code></td>\n    <td>The overall outcome: completed, crashed, timed out, hit a limit, failed to\n        compile, and so on — with exit code and signal.</td>\n    <td>\"How did the run end?\"</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>stage_results</code></td>\n    <td>Health report per stage (compiler, debugger, Valgrind, sanitizer, allocation\n        tracker): status, duration, and a reason whenever something did not complete.</td>\n    <td>\"Did each part finish, and if not, why?\"</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>coverage</code>, <code>trace_gaps</code></td>\n    <td>Which parts of execution were observed (<code>user_code</code> scope) and which\n        intervals were not (program startup, skipped library code), with explicit gap\n        records — never guessed counts.</td>\n    <td>\"What did we NOT see?\"</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>resource_usage</code>, <code>profiling</code></td>\n    <td>Measured consumption: wall time, number of debugger commands issued, snapshot\n        count, which limits fired, timing breakdowns.</td>\n    <td>\"What did the recording cost?\"</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>analysis_notes</code>, <code>session_meta</code>,\n        <code>execution_limits</code>, <code>tracing_configuration</code>,\n        <code>compile_errors</code>, <code>storage</code></td>\n    <td>Everything else a careful reader needs: warnings and degradations, tool\n        versions, the effective limits, the configuration used, compiler diagnostics,\n        and storage/bookkeeping details.</td>\n    <td>\"The fine print, in the document itself\"</td>\n  </tr>\n</table>\n\n<h3>A single instruction event, annotated</h3>\n\n<p class=\"small muted\">Real values from <code>examples/v21_dual.json</code>, annotated:</p>\n\n<pre><code>{\n  <span class=\"k\">\"event_id\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">0</span>,              <span class=\"cm\">// ordered, zero-based: this is the 1st attempt</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"address\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"0x0000000000400586\"</span>,   <span class=\"cm\">// the instruction that was ABOUT to run</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"next_address\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"0x0000000000400587\"</span>, <span class=\"cm\">// actually observed next stop — never guessed</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"instruction_id\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">0</span>,         <span class=\"cm\">// index into disassembly_table (no repeated text)</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"source\"</span>: { <span class=\"k\">\"line\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">29</span>, <span class=\"k\">\"func\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"main\"</span> },\n  <span class=\"k\">\"outcome\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"completed\"</span>,      <span class=\"cm\">// completed | faulted | interrupted | unknown</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"stopped_reason\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"end-stepping-range\"</span>,\n  <span class=\"k\">\"memory\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">[]</span>,               <span class=\"cm\">// reads of user-configured watch addresses appear</span>\n                                 <span class=\"cm\">// here (e.g. {\"expression\":\"&amp;x\",\"status\":\"valid\",</span>\n                                 <span class=\"cm\">//  \"raw_bytes_hex\":\"0a000000\"}) — none configured here</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"checkpoint_id\"</span>: <span class=\"hl\">0</span>           <span class=\"cm\">// links to the nearest snapshot (the C-level state)</span>\n  <span class=\"cm\">// note: no \"registers\" key — see the performance section</span>\n}</code></pre>\n\n<h3>A single variable record, annotated</h3>\n\n<p class=\"small muted\">Real values from <code>examples/v21_dual.json</code> (the fixture's <code>int *arr</code> pointing into a heap block):</p>\n\n<pre><code>{\n  <span class=\"k\">\"name\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"arr\"</span>, <span class=\"k\">\"c_type\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"int *\"</span>,\n  <span class=\"k\">\"value\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"0x705010\"</span>,            <span class=\"cm\">// what the pointer CONTAINS</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"address\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"0x7fffffffda48\"</span>,   <span class=\"cm\">// where the pointer variable itself lives</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"points_to\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"0x705010\"</span>,\n  <span class=\"k\">\"target\"</span>: { <span class=\"k\">\"kind\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"heap\"</span>, <span class=\"k\">\"allocation_id\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">1</span>,\n              <span class=\"k\">\"base_address\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"0x705010\"</span>, <span class=\"k\">\"offset_bytes\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">0</span> },\n  <span class=\"k\">\"raw_bytes_hex\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"10507000…\"</span>,  <span class=\"cm\">// the pointer's own bytes, as observed</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"read_status\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"valid\"</span>\n}</code></pre>\n\n<p class=\"small muted\">\n  Pointer targets are classified as <code>stack</code>, <code>heap</code> (with the\n  allocation ID it belongs to), <code>global</code>, <code>code</code>,\n  <code>null</code>, <code>unmapped</code> or <code>unknown</code> — so the interface\n  can draw \"this pointer goes to that heap block\" without guessing.\n</p>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"sync\">5. How the C view and assembly view stay in sync<a class=\"pilcrow\" href=\"#sync\">¶</a></h2>\n\n<p>\n  Both views come from <strong>one run of the program under one GDB session</strong>.\n  Every event in the assembly view carries a <code>stop_id</code> pair and optionally a\n  <code>checkpoint_id</code> pointing into the source view's snapshots. Concretely:\n</p>\n<ul class=\"tight\">\n  <li>Each recorded instruction event names the source file, line and function it was\n      paused in — that is the link from assembly back to the C statement.</li>\n  <li>Snapshots (the C-level state photos) record how many instruction attempts had\n      happened before them, so either timeline can be navigated from the other.</li>\n  <li>Instruction addresses are taken from the debugger's own stop reports. The\n      <em>next</em> address is always the actually observed next stop — crucial,\n      because machine code frequently does <em>not</em> run sequentially (branches,\n      calls, returns, faults).</li>\n</ul>\n\n<div class=\"admonition note\">\n  <span class=\"title\">Why this matters for Visual C</span>\n  <p>The interface can highlight a C statement, show the exact machine instructions\n  that executed for it, and step through them — all from one file, with no risk of\n  the two views disagreeing.</p>\n</div>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"honesty\">6. What is exact, and what is not<a class=\"pilcrow\" href=\"#honesty\">¶</a></h2>\n\n<p>\n  A learning tool must never show invented data as if it were real. The trace follows\n  a strict honesty policy:\n</p>\n<ul class=\"tight\">\n  <li><strong>Values are exact only at their recorded stop.</strong> A snapshot shows the\n      program's state at that moment; nothing claims to know intermediate values\n      between stops.</li>\n  <li><strong>Nothing is fabricated.</strong> Unobservable data is <code>null</code>,\n      with a machine-readable <em>why</em>: validity flags such as\n      <code>valid</code>, <code>unavailable</code>, <code>unreadable</code>,\n      <code>optimized_out</code>, <code>truncated</code>, <code>not_captured</code>.</li>\n  <li><strong>Gaps are explicit.</strong> Startup before <code>main</code>, and code the\n      engine deliberately steps over (library internals), appear as\n      <code>trace_gaps</code> with observed boundary addresses — the number of unseen\n      instructions is never invented.</li>\n  <li><strong>Partial beats silent.</strong> A timeout, a limit or a crash still yields\n      a trace containing everything captured up to that point, clearly marked as\n      incomplete.</li>\n  <li><strong>A freed block's bytes are the last bytes seen while it was alive.</strong>\n      Memory is not read after the block was freed — the trace says so rather than\n      implying the bytes are current.</li>\n</ul>\n\n<div class=\"admonition warning\">\n  <span class=\"title\">Rule for the interface</span>\n  <p>Never present a memory value as \"current\" unless its record says it was observed\n  at the displayed stop. The trace gives you the status flags to enforce this.</p>\n</div>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"limits\">7. Safety limits, timeouts, partial traces<a class=\"pilcrow\" href=\"#limits\">¶</a></h2>\n\n<p>\n  The engine wraps everything in budgets so a runaway student program cannot hang the\n  session. Limits are configurable on the command line or in a JSON config file;\n  hitting one terminates collection <em>gracefully</em> and keeps the partial trace.\n</p>\n\n<table>\n  <tr><th>Limit (flag)</th><th>Default</th><th>What it bounds</th></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--timeout</code></td><td>10 s</td><td>The whole session: compile + run + analyses</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-steps</code></td><td>1,000</td><td>Debugger stepping commands</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-memory-mb</code></td><td>256 MB</td><td>Address space of the program being traced</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-output-bytes</code></td><td>1 MiB</td><td>Captured program output (ends the run as <code>output_limit_reached</code>)</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-heap-allocations</code></td><td>10,000</td><td>Tracked allocation records</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-snapshots</code></td><td>1,000</td><td>State photos</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-snapshot-memory-bytes</code></td><td>1 MiB</td><td>Variable + heap bytes read per snapshot</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-memory-read-bytes</code></td><td>4 KiB</td><td>A single memory read</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-instruction-events</code></td><td>100,000</td><td>Recorded instruction attempts</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-gdb-commands</code></td><td>1,000,000</td><td>Total debugger traffic</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-processes</code></td><td>16</td><td>Child processes (when cgroups are available)</td></tr>\n</table>\n\n<div class=\"admonition warning\">\n  <span class=\"title\">Not a security sandbox</span>\n  <p><strong>These limits are not a security sandbox.</strong> They protect the session\n  from runaway programs, not the machine from malicious ones. Real isolation needs a\n  container or VM.</p>\n</div>\n\n<p>\n  Every limit that fires is recorded in <code>resource_usage.limits_triggered</code>\n  (each limit appears at most once), and the overall outcome reflects the\n  <em>real</em> cause — e.g. ending because the output cap was hit is reported as\n  <code>output_limit_reached</code>, not disguised as a step limit.\n</p>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"memory-errors\">8. Crashes and memory errors<a class=\"pilcrow\" href=\"#memory-errors\">¶</a></h2>\n\n<p>Three independent sources of truth, kept strictly separate:</p>\n\n<ol class=\"tight\">\n  <li><strong>The debugger observes the crash itself.</strong> The trace keeps the\n      signal, the exact faulting instruction (its address matches the last assembly\n      event, marked <code>faulted</code>) and the source line. No events are invented\n      after the crash.</li>\n  <li><strong>Valgrind is the second opinion.</strong> The program runs a second time\n      under Valgrind's memcheck, which can catch errors that did not crash —\n      use-after-free, out-of-bounds accesses, leaks — and reports them with stacks\n      and source locations. Findings are correlated with the heap timeline by\n      file and line.</li>\n  <li><strong>The sanitizer pass is the reproduction attempt.</strong> A second binary\n      built with AddressSanitizer (plus UBSan when installed) runs on its own. What\n      it found, and whether it truly <em>reproduced</em> the recorded crash, is kept\n      separate from the debugger's observations — an ASan finding that does not\n      match the crash is labeled <code>diagnostic_observed</code>, never forced into\n      agreement.</li>\n</ol>\n\n<h3>When does the sanitizer pass run?</h3>\n<p>Configurable with <code>--sanitizer-trigger</code>:</p>\n<table>\n  <tr><th>Mode</th><th>Meaning</th></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>never</code></td><td>Skip the pass entirely.</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>on_crash</code></td><td>Run only when the traced run crashed (the V2 behavior).</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>on_crash_or_valgrind_error</code></td><td><span class=\"pill\">default</span> Run on a crash, <em>or</em> when Valgrind found memory errors even though the program exited cleanly.</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>always</code></td><td>Run for every successful build, budget permitting.</td></tr>\n</table>\n\n<div class=\"admonition note\">\n  <span class=\"title\">Note</span>\n  <p>Valgrind and the sanitizer never run in the same process, global time budgets are\n  always respected, and a skipped pass records the reason in\n  <code>stage_results.sanitizer</code>.</p>\n</div>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"performance\">9. Performance at a glance<a class=\"pilcrow\" href=\"#performance\">¶</a></h2>\n\n<p>\n  The engine was profiled with a formal audit. The original design polled the CPU\n  registers after every single instruction — useful for a register panel, but it\n  consumed about <strong>90&nbsp;% of all debugger time</strong>. Visual C will not show\n  register panels, so version&nbsp;2.1 removed that collection entirely.\n</p>\n\n<p>Result on the audit benchmark suite (median of 3 runs, same machine):</p>\n\n<table>\n  <tr><th>Workload</th><th>Before</th><th>After</th><th>Speed-up</th></tr>\n  <tr><td>Finite loop (1,012 instructions)</td><td>19.1 s</td><td>6.1 s</td><td>3.1×</td></tr>\n  <tr><td>Function calls (1,413)</td><td>28.5 s</td><td>8.9 s</td><td>3.2×</td></tr>\n  <tr><td>Heap churn (1,363)</td><td>31.1 s</td><td>12.3 s</td><td>2.5×</td></tr>\n  <tr><td>Nested loops (1,352)</td><td>29.9 s</td><td>13.3 s</td><td>2.2×</td></tr>\n  <tr><td>Recursion (671)</td><td>20.0 s</td><td>10.1 s</td><td>2.0×</td></tr>\n  <tr><td>Simple arithmetic (18)</td><td>3.6 s</td><td>3.8 s</td><td>— (fixed startup cost dominates)</td></tr>\n</table>\n\n<div class=\"admonition seealso\">\n  <span class=\"title\">See also</span>\n  <p>Instruction addresses were never taken from registers — they come from the\n  debugger's stop reports — so nothing about the recorded execution changed. The\n  same audit confirmed the remaining big cost is capturing the C-level state\n  photos, which is the core educational feature and stays. Full methodology and\n  numbers: <a href=\"v2.1/performance.md\"><code>docs/v2.1/performance.md</code></a>.</p>\n</div>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"run-it\">10. Running it yourself<a class=\"pilcrow\" href=\"#run-it\">¶</a></h2>\n\n<pre><code><span class=\"cm\"># the basics: compile, run, write trace.json, print the trace to stdout</span>\ncargo run -- sample.c\n\n<span class=\"cm\"># save to a file; give the program some arguments</span>\ncargo run -- sample.c --output trace.json --  --verbose 42\n\n<span class=\"cm\"># common knobs</span>\ncargo run -- sample.c --timeout 3 --max-steps 200\ncargo run -- sample.c --trace-mode source          <span class=\"cm\"># cheaper, C-level only</span>\ncargo run -- sample.c --sanitizer-trigger always\ncargo run -- sample.c --gdb-path /usr/bin/gdb-14   <span class=\"cm\"># override tool discovery</span>\n\n<span class=\"cm\"># a failed build still produces a trace with the compiler diagnostics</span>\ncargo run -- broken.c</code></pre>\n\n<table>\n  <tr><th>Exit code</th><th>Meaning</th></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>0</code></td><td>A trace was produced (completed, crashed, timed out, or hit a limit are all \"success\" for the recorder).</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>2</code></td><td>Compilation failed; a partial trace with the diagnostics is still emitted.</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>1</code></td><td>Operational error (bad arguments, missing source, missing required tool). No trace.</td></tr>\n</table>\n\n<h3>The optional journal</h3>\n<p>\n  With <code>--journal run.jsonl</code> the engine additionally streams every record\n  (configuration, disassembly entries, instruction events, checkpoints, gaps, …) to a\n  line-oriented log as execution proceeds, and finalizes it with a footer record.\n  This is what allows very long runs to keep a complete, durable record even when the\n  JSON is instructed to keep only a bounded index in memory\n  (<code>--journal-only</code>).\n</p>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"limitations\">11. Known limitations<a class=\"pilcrow\" href=\"#limitations\">¶</a></h2>\n\n<ul class=\"tight\">\n  <li>Instruction coverage is <strong>user code only</strong>: program startup and\n      excluded library internals appear as explicit gaps, not recordings.</li>\n  <li>In multi-threaded programs the engine records the <strong>selected\n      thread's</strong> steps; a complete interleaving of all threads is out of scope\n      (the trace marks coverage incomplete and explains why).</li>\n  <li>Children created by <code>fork</code> are not instruction-traced (their\n      allocations may still be recorded).</li>\n  <li>Self-modifying / JIT code is unsupported; the disassembly cache assumes code\n      does not change under the engine.</li>\n  <li>The allocator wrapper sees the program's own allocation calls; memory allocated\n      <em>inside</em> libc or other libraries is invisible to the heap timeline\n      (Valgrind still sees all of it).</li>\n  <li>Per-instruction <strong>CPU register values are not collected</strong> (removed\n      in V2.1 with the feature they served). Old traces that contain them still load.</li>\n  <li>The trace is produced by a development machine, not a security sandbox —\n      see the limits section.</li>\n</ul>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"glossary\">12. Glossary<a class=\"pilcrow\" href=\"#glossary\">¶</a></h2>\n\n<dl class=\"glossary\">\n  <dt>Trace</dt><dd>The versioned JSON document this engine produces — the complete, replayable record of one program run. Schema version 2.</dd>\n  <dt>Snapshot / checkpoint</dt><dd>A \"state photo\": the source location, call stack, variables, heap contents and output captured at one debugger stop in user code.</dd>\n  <dt>Instruction event</dt><dd>One attempted machine instruction: where it was, where execution went next, and what happened. Attempts are recorded even when they fault.</dd>\n  <dt>Disassembly table</dt><dd>A de-duplicated catalog of instruction definitions (text, bytes, function). Events reference it by ID instead of repeating assembly text.</dd>\n  <dt>GDB / MI2</dt><dd>The GNU debugger, and its machine-oriented command interface (\"MI\") that the engine uses to drive it reliably.</dd>\n  <dt>Inferior</dt><dd>Debugger jargon for the program being debugged.</dd>\n  <dt>Valgrind / memcheck</dt><dd>An independent analysis tool that re-runs the program and detects memory errors and leaks without a crash.</dd>\n  <dt>Sanitizer (ASan/UBSan)</dt><dd>Compiler-instrumented error detection linked into a second build of the program; used here as a reproduction pass.</dd>\n  <dt>DWARF</dt><dd>The debug information format GCC embeds in the binary; it is how addresses map back to source lines, variables and types.</dd>\n  <dt>Heap timeline</dt><dd>The ordered story of <code>allocated</code> / <code>reallocated</code> / <code>freed</code> events reconstructed from the program's own allocator calls.</dd>\n  <dt>Trace gap</dt><dd>An explicit record of an interval that was deliberately or necessarily not observed (startup, skipped library code), with observed boundary addresses.</dd>\n  <dt>Stage result</dt><dd>Per-stage health report (compiler, debugger, Valgrind, sanitizer, allocation tracker): completed, failed, timed out, skipped or cancelled — with a reason.</dd>\n  <dt>Journal</dt><dd>The optional line-by-line log the engine writes while running; enables durable recording and memory-bounded operation.</dd>\n</dl>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<footer class=\"docinfo\">\n  <p>\n    <strong>Document info.</strong> Trace engine version: V2.1 (schema version 2),\n    November 2026. Yes — Fumadocs is a documentation framework for Next.js (App Router), and it's probably the strongest fit among JS-based docs frameworks if you're already comfortable with React/Next.

What it gives you:
- **Content pipeline**: MDX files in `content/docs/`, compiled by `fumadocs-mdx` (their own compiler, replacing the deprecated Contentlayer approach). Frontmatter for title/description, `meta.json` files control the sidebar page tree (order, separators, folders, icons).
- **UI**: `fumadocs-ui` ships the full docs chrome — sticky sidebar, right-hand TOC, `⌘K` search dialog, dark mode (via next-themes), breadcrumbs. The default look is the modern shadcn-style design with CSS-variable theming, so our dark palette translates directly.
- **Search**: built-in full-text search powered by Orama (client-side, no server needed), with Algolia/Fuse/custom adapters available.
- **Extras**: `fumadocs-typescript` (auto API tables), `fumadocs-openapi`, twoslash for TS code, `remark-include` so you can `{{{include}}}` existing .md files — that last one matters for us (more below).

How it maps to what we built:
- The `trace-engine.html` page was deliberately structured like a docs page already — sidebar groups, numbered sections, ¶ anchors, admonitions, TOC-able headings. Converting to Fumadocs is mostly mechanical: frontmatter + MDX, Callout instead of `.admonition`, Shiki code blocks instead of our hand-span'd highlighting, TOC auto-generated from h2/h3, sidebar from `meta.json` mirroring our nav groups.
- The stable anchor IDs (`#overview`, `#pipeline`, …) can be preserved so any deep links keep working.
- One decision to make early: our repo has `docs/*.md` (v2 schema, V2.1 reports, architecture) that must stay readable on GitHub. With `remark-include`, the Fumadocs pages can literally embed those same .md files, so there's one source of truth and the site stays in sync without duplication.

What adopting it means for this repo:
- A separate Next.js app (e.g. `docs-site/`), TypeScript + Tailwind, Node toolchain — it doesn't touch the Rust engine, it's just a sibling app. No engine changes.
- MDX content = our existing docs + the trace-engine page, organized into groups (Engine / Reference / Examples), RootToggle later when the app grows GUI/CLI sections.

Caveats: it's Next.js-specific; a build needs Node + pnpm; and my knowledge is current to ~mid-2025 — Fumadocs moves fast (it tracks Next.js majors), so if we adopt, step 1 of the plan would be verifying the current version/API before scaffolding.

Then the question: what are you thinking — adopt it now as the docs platform, keep the HTML page as the standalone artifact and just plan ahead, or want me to research the current state first?

Yes — **Fumadocs** is a documentation framework for **Next.js** (App Router), and it's arguably the most popular choice right now for JS/TS-based docs sites. Very relevant question, since the `trace-engine.html` page was built with "future docs site" in mind.

## What it is

- **Content pipeline** — MDX files in `content/docs/`, compiled by `fumadocs-mdx` (their own compiler, which replaced the abandoned Contentlayer approach). Frontmatter for title/description, and `meta.json` files control the sidebar page tree — order, folders, separators, icons.
- **UI (`fumadocs-ui`)** — ships the entire docs chrome out of the box: sticky left sidebar, right-hand table of contents, `⌘K` search dialog, breadcrumbs, dark mode via next-themes. The default look is the modern shadcn-style design built on CSS variables.
- **Search** — built-in full-text search (Orama-based, works client-side with no server), with Algolia / Fuse.js / custom adapters as alternatives.
- **Extras** — `fumadocs-typescript` (auto API reference tables), `fumadocs-openapi`, Twoslash for typed code blocks, and `remark-include` so a page can embed an existing `.md` file directly.

## How it maps to what we already built

The HTML page was deliberately structured like a docs page already, so conversion is mostly mechanical:

| We have | Fumadocs equivalent |
|---|---|
| Sidebar nav groups | `meta.json` page tree |
| Numbered h2 sections + ¶ anchors | Auto-generated TOC, stable heading IDs preserved |
| `.admonition` boxes | `<Callout>` component |
| Hand-highlighted `<pre>` blocks | Shiki code blocks |
| CSS-variable theming | Same concept — our dark palette translates directly |

One important decision if you adopt it: this repo's `docs/*.md` files (V2 schema, V2.1 reports, architecture) must stay readable on GitHub. With `remark-include`, the site pages can **embed those same .md files** — one source of truth, no duplication, and the site stays in sync automatically.

## What adopting means for this repo

- A separate Next.js app (e.g. `docs-site/`) — TypeScript + Tailwind + Node toolchain, sitting next to the Rust engine. Zero engine changes.
- Trace-engine page becomes an MDX page; docs groups mirror our sidebar (Engine / Reference / Examples); a `RootToggle` can later split Engine vs. GUI vs. CLI docs as the app grows.

One caveat: Fumadocs tracks Next.js majors and moves fast — my knowledge is solid to ~mid-2025, so if we adopt, the first plan step would be verifying the current version/API before scaffolding.
