267: <main class="main">
268: 
269: <h1>The Trace Engine: how Visual C records a running C&nbsp;program</h1>
270: 
271: <p class="lede">
272:   The <strong>trace engine</strong> (<code>c-trace-engine</code>) is the part of Visual C
273:   that actually <em>runs</em> a student's C program and turns what happens into one
274:   detailed, replayable file — the <strong>trace</strong>. Everything the future Visual C
275:   interface shows (the C view, the assembly view, memory, pointers, the heap, crashes)
276:   is read back from that file. This page explains what the engine does and what the
277:   trace contains, in plain language.
278: </p>
279: 
280: <!-- ==================================================================== -->
281: <h2 id="overview">1. What the trace engine is<a class="pilcrow" href="#overview">¶</a></h2>
282: 
283: <p>
284:   Visual C is an <strong>offline-first</strong> learning tool: a student writes a small C
285:   program, and Visual C shows them how it really executed — statement by statement,
286:   instruction by instruction, allocation by allocation. The trace engine is the
287:   command-line component that makes this possible.
288: </p>
289: 
290: <div class="admonition note">
291:   <span class="title">In one sentence</span>
292:   <p><strong>Compile the program, run it once under a debugger, and record
293:   everything observable about that single run into a versioned JSON
294:   file — the trace.</strong></p>
295: </div>
296: 
297: <p>Three principles guide every design decision:</p>
298: <ul class="tight">
299:   <li><strong>Real execution only.</strong> The engine never simulates loops or invents
300:       instruction events. If something is not in the trace, it was not observed.</li>
301:   <li><strong>One timeline.</strong> The C-level view and the machine-instruction view come
302:       from the <em>same</em> debugger run, so they can never disagree about what happened.</li>
303:   <li><strong>Honesty about gaps.</strong> Whenever data could not be observed (timeout,
304:       limit, unreadable memory, optimized-out variable), the trace says so explicitly
305:       instead of guessing.</li>
306: </ul>
307: 
308: <!-- ==================================================================== -->
309: <h2 id="pipeline">2. The big picture<a class="pilcrow" href="#pipeline">¶</a></h2>
310: 
311: <div class="flow">
312:   <div class="stage"><b>Your C sources</b><span class="small">one or more <code>.c</code> files, plus build settings</span></div>
313:   <div class="arrow">→</div>
314:   <div class="stage"><b>Compiler stage</b><span class="small">GCC builds a debug binary; a second sanitizer binary is built for crash diagnosis</span></div>
315:   <div class="arrow">→</div>
316:   <div class="stage main"><b>Debug run</b><span class="small">the program runs once under GDB; the engine single-steps user code and records stops</span></div>
317:   <div class="arrow">→</div>
318:   <div class="stage"><b>Analysis stages</b><span class="small">Valgrind re-runs the program; the sanitizer pass runs when triggered; caller locations resolved</span></div>
319:   <div class="arrow">→</div>
320:   <div class="stage"><b>The trace (JSON)</b><span class="small">one file describing the whole run</span></div>
321: </div>
322: 
323: <p class="small muted">
324:   The compiler, debugger and analyses are real external tools (GCC, GDB, Valgrind,
325:   addr2line). The engine drives them, enforces time and memory budgets, and stitches
326:   their outputs into one coherent document.
327: </p>
328: 
329: <!-- ==================================================================== -->
330: <h2 id="steps">3. What happens, step by step<a class="pilcrow" href="#steps">¶</a></h2>
331: 
332: <ol class="tight">
333:   <li><strong>Compile.</strong> Every translation unit is compiled with debug info
334:       (<code>-g -O0</code>). Compiler errors are captured in a machine-readable form and
335:       end up in the trace, so even a failed build produces a useful partial trace.
336:       A small runtime is linked in that records every <code>malloc</code>/<code>calloc</code>/
337:       <code>realloc</code>/<code>free</code> the program makes to a side file.</li>
338:   <li><strong>Run under GDB.</strong> The engine launches GDB in its machine-facing mode
339:       (MI2), breaks at <code>main</code>, and steps through the student's code —
340:       instruction by instruction in dual mode, or line by line in the cheaper
341:       source-only mode. Program output is captured through a separate channel so it
342:       never mixes with debugger chatter.</li>
343:   <li><strong>Record at every stop.</strong> Each time the program pauses, the engine
344:       records where it stopped (file, line, function, call stack), every visible
345:       variable (name, type, value, its own address, and for pointers the address it
346:       points to), the live contents of heap blocks, and the program's output so far.
347:       In dual mode each attempted machine instruction is recorded too: its address,
348:       the address of the <em>next</em> instruction, what happened (completed, faulted,
349:       interrupted), and selected memory reads.</li>
350:   <li><strong>Analyze independently.</strong> Valgrind re-runs the program on its own to
351:       hunt for memory errors with a second opinion. When triggered — a crash, or
352:       Valgrind findings — the sanitizer-built binary also runs once as a diagnostic
353:       pass. Allocation callers are resolved to <code>file:line</code> in one batched
354:       <code>addr2line</code> call.</li>
355:   <li><strong>Assemble the trace.</strong> Everything is written as one JSON document
356:       with a schema version, per-stage health reports, resource usage, and honest
357:       notes about anything that was skipped or degraded.</li>
358: </ol>
359: 
360: <!-- ==================================================================== -->
361: <h2 id="trace-tour">4. A guided tour of the trace file<a class="pilcrow" href="#trace-tour">¶</a></h2>
362: 
363: <p>
364:   A trace is a single JSON object. These are its main sections, grouped by what a
365:   reader (and later the Visual C interface) uses them for. A full real example lives
366:   at <a href="../examples/v21_dual.json"><code>examples/v21_dual.json</code></a>.
367: </p>
368: 
369: <table>
370:   <tr><th>Section</th><th>What it contains</th><th>Think of it as…</th></tr>
371:   <tr>
372:     <td><code>snapshots</code></td>
373:     <td>One record per stop in the student's code: source file/line/function, the call
374:         stack, all visible variables with addresses and raw bytes, live heap-block
375:         contents, and program output so far.</td>
376:     <td>"A photo of the program's state" at each C statement</td>
377:   </tr>
378:   <tr>
379:     <td><code>instruction_events</code><br><code>disassembly_table</code></td>
380:     <td>Every <em>attempted</em> machine instruction in order (address, next address,
381:         outcome, source line it belongs to), plus a de-duplicated table of instruction
382:         definitions (text, bytes, function) referenced by ID.</td>
383:     <td>"The assembly view" — what the CPU really did</td>
384:   </tr>
385:   <tr>
386:     <td><code>heap_events</code><br><code>heap_state</code><br><code>allocation_lifetimes</code></td>
387:     <td>The full allocation story: every <code>allocated</code>/<code>reallocated</code>/
388:         <code>freed</code> event, the final state of every block (live or freed, with
389:         contents), and each block's lifetime boundaries with stable IDs.</td>
390:     <td>"The memory view" — the heap's biography</td>
391:   </tr>
392:   <tr>
393:     <td><code>crash_report</code></td>
394:     <td>For a crash: the signal (e.g. <code>SIGSEGV</code>), the exact source line and
395:         faulting instruction address, and a backtrace.</td>
396:     <td>"Why did it die?"</td>
397:   </tr>
398:   <tr>
399:     <td><code>valgrind_report</code><br><code>sanitizer_report</code></td>
400:     <td>The independent memory analyses: Valgrind errors (with stacks and leak
401:         classification) and the sanitizer reproduction attempt, each with its own
402:         completeness flags.</td>
403:     <td>"Second opinions" from other tools</td>
404:   </tr>
405:   <tr>
406:     <td><code>execution</code>, <code>execution_status</code></td>
407:     <td>The overall outcome: completed, crashed, timed out, hit a limit, failed to
408:         compile, and so on — with exit code and signal.</td>
409:     <td>"How did the run end?"</td>
410:   </tr>
411:   <tr>
412:     <td><code>stage_results</code></td>
413:     <td>Health report per stage (compiler, debugger, Valgrind, sanitizer, allocation
414:         tracker): status, duration, and a reason whenever something did not complete.</td>
415:     <td>"Did each part finish, and if not, why?"</td>
416:   </tr>
417:   <tr>
418:     <td><code>coverage</code>, <code>trace_gaps</code></td>
419:     <td>Which parts of execution were observed (<code>user_code</code> scope) and which
420:         intervals were not (program startup, skipped library code), with explicit gap
421:         records — never guessed counts.</td>
422:     <td>"What did we NOT see?"</td>
423:   </tr>
424:   <tr>
425:     <td><code>resource_usage</code>, <code>profiling</code></td>
426:     <td>Measured consumption: wall time, number of debugger commands issued, snapshot
427:         count, which limits fired, timing breakdowns.</td>
428:     <td>"What did the recording cost?"</td>
429:   </tr>
430:   <tr>
431:     <td><code>analysis_notes</code>, <code>session_meta</code>,
432:         <code>execution_limits</code>, <code>tracing_configuration</code>,
433:         <code>compile_errors</code>, <code>storage</code></td>
434:     <td>Everything else a careful reader needs: warnings and degradations, tool
435:         versions, the effective limits, the configuration used, compiler diagnostics,
436:         and storage/bookkeeping details.</td>
437:     <td>"The fine print, in the document itself"</td>
438:   </tr>
439: </table>
440: 
441: <h3>A single instruction event, annotated</h3>
442: 
443: <p class="small muted">Real values from <code>examples/v21_dual.json</code>, annotated:</p>
444: 
445: <pre><code>{
446:   <span class="k">"event_id"</span>: <span class="s">0</span>,              <span class="cm">// ordered, zero-based: this is the 1st attempt</span>
447:   <span class="k">"address"</span>: <span class="s">"0x0000000000400586"</span>,   <span class="cm">// the instruction that was ABOUT to run</span>
448:   <span class="k">"next_address"</span>: <span class="s">"0x0000000000400587"</span>, <span class="cm">// actually observed next stop — never guessed</span>
449:   <span class="k">"instruction_id"</span>: <span class="s">0</span>,         <span class="cm">// index into disassembly_table (no repeated text)</span>
450:   <span class="k">"source"</span>: { <span class="k">"line"</span>: <span class="s">29</span>, <span class="k">"func"</span>: <span class="s">"main"</span> },
451:   <span class="k">"outcome"</span>: <span class="s">"completed"</span>,      <span class="cm">// completed | faulted | interrupted | unknown</span>
452:   <span class="k">"stopped_reason"</span>: <span class="s">"end-stepping-range"</span>,
453:   <span class="k">"memory"</span>: <span class="s">[]</span>,               <span class="cm">// reads of user-configured watch addresses appear</span>
454:                                  <span class="cm">// here (e.g. {"expression":"&amp;x","status":"valid",</span>
455:                                  <span class="cm">//  "raw_bytes_hex":"0a000000"}) — none configured here</span>
456:   <span class="k">"checkpoint_id"</span>: <span class="hl">0</span>           <span class="cm">// links to the nearest snapshot (the C-level state)</span>
457:   <span class="cm">// note: no "registers" key — see the performance section</span>
458: }</code></pre>
459: 
460: <h3>A single variable record, annotated</h3>
461: 
462: <p class="small muted">Real values from <code>examples/v21_dual.json</code> (the fixture's <code>int *arr</code> pointing into a heap block):</p>
463: 
464: <pre><code>{
465:   <span class="k">"name"</span>: <span class="s">"arr"</span>, <span class="k">"c_type"</span>: <span class="s">"int *"</span>,
466:   <span class="k">"value"</span>: <span class="s">"0x705010"</span>,            <span class="cm">// what the pointer CONTAINS</span>
467:   <span class="k">"address"</span>: <span class="s">"0x7fffffffda48"</span>,   <span class="cm">// where the pointer variable itself lives</span>
468:   <span class="k">"points_to"</span>: <span class="s">"0x705010"</span>,
469:   <span class="k">"target"</span>: { <span class="k">"kind"</span>: <span class="s">"heap"</span>, <span class="k">"allocation_id"</span>: <span class="s">1</span>,
470:               <span class="k">"base_address"</span>: <span class="s">"0x705010"</span>, <span class="k">"offset_bytes"</span>: <span class="s">0</span> },
471:   <span class="k">"raw_bytes_hex"</span>: <span class="s">"10507000…"</span>,  <span class="cm">// the pointer's own bytes, as observed</span>
472:   <span class="k">"read_status"</span>: <span class="s">"valid"</span>
473: }</code></pre>
474: 
475: <p class="small muted">
476:   Pointer targets are classified as <code>stack</code>, <code>heap</code> (with the
477:   allocation ID it belongs to), <code>global</code>, <code>code</code>,
478:   <code>null</code>, <code>unmapped</code> or <code>unknown</code> — so the interface
479:   can draw "this pointer goes to that heap block" without guessing.
480: </p>
481: 
482: <!-- ==================================================================== -->
483: <h2 id="sync">5. How the C view and assembly view stay in sync<a class="pilcrow" href="#sync">¶</a></h2>
484: 
485: <p>
486:   Both views come from <strong>one run of the program under one GDB session</strong>.
487:   Every event in the assembly view carries a <code>stop_id</code> pair and optionally a
488:   <code>checkpoint_id</code> pointing into the source view's snapshots. Concretely:
489: </p>
490: <ul class="tight">
491:   <li>Each recorded instruction event names the source file, line and function it was
492:       paused in — that is the link from assembly back to the C statement.</li>
493:   <li>Snapshots (the C-level state photos) record how many instruction attempts had
494:       happened before them, so either timeline can be navigated from the other.</li>
495:   <li>Instruction addresses are taken from the debugger's own stop reports. The
496:       <em>next</em> address is always the actually observed next stop — crucial,
497:       because machine code frequently does <em>not</em> run sequentially (branches,
498:       calls, returns, faults).</li>
499: </ul>
500: 
501: <div class="admonition note">
502:   <span class="title">Why this matters for Visual C</span>
503:   <p>The interface can highlight a C statement, show the exact machine instructions
504:   that executed for it, and step through them — all from one file, with no risk of
505:   the two views disagreeing.</p>
506: </div>
507: 
508: <!-- ==================================================================== -->
509: <h2 id="honesty">6. What is exact, and what is not<a class="pilcrow" href="#honesty">¶</a></h2>
510: 
511: <p>
512:   A learning tool must never show invented data as if it were real. The trace follows
513:   a strict honesty policy:
514: </p>
515: <ul class="tight">
516:   <li><strong>Values are exact only at their recorded stop.</strong> A snapshot shows the
517:       program's state at that moment; nothing claims to know intermediate values
518:       between stops.</li>
519:   <li><strong>Nothing is fabricated.</strong> Unobservable data is <code>null</code>,
520:       with a machine-readable <em>why</em>: validity flags such as
521:       <code>valid</code>, <code>unavailable</code>, <code>unreadable</code>,
522:       <code>optimized_out</code>, <code>truncated</code>, <code>not_captured</code>.</li>
523:   <li><strong>Gaps are explicit.</strong> Startup before <code>main</code>, and code the
524:       engine deliberately steps over (library internals), appear as
525:       <code>trace_gaps</code> with observed boundary addresses — the number of unseen
526:       instructions is never invented.</li>
527:   <li><strong>Partial beats silent.</strong> A timeout, a limit or a crash still yields
528:       a trace containing everything captured up to that point, clearly marked as
529:       incomplete.</li>
530:   <li><strong>A freed block's bytes are the last bytes seen while it was alive.</strong>
531:       Memory is not read after the block was freed — the trace says so rather than
532:       implying the bytes are current.</li>
533: </ul>
534: 
535: <div class="admonition warning">
536:   <span class="title">Rule for the interface</span>
537:   <p>Never present a memory value as "current" unless its record says it was observed
538:   at the displayed stop. The trace gives you the status flags to enforce this.</p>
539: </div>
540: 
541: <!-- ==================================================================== -->
542: <h2 id="limits">7. Safety limits, timeouts, partial traces<a class="pilcrow" href="#limits">¶</a></h2>
543: 
544: <p>
545:   The engine wraps everything in budgets so a runaway student program cannot hang the
546:   session. Limits are configurable on the command line or in a JSON config file;
547:   hitting one terminates collection <em>gracefully</em> and keeps the partial trace.
548: </p>
549: 
550: <table>
551:   <tr><th>Limit (flag)</th><th>Default</th><th>What it bounds</th></tr>
552:   <tr><td><code>--timeout</code></td><td>10 s</td><td>The whole session: compile + run + analyses</td></tr>
553:   <tr><td><code>--max-steps</code></td><td>1,000</td><td>Debugger stepping commands</td></tr>
554:   <tr><td><code>--max-memory-mb</code></td><td>256 MB</td><td>Address space of the program being traced</td></tr>
555:   <tr><td><code>--max-output-bytes</code></td><td>1 MiB</td><td>Captured program output (ends the run as <code>output_limit_reached</code>)</td></tr>
556:   <tr><td><code>--max-heap-allocations</code></td><td>10,000</td><td>Tracked allocation records</td></tr>
557:   <tr><td><code>--max-snapshots</code></td><td>1,000</td><td>State photos</td></tr>
558:   <tr><td><code>--max-snapshot-memory-bytes</code></td><td>1 MiB</td><td>Variable + heap bytes read per snapshot</td></tr>
559:   <tr><td><code>--max-memory-read-bytes</code></td><td>4 KiB</td><td>A single memory read</td></tr>
560:   <tr><td><code>--max-instruction-events</code></td><td>100,000</td><td>Recorded instruction attempts</td></tr>
561:   <tr><td><code>--max-gdb-commands</code></td><td>1,000,000</td><td>Total debugger traffic</td></tr>
562:   <tr><td><code>--max-processes</code></td><td>16</td><td>Child processes (when cgroups are available)</td></tr>
563: </table>
564: 
565: <div class="admonition warning">
566:   <span class="title">Not a security sandbox</span>
567:   <p><strong>These limits are not a security sandbox.</strong> They protect the session
568:   from runaway programs, not the machine from malicious ones. Real isolation needs a
569:   container or VM.</p>
570: </div>
571: 
572: <p>
573:   Every limit that fires is recorded in <code>resource_usage.limits_triggered</code>
574:   (each limit appears at most once), and the overall outcome reflects the
575:   <em>real</em> cause — e.g. ending because the output cap was hit is reported as
576:   <code>output_limit_reached</code>, not disguised as a step limit.
577: </p>
578: 
579: <!-- ==================================================================== -->
580: <h2 id="memory-errors">8. Crashes and memory errors<a class="pilcrow" href="#memory-errors">¶</a></h2>
581: 
582: <p>Three independent sources of truth, kept strictly separate:</p>
583: 
584: <ol class="tight">
585:   <li><strong>The debugger observes the crash itself.</strong> The trace keeps the
586:       signal, the exact faulting instruction (its address matches the last assembly
587:       event, marked <code>faulted</code>) and the source line. No events are invented
588:       after the crash.</li>
589:   <li><strong>Valgrind is the second opinion.</strong> The program runs a second time
590:       under Valgrind's memcheck, which can catch errors that did not crash —
591:       use-after-free, out-of-bounds accesses, leaks — and reports them with stacks
592:       and source locations. Findings are correlated with the heap timeline by
593:       file and line.</li>
594:   <li><strong>The sanitizer pass is the reproduction attempt.</strong> A second binary
595:       built with AddressSanitizer (plus UBSan when installed) runs on its own. What
596:       it found, and whether it truly <em>reproduced</em> the recorded crash, is kept
597:       separate from the debugger's observations — an ASan finding that does not
598:       match the crash is labeled <code>diagnostic_observed</code>, never forced into
599:       agreement.</li>
600: </ol>
601: 
602: <h3>When does the sanitizer pass run?</h3>
603: <p>Configurable with <code>--sanitizer-trigger</code>:</p>
604: <table>
605:   <tr><th>Mode</th><th>Meaning</th></tr>
606:   <tr><td><code>never</code></td><td>Skip the pass entirely.</td></tr>
607:   <tr><td><code>on_crash</code></td><td>Run only when the traced run crashed (the V2 behavior).</td></tr>
608:   <tr><td><code>on_crash_or_valgrind_error</code></td><td><span class="pill">default</span> Run on a crash, <em>or</em> when Valgrind found memory errors even though the program exited cleanly.</td></tr>
609:   <tr><td><code>always</code></td><td>Run for every successful build, budget permitting.</td></tr>
610: </table>
611: 
612: <div class="admonition note">
613:   <span class="title">Note</span>
614:   <p>Valgrind and the sanitizer never run in the same process, global time budgets are
615:   always respected, and a skipped pass records the reason in
616:   <code>stage_results.sanitizer</code>.</p>
617: </div>
618: 
619: <!-- ==================================================================== -->
620: <h2 id="performance">9. Performance at a glance<a class="pilcrow" href="#performance">¶</a></h2>
621: 
622: <p>
623:   The engine was profiled with a formal audit. The original design polled the CPU
624:   registers after every single instruction — useful for a register panel, but it
625:   consumed about <strong>90&nbsp;% of all debugger time</strong>. Visual C will not show
626:   register panels, so version&nbsp;2.1 removed that collection entirely.
627: </p>
628: 
629: <p>Result on the audit benchmark suite (median of 3 runs, same machine):</p>
630: 
631: <table>
632:   <tr><th>Workload</th><th>Before</th><th>After</th><th>Speed-up</th></tr>
633:   <tr><td>Finite loop (1,012 instructions)</td><td>19.1 s</td><td>6.1 s</td><td>3.1×</td></tr>
634:   <tr><td>Function calls (1,413)</td><td>28.5 s</td><td>8.9 s</td><td>3.2×</td></tr>
635:   <tr><td>Heap churn (1,363)</td><td>31.1 s</td><td>12.3 s</td><td>2.5×</td></tr>
636:   <tr><td>Nested loops (1,352)</td><td>29.9 s</td><td>13.3 s</td><td>2.2×</td></tr>
637:   <tr><td>Recursion (671)</td><td>20.0 s</td><td>10.1 s</td><td>2.0×</td></tr>
638:   <tr><td>Simple arithmetic (18)</td><td>3.6 s</td><td>3.8 s</td><td>— (fixed startup cost dominates)</td></tr>
639: </table>
640: 
641: <div class="admonition seealso">
642:   <span class="title">See also</span>
643:   <p>Instruction addresses were never taken from registers — they come from the
644:   debugger's stop reports — so nothing about the recorded execution changed. The
645:   same audit confirmed the remaining big cost is capturing the C-level state
646:   photos, which is the core educational feature and stays. Full methodology and
647:   numbers: <a href="v2.1/performance.md"><code>docs/v2.1/performance.md</code></a>.</p>
648: </div>
649: 
650: <!-- ==================================================================== -->
651: <h2 id="run-it">10. Running it yourself<a class="pilcrow" href="#run-it">¶</a></h2>
652: 
653: <pre><code><span class="cm"># the basics: compile, run, write trace.json, print the trace to stdout</span>
654: cargo run -- sample.c
655: 
656: <span class="cm"># save to a file; give the program some arguments</span>
657: cargo run -- sample.c --output trace.json --  --verbose 42
658: 
659: <span class="cm"># common knobs</span>
660: cargo run -- sample.c --timeout 3 --max-steps 200
661: cargo run -- sample.c --trace-mode source          <span class="cm"># cheaper, C-level only</span>
662: cargo run -- sample.c --sanitizer-trigger always
663: cargo run -- sample.c --gdb-path /usr/bin/gdb-14   <span class="cm"># override tool discovery</span>
664: 
665: <span class="cm"># a failed build still produces a trace with the compiler diagnostics</span>
666: cargo run -- broken.c</code></pre>
667: 
668: <table>
669:   <tr><th>Exit code</th><th>Meaning</th></tr>
670:   <tr><td><code>0</code></td><td>A trace was produced (completed, crashed, timed out, or hit a limit are all "success" for the recorder).</td></tr>
671:   <tr><td><code>2</code></td><td>Compilation failed; a partial trace with the diagnostics is still emitted.</td></tr>
672:   <tr><td><code>1</code></td><td>Operational error (bad arguments, missing source, missing required tool). No trace.</td></tr>
673: </table>
674: 
675: <h3>The optional journal</h3>
676: <p>
677:   With <code>--journal run.jsonl</code> the engine additionally streams every record
678:   (configuration, disassembly entries, instruction events, checkpoints, gaps, …) to a
679:   line-oriented log as execution proceeds, and finalizes it with a footer record.
680:   This is what allows very long runs to keep a complete, durable record even when the
681:   JSON is instructed to keep only a bounded index in memory
682:   (<code>--journal-only</code>).
683: </p>
684: 
685: <!-- ==================================================================== -->
686: <h2 id="limitations">11. Known limitations<a class="pilcrow" href="#limitations">¶</a></h2>
687: 
688: <ul class="tight">
689:   <li>Instruction coverage is <strong>user code only</strong>: program startup and
690:       excluded library internals appear as explicit gaps, not recordings.</li>
691:   <li>In multi-threaded programs the engine records the <strong>selected
692:       thread's</strong> steps; a complete interleaving of all threads is out of scope
693:       (the trace marks coverage incomplete and explains why).</li>
694:   <li>Children created by <code>fork</code> are not instruction-traced (their
695:       allocations may still be recorded).</li>
696:   <li>Self-modifying / JIT code is unsupported; the disassembly cache assumes code
697:       does not change under the engine.</li>
698:   <li>The allocator wrapper sees the program's own allocation calls; memory allocated
699:       <em>inside</em> libc or other libraries is invisible to the heap timeline
700:       (Valgrind still sees all of it).</li>
701:   <li>Per-instruction <strong>CPU register values are not collected</strong> (removed
702:       in V2.1 with the feature they served). Old traces that contain them still load.</li>
703:   <li>The trace is produced by a development machine, not a security sandbox —
704:       see the limits section.</li>
705: </ul>
706: 
707: <!-- ==================================================================== -->
708: <h2 id="glossary">12. Glossary<a class="pilcrow" href="#glossary">¶</a></h2>
709: 
710: <dl class="glossary">
711:   <dt>Trace</dt><dd>The versioned JSON document this engine produces — the complete, replayable record of one program run. Schema version 2.</dd>
712:   <dt>Snapshot / checkpoint</dt><dd>A "state photo": the source location, call stack, variables, heap contents and output captured at one debugger stop in user code.</dd>
713:   <dt>Instruction event</dt><dd>One attempted machine instruction: where it was, where execution went next, and what happened. Attempts are recorded even when they fault.</dd>
714:   <dt>Disassembly table</dt><dd>A de-duplicated catalog of instruction definitions (text, bytes, function). Events reference it by ID instead of repeating assembly text.</dd>
715:   <dt>GDB / MI2</dt><dd>The GNU debugger, and its machine-oriented command interface ("MI") that the engine uses to drive it reliably.</dd>
716:   <dt>Inferior</dt><dd>Debugger jargon for the program being debugged.</dd>
717:   <dt>Valgrind / memcheck</dt><dd>An independent analysis tool that re-runs the program and detects memory errors and leaks without a crash.</dd>
718:   <dt>Sanitizer (ASan/UBSan)</dt><dd>Compiler-instrumented error detection linked into a second build of the program; used here as a reproduction pass.</dd>
719:   <dt>DWARF</dt><dd>The debug information format GCC embeds in the binary; it is how addresses map back to source lines, variables and types.</dd>
720:   <dt>Heap timeline</dt><dd>The ordered story of <code>allocated</code> / <code>reallocated</code> / <code>freed</code> events reconstructed from the program's own allocator calls.</dd>
721:   <dt>Trace gap</dt><dd>An explicit record of an interval that was deliberately or necessarily not observed (startup, skipped library code), with observed boundary addresses.</dd>
722:   <dt>Stage result</dt><dd>Per-stage health report (compiler, debugger, Valgrind, sanitizer, allocation tracker): completed, failed, timed out, skipped or cancelled — with a reason.</dd>
723:   <dt>Journal</dt><dd>The optional line-by-line log the engine writes while running; enables durable recording and memory-bounded operation.</dd>
724: </dl>

Let me write the JS concretely:

```js
<script>
(function () {
  'use strict';
  var $ = function (s, r) { return (r || document).querySelector(s); };
  var $$ = function (s, r) { return Array.prototype.slice.call((r || document).querySelectorAll(s)); };

  /* ---------- scrollspy (right-hand TOC) ---------- */
  var tocLinks = $$('.toc a[href^="#"]');
  var headings = $$('main h2[id]');
  function spy() {
    var cur = headings.length ? headings[0] : null;
    for (var i = 0; i < headings.length; i++) {
      if (headings[i].getBoundingClientRect().top <= 110) cur = headings[i];
      else break;
    }
    var id = cur ? cur.id : null;
    tocLinks.forEach(function (a) {
      a.classList.toggle('active', !!id && a.getAttribute('href') === '#' + id);
    });
  }
  var ticking = false;
  window.addEventListener('scroll', function () {
    if (!ticking) { ticking = true; requestAnimationFrame(function(){ ticking = false; spy(); }); }
  }, { passive: true });
  spy();

  /* ---------- copy buttons ---------- */
  $$('.codeblock .copy').forEach(function (btn) {
    btn.addEventListener('click', function () {
      var pre = $('pre', btn.closest('.codeblock'));
      var text = pre ? pre.innerText : '';
      var done = function (ok) {
        btn.classList.add(ok ? 'ok' : 'bad');
        btn.textContent = ok ? 'Copied ✓' : 'Failed';
        setTimeout(function () { btn.className = 'copy'; btn.textContent = 'Copy'; }, 1600);
      };
      if (navigator.clipboard && navigator.clipboard.writeText) {
        navigator.clipboard.writeText(text).then(function () { done(true); }, function () { fallback(); });
      } else { fallback(); }
      function fallback() {
        var ta = document.createElement('textarea');
        ta.value = text; ta.style.cssText = 'position:fixed;opacity:0';
        document.body.appendChild(ta); ta.select();
        var ok = false;
        try { ok = document.execCommand('copy'); } catch (e) {}
        document.body.removeChild(ta);
        done(ok);
      }
    });
  });

  /* ---------- ⌘K search ---------- */
  var overlay = $('#search'), inputEl = $('#search-input'), listEl = $('#search-results');
  var index = [];
  $$('main h2[id]').forEach(function (h) {
    index.push({ title: h.textContent.replace(/[#¶]/g, '').trim(), kind: 'Section', href: '#' + h.id });
  });
  $$('.sidebar a[href]:not([href="#"])').forEach(function (a) {
    index.push({ title: a.textContent.trim(), kind: 'Page', href: a.getAttribute('href') });
  });
  var sel = 0, rows = [];
  function render(q) {
    q = (q || '').trim().toLowerCase();
    var matches = index.filter(function (it) {
      return !q || it.title.toLowerCase().indexOf(q) !== -1;
    });
    if (q) {
      matches.sort(function (a, b) {
        var as = a.title.toLowerCase().indexOf(q) === 0 ? 0 : 1;
        var bs = b.title.toLowerCase().indexOf(q) === 0 ? 0 : 1;
        return as - bs;
      });
    }
    sel = 0; rows = matches.slice(0, 12);
    if (!rows.length) {
      listEl.innerHTML = '<p class="empty">No results for “' + q.replace(/[<>&]/g, '') + '”</p>';
      return;
    }
    listEl.innerHTML = rows.map(function (it, i) {
      return '<a role="option" class="row' + (i === 0 ? ' selected' : '') + '" href="' + it.href + '">' +
             '<span class="kind">' + it.kind + '</span>' + it.title + '</a>';
    }).join('');
  }
  function highlight(i) {
    sel = Math.max(0, Math.min(rows.length - 1, i));
    $$('.row', listEl).forEach(function (r, j) { r.classList.toggle('selected', j === sel); });
    var el = $$('.row', listEl)[sel];
    if (el) el.scrollIntoView({ block: 'nearest' });
  }
  function openSearch() {
    overlay.hidden = false; inputEl.value = ''; render(''); inputEl.focus();
    document.body.classList.add('locked');
  }
  function closeSearch() {
    overlay.hidden = true; document.body.classList.remove('locked');
  }
  document.addEventListener('keydown', function (e) {
    if ((e.metaKey || e.ctrlKey) && (e.key === 'k' || e.key === 'K')) {
      e.preventDefault();
      overlay.hidden ? openSearch() : closeSearch();
    } else if (e.key === 'Escape' && !overlay.hidden) {
      closeSearch();
    }
  });
  inputEl.addEventListener('input', function () { render(inputEl.value); });
  inputEl.addEventListener('keydown', function (e) {
    if (e.key === 'ArrowDown') { e.preventDefault(); highlight(sel + 1); }
    else if (e.key === 'ArrowUp') { e.preventDefault(); highlight(sel - 1); }
    else if (e.key === 'Enter') {
      var el = $$('.row', listEl)[sel];
      if (el) { closeSearch(); el.click(); }
    }
  });
  listEl.addEventListener('click', function (e) { if (e.target.closest('a')) closeSearch(); });
  var trigger = $('.search-trigger');
  if (trigger) trigger.addEventListener('click', openSearch);
  $('.search-backdrop').addEventListener('click', closeSearch);
})();
</script>
```

Notes: `q.replace(/[<>&]/g,'')` for XSS-safety of the empty-state string; titles come from our own DOM so fine, but strip <>& anyway when inserting titles? They're from static markup, fine. But add a tiny escape function to be tidy:

```js
function esc(s){return s.replace(/[&<>"]/g,function(c){return{'&':'&amp;','<':'&lt;','>':'&gt;','"':'&quot;'}[c];});}
```
Use it in render for title and empty message. Titles contain `&amp;` already in HTML ("V2 schema & semantics" — textContent gives "V2 schema & semantics" raw &, esc re-escapes → good).

Also body.locked { overflow: hidden }.

Also clicking overlay panel shouldn't close (only backdrop).

Search trigger button in sidebar. On mobile, sidebar static — trigger still works.

Also add `aria-expanded` on trigger? Minor; skip extra.

Escape key: global handler covers it.

One more detail: `overlay.hidden ? openSearch() : closeSearch();` — expression statement fine.

Also initial spy() call — headings top positions; fine.

margin-top: 14px; color: var(--strong); }\n  dl.glossary dd { margin: 2px 0 0 0; }\n  ul.tight li, ol.tight li { margin: 5px 0; }\n  .pill {\n    display: inline-block; font-size: 11px; font-weight: 600;\n    border-radius: 999px; padding: 1px 9px; margin-right: 4px;\n    border: 1px solid rgba(59,130,246,.4); background: var(--primary-soft);\n    color: var(--primary-bright); text-transform: uppercase; letter-spacing: .04em;\n  }\n\n  /* ------------------------------------------------------------------ */\n  /* prev/next pager + footer                                            */\n  .pager { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr 1fr; gap: 12px; margin: 48px 0 0; }\n  .pager a {\n    display: block; border: 1px solid var(--line-soft); border-radius: var(--radius);\n    background: var(--card); padding: 12px 16px;\n  }\n  .pager a:hover { border-color: var(--line); overflow: hidden;\n  }\n  .search-head { display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 10px; padding: 12px 14px; border-bottom: 1px solid var(--line-soft); }\n  .search-head svg { color: var(--muted); flex: none; }\n    .table-wrap, .codeblock, .callout, .pager a { border-color: #bbb; background: #fff; }\n    .codeblock figcaption { background: #eee; }\n    .codeblock, pre code { color: #111; }\n    pre .cm { color: #666; }\n    a { color: #0645ad; }\n  }\n</style>\n</head>\n<body>\n\n<!-- ================================================================== -->\n<aside class=\"sidebar\">\n  <div class=\"side-header\">\n    <span class=\"logo-mark\">V</span>\n    <span class=\"brand\"><b>Visual C Docs</b><span>engine V2.1 · schema 2</span></span>\n  </div>\n\n  <button class=\"search-trigger\" type=\"button\" aria-haspopup=\"dialog\" aria-controls=\"search\">\n    <svg width=\"14\" height=\"14\" viewBox=\"0 0 24 24\" fill=\"none\" stroke=\"currentColor\" stroke-width=\"2\" stroke-linecap=\"round\" stroke-linejoin=\"round\"><circle cx=\"11\" cy=\"11\" r=\"7\"/><path d=\"m21 21-4.3-4.3\"/></svg>\n    <span>Search…</span>\n    <kbd>⌘K</kbd>\n  </button>\n\n  <details class=\"navgroup\" open>\n    <summary><span class=\"chev\">›</span>The Engine</summary>\n    <div class=\"links\">\n      <a class=\"current\" href=\"#\" aria-current=\"page\">The Trace Engine</a>\n      <a href=\"architecture.md\">Engine architecture</a>\n      <a href=\"engine-internals.md\">Engine internals</a>\n    </div>\n  </details>\n\n  <details class=\"navgroup\" open>\n    <summary><span class=\"chev\">›</span>Reference</summary>\n    <div class=\"links\">\n      <a href=\"v2.md\">V2 schema &amp; semantics</a>\n      <a href=\"build-config.md\">Build configuration</a>\n      <a href=\"v2.1/summary.md\">V2.1 update reports</a>\n    </div>\n  </details>\n\n  <details class=\"navgroup\" open>\n    <summary><span class=\"chev\">›</span>Examples</summary>\n    <div class=\"links\">\n      <a href=\"../examples/v21_manifest.json\">Trace manifest</a>\n      <a href=\"../examples/v21_dual.json\">Example dual trace</a>\n    </div>\n  </details>\n</aside>\n\n<!-- ================================================================== -->\n<div class=\"page\">\n<div class=\"page-inner\">\n\n<main class=\"content\">\n\n<div class=\"breadcrumb\">Docs <span class=\"sep\">/</span> Engine <span class=\"sep\">/</span> <b>The Trace Engine</b></div>\n\n<h1>The Trace Engine: how Visual C records a running C&nbsp;program</h1>\n\n<p class=\"lede\">\n  The <strong>trace engine</strong> (<code>c-trace-engine</code>) is the part of Visual C\n  that actually <em>runs</em> a student's C program and turns what happens into one\n  detailed, replayable file — the <strong>trace</strong>. Everything the future Visual C\n  interface shows (the C view, the assembly view, memory, pointers, the heap, crashes)\n  is read back from that file. This page explains what the engine does and what the\n  trace contains, in plain language.\n</p>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"overview\">1. What the trace engine is<a class=\"anchor\" href=\"#overview\">#</a></h2>\n\n<p>\n  Visual C is an <strong>offline-first</strong> learning tool: a student writes a small C\n  program, and Visual C shows them how it really executed — statement by statement,\n  instruction by instruction, allocation by allocation. The trace engine is the\n  command-line component that makes this possible.\n</p>\n\n<div class=\"callout note\">\n  <span class=\"co-icon\"><svg width=\"16\" height=\"16\" viewBox=\"0 0 24 24\" fill=\"none\" stroke=\"currentColor\" stroke-width=\"2\" stroke-linecap=\"round\" stroke-linejoin=\"round\"><circle cx=\"12\" cy=\"12\" r=\"10\"/><path d=\"M12 16v-4\"/><path d=\"M12 8h.01\"/></svg></span>\n  <div>\n    <p class=\"title\">In one sentence</p>\n    <p><strong>Compile the program, run it once under a debugger, and record\n    everything observable about that single run into a versioned JSON\n    file — the trace.</strong></p>\n  </div>\n</div>\n\n<p>Three principles guide every design decision:</p>\n<ul class=\"tight\">\n  <li><strong>Real execution only.</strong> The engine never simulates loops or invents\n      instruction events. If something is not in the trace, it was not observed.</li>\n  <li><strong>One timeline.</strong> The C-level view and the machine-instruction view come\n      from the <em>same</em> debugger run, so they can never disagree about what happened.</li>\n  <li><strong>Honesty about gaps.</strong> Whenever data could not be observed (timeout,\n      limit, unreadable memory, optimized-out variable), the trace says so explicitly\n      instead of guessing.</li>\n</ul>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"pipeline\">2. The big picture<a class=\"anchor\" href=\"#pipeline\">#</a></h2>\n\n<div class=\"flow\">\n  <div class=\"stage\"><b>Your C sources</b><span class=\"small\">one or more <code>.c</code> files, plus build settings</span></div>\n  <div class=\"arrow\">→</div>\n  <div class=\"stage\"><b>Compiler stage</b><span class=\"small\">GCC builds a debug binary; a second sanitizer binary is built for crash diagnosis</span></div>\n  <div class=\"arrow\">→</div>\n  <div class=\"stage main\"><b>Debug run</b><span class=\"small\">the program runs once under GDB; the engine single-steps user code and records stops</span></div>\n  <div class=\"arrow\">→</div>\n  <div class=\"stage\"><b>Analysis stages</b><span class=\"small\">Valgrind re-runs the program; the sanitizer pass runs when triggered; caller locations resolved</span></div>\n  <div class=\"arrow\">→</div>\n  <div class=\"stage\"><b>The trace (JSON)</b><span class=\"small\">one file describing the whole run</span></div>\n</div>\n\n<p class=\"small muted\">\n  The compiler, debugger and analyses are real external tools (GCC, GDB, Valgrind,\n  addr2line). The engine drives them, enforces time and memory budgets, and stitches\n  their outputs into one coherent document.\n</p>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"steps\">3. What happens, step by step<a class=\"anchor\" href=\"#steps\">#</a></h2>\n\n<ol class=\"tight\">\n  <li><strong>Compile.</strong> Every translation unit is compiled with debug info\n      (<code>-g -O0</code>). Compiler errors are captured in a machine-readable form and\n      end up in the trace, so even a failed build produces a useful partial trace.\n      A small runtime is linked in that records every <code>malloc</code>/<code>calloc</code>/\n      <code>realloc</code>/<code>free</code> the program makes to a side file.</li>\n  <li><strong>Run under GDB.</strong> The engine launches GDB in its machine-facing mode\n      (MI2), breaks at <code>main</code>, and steps through the student's code —\n      instruction by instruction in dual mode, or line by line in the cheaper\n      source-only mode. Program output is captured through a separate channel so it\n      never mixes with debugger chatter.</li>\n  <li><strong>Record at every stop.</strong> Each time the program pauses, the engine\n      records where it stopped (file, line, function, call stack), every visible\n      variable (name, type, value, its own address, and for pointers the address it\n      points to), the live contents of heap blocks, and the program's output so far.\n      In dual mode each attempted machine instruction is recorded too: its address,\n      the address of the <em>next</em> instruction, what happened (completed, faulted,\n      interrupted), and selected memory reads.</li>\n  <li><strong>Analyze independently.</strong> Valgrind re-runs the program on its own to\n      hunt for memory errors with a second opinion. When triggered — a crash, or\n      Valgrind findings — the sanitizer-built binary also runs once as a diagnostic\n      pass. Allocation callers are resolved to <code>file:line</code> in one batched\n      <code>addr2line</code> call.</li>\n  <li><strong>Assemble the trace.</strong> Everything is written as one JSON document\n      with a schema version, per-stage health reports, resource usage, and honest\n      notes about anything that was skipped or degraded.</li>\n</ol>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"trace-tour\">4. A guided tour of the trace file<a class=\"anchor\" href=\"#trace-tour\">#</a></h2>\n\n<p>\n  A trace is a single JSON object. These are its main sections, grouped by what a\n  reader (and later the Visual C interface) uses them for. A full real example lives\n  at <a href=\"../examples/v21_dual.json\"><code>examples/v21_dual.json</code></a>.\n</p>\n\n<div class=\"table-wrap\">\n<table>\n  <tr><th>Section</th><th>What it contains</th><th>Think of it as…</th></tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>snapshots</code></td>\n    <td>One record per stop in the student's code: source file/line/function, the call\n        stack, all visible variables with addresses and raw bytes, live heap-block\n        contents, and program output so far.</td>\n    <td>\"A photo of the program's state\" at each C statement</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>instruction_events</code><br><code>disassembly_table</code></td>\n    <td>Every <em>attempted</em> machine instruction in order (address, next address,\n        outcome, source line it belongs to), plus a de-duplicated table of instruction\n        definitions (text, bytes, function) referenced by ID.</td>\n    <td>\"The assembly view\" — what the CPU really did</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>heap_events</code><br><code>heap_state</code><br><code>allocation_lifetimes</code></td>\n    <td>The full allocation story: every <code>allocated</code>/<code>reallocated</code>/\n        <code>freed</code> event, the final state of every block (live or freed, with\n        contents), and each block's lifetime boundaries with stable IDs.</td>\n    <td>\"The memory view\" — the heap's biography</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>crash_report</code></td>\n    <td>For a crash: the signal (e.g. <code>SIGSEGV</code>), the exact source line and\n        faulting instruction address, and a backtrace.</td>\n    <td>\"Why did it die?\"</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>valgrind_report</code><br><code>sanitizer_report</code></td>\n    <td>The independent memory analyses: Valgrind errors (with stacks and leak\n        classification) and the sanitizer reproduction attempt, each with its own\n        completeness flags.</td>\n    <td>\"Second opinions\" from other tools</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>execution</code>, <code>execution_status</code></td>\n    <td>The overall outcome: completed, crashed, timed out, hit a limit, failed to\n        compile, and so on — with exit code and signal.</td>\n    <td>\"How did the run end?\"</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>stage_results</code></td>\n    <td>Health report per stage (compiler, debugger, Valgrind, sanitizer, allocation\n        tracker): status, duration, and a reason whenever something did not complete.</td>\n    <td>\"Did each part finish, and if not, why?\"</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>coverage</code>, <code>trace_gaps</code></td>\n    <td>Which parts of execution were observed (<code>user_code</code> scope) and which\n        intervals were not (program startup, skipped library code), with explicit gap\n        records — never guessed counts.</td>\n    <td>\"What did we NOT see?\"</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>resource_usage</code>, <code>profiling</code></td>\n    <td>Measured consumption: wall time, number of debugger commands issued, snapshot\n        count, which limits fired, timing breakdowns.</td>\n    <td>\"What did the recording cost?\"</td>\n  </tr>\n  <tr>\n    <td><code>analysis_notes</code>, <code>session_meta</code>,\n        <code>execution_limits</code>, <code>tracing_configuration</code>,\n        <code>compile_errors</code>, <code>storage</code></td>\n    <td>Everything else a careful reader needs: warnings and degradations, tool\n        versions, the effective limits, the configuration used, compiler diagnostics,\n        and storage/bookkeeping details.</td>\n    <td>\"The fine print, in the document itself\"</td>\n  </tr>\n</table>\n</div>\n\n<h3>A single instruction event, annotated</h3>\n\n<p class=\"small muted\">Real values from <code>examples/v21_dual.json</code>, annotated:</p>\n\n<figure class=\"codeblock\">\n  <figcaption><span class=\"lang\">json</span><button class=\"copy\" type=\"button\">Copy</button></figcaption>\n<pre><code>{\n  <span class=\"k\">\"event_id\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">0</span>,              <span class=\"cm\">// ordered, zero-based: this is the 1st attempt</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"address\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"0x0000000000400586\"</span>,   <span class=\"cm\">// the instruction that was ABOUT to run</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"next_address\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"0x0000000000400587\"</span>, <span class=\"cm\">// actually observed next stop — never guessed</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"instruction_id\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">0</span>,         <span class=\"cm\">// index into disassembly_table (no repeated text)</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"source\"</span>: { <span class=\"k\">\"line\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">29</span>, <span class=\"k\">\"func\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"main\"</span> },\n  <span class=\"k\">\"outcome\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"completed\"</span>,      <span class=\"cm\">// completed | faulted | interrupted | unknown</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"stopped_reason\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"end-stepping-range\"</span>,\n  <span class=\"k\">\"memory\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">[]</span>,               <span class=\"cm\">// reads of user-configured watch addresses appear</span>\n                                 <span class=\"cm\">// here (e.g. {\"expression\":\"&amp;x\",\"status\":\"valid\",</span>\n                                 <span class=\"cm\">//  \"raw_bytes_hex\":\"0a000000\"}) — none configured here</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"checkpoint_id\"</span>: <span class=\"hl\">0</span>           <span class=\"cm\">// links to the nearest snapshot (the C-level state)</span>\n  <span class=\"cm\">// note: no \"registers\" key — see the performance section</span>\n}</code></pre>\n</figure>\n\n<h3>A single variable record, annotated</h3>\n\n<p class=\"small muted\">Real values from <code>examples/v21_dual.json</code> (the fixture's <code>int *arr</code> pointing into a heap block):</p>\n\n<figure class=\"codeblock\">\n  <figcaption><span class=\"lang\">json</span><button class=\"copy\" type=\"button\">Copy</button></figcaption>\n<pre><code>{\n  <span class=\"k\">\"name\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"arr\"</span>, <span class=\"k\">\"c_type\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"int *\"</span>,\n  <span class=\"k\">\"value\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"0x705010\"</span>,            <span class=\"cm\">// what the pointer CONTAINS</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"address\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"0x7fffffffda48\"</span>,   <span class=\"cm\">// where the pointer variable itself lives</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"points_to\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"0x705010\"</span>,\n  <span class=\"k\">\"target\"</span>: { <span class=\"k\">\"kind\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"heap\"</span>, <span class=\"k\">\"allocation_id\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">1</span>,\n              <span class=\"k\">\"base_address\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"0x705010\"</span>, <span class=\"k\">\"offset_bytes\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">0</span> },\n  <span class=\"k\">\"raw_bytes_hex\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"10507000…\"</span>,  <span class=\"cm\">// the pointer's own bytes, as observed</span>\n  <span class=\"k\">\"read_status\"</span>: <span class=\"s\">\"valid\"</span>\n}</code></pre>\n</figure>\n\n<p class=\"small muted\">\n  Pointer targets are classified as <code>stack</code>, <code>heap</code> (with the\n  allocation ID it belongs to), <code>global</code>, <code>code</code>,\n  <code>null</code>, <code>unmapped</code> or <code>unknown</code> — so the interface\n  can draw \"this pointer goes to that heap block\" without guessing.\n</p>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"sync\">5. How the C view and assembly view stay in sync<a class=\"anchor\" href=\"#sync\">#</a></h2>\n\n<p>\n  Both views come from <strong>one run of the program under one GDB session</strong>.\n  Every event in the assembly view carries a <code>stop_id</code> pair and optionally a\n  <code>checkpoint_id</code> pointing into the source view's snapshots. Concretely:\n</p>\n<ul class=\"tight\">\n  <li>Each recorded instruction event names the source file, line and function it was\n      paused in — that is the link from assembly back to the C statement.</li>\n  <li>Snapshots (the C-level state photos) record how many instruction attempts had\n      happened before them, so either timeline can be navigated from the other.</li>\n  <li>Instruction addresses are taken from the debugger's own stop reports. The\n      <em>next</em> address is always the actually observed next stop — crucial,\n      because machine code frequently does <em>not</em> run sequentially (branches,\n      calls, returns, faults).</li>\n</ul>\n\n<div class=\"callout note\">\n  <span class=\"co-icon\"><svg width=\"16\" height=\"16\" viewBox=\"0 0 24 24\" fill=\"none\" stroke=\"currentColor\" stroke-width=\"2\" stroke-linecap=\"round\" stroke-linejoin=\"round\"><circle cx=\"12\" cy=\"12\" r=\"10\"/><path d=\"M12 16v-4\"/><path d=\"M12 8h.01\"/></svg></span>\n  <div>\n    <p class=\"title\">Why this matters for Visual C</p>\n    <p>The interface can highlight a C statement, show the exact machine instructions\n    that executed for it, and step through them — all from one file, with no risk of\n    the two views disagreeing.</p>\n  </div>\n</div>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"honesty\">6. What is exact, and what is not<a class=\"anchor\" href=\"#honesty\">#</a></h2>\n\n<p>\n  A learning tool must never show invented data as if it were real. The trace follows\n  a strict honesty policy:\n</p>\n<ul class=\"tight\">\n  <li><strong>Values are exact only at their recorded stop.</strong> A snapshot shows the\n      program's state at that moment; nothing claims to know intermediate values\n      between stops.</li>\n  <li><strong>Nothing is fabricated.</strong> Unobservable data is <code>null</code>,\n      with a machine-readable <em>why</em>: validity flags such as\n      <code>valid</code>, <code>unavailable</code>, <code>unreadable</code>,\n      <code>optimized_out</code>, <code>truncated</code>, <code>not_captured</code>.</li>\n  <li><strong>Gaps are explicit.</strong> Startup before <code>main</code>, and code the\n      engine deliberately steps over (library internals), appear as\n      <code>trace_gaps</code> with observed boundary addresses — the number of unseen\n      instructions is never invented.</li>\n  <li><strong>Partial beats silent.</strong> A timeout, a limit or a crash still yields\n      a trace containing everything captured up to that point, clearly marked as\n      incomplete.</li>\n  <li><strong>A freed block's bytes are the last bytes seen while it was alive.</strong>\n      Memory is not read after the block was freed — the trace says so rather than\n      implying the bytes are current.</li>\n</ul>\n\n<div class=\"callout warning\">\n  <span class=\"co-icon\"><svg width=\"16\" height=\"16\" viewBox=\"0 0 24 24\" fill=\"none\" stroke=\"currentColor\" stroke-width=\"2\" stroke-linecap=\"round\" stroke-linejoin=\"round\"><path d=\"m21.73 18-8-14a2 2 0 0 0-3.46 0l-8 14A2 2 0 0 0 4 21h16a2 2 0 0 0 1.73-3\"/><path d=\"M12 9v4\"/><path d=\"M12 17h.01\"/></svg></span>\n  <div>\n    <p class=\"title\">Rule for the interface</p>\n    <p>Never present a memory value as \"current\" unless its record says it was observed\n    at the displayed stop. The trace gives you the status flags to enforce this.</p>\n  </div>\n</div>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"limits\">7. Safety limits, timeouts, partial traces<a class=\"anchor\" href=\"#limits\">#</a></h2>\n\n<p>\n  The engine wraps everything in budgets so a runaway student program cannot hang the\n  session. Limits are configurable on the command line or in a JSON config file;\n  hitting one terminates collection <em>gracefully</em> and keeps the partial trace.\n</p>\n\n<div class=\"table-wrap\">\n<table>\n  <tr><th>Limit (flag)</th><th>Default</th><th>What it bounds</th></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--timeout</code></td><td>10 s</td><td>The whole session: compile + run + analyses</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-steps</code></td><td>1,000</td><td>Debugger stepping commands</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-memory-mb</code></td><td>256 MB</td><td>Address space of the program being traced</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>--max-output-bytes</code></td><td>1 MiB</td><td>Captured program output (ends the run as <code>output_limit_reached</code>)</td></tr>\n Crashes and memory errors<a class=\"anchor\" href=\"#memory-errors\">#</a></h2>\n\n<p>Three independent sources of truth, kept strictly separate:</p>\n\n<ol class=\"tight\">\n  <li><strong>The debugger observes the crash itself.</strong> The trace keeps the\n      signal, the exact faulting instruction (its address matches the last assembly\n      event, marked <code>faulted</code>) and the source line. No events are invented\n      after the crash.</li>\n  <li><strong>Valgrind is the second opinion.</strong> The program runs a second time\n      under Valgrind's memcheck, which can catch errors that did not crash —\n      use-after-free, out-of-bounds accesses, leaks — and reports them with stacks\n      and source locations. Findings are correlated with the heap timeline by\n      file and line.</li>\n  <li><strong>The sanitizer pass is the reproduction attempt.</strong> A second binary\n      built with AddressSanitizer (plus UBSan when installed) runs on its own. What\n      it found, and whether it truly <em>reproduced</em> the recorded crash, is kept\n      separate from the debugger's observations — an ASan finding that does not\n      match the crash is labeled <code>diagnostic_observed</code>, never forced into\n      agreement.</li>\n</ol>\n\n<h3>When does the sanitizer pass run?</h3>\n<p>Configurable with <code>--sanitizer-trigger</code>:</p>\n<div class=\"table-wrap\">\n<table>\n  <tr><th>Mode</th><th>Meaning</th></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>never</code></td><td>Skip the pass entirely.</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>on_crash</code></td><td>Run only when the traced run crashed (the V2 behavior).</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>on_crash_or_valgrind_error</code></td><td><span class=\"pill\">default</span> Run on a crash, <em>or</em> when Valgrind found memory errors even though the program exited cleanly.</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>always</code></td><td>Run for every successful build, budget permitting.</td></tr>\n</table>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"callout note\">\n  <span class=\"co-icon\"><svg width=\"16\" height=\"16\" viewBox=\"0 0 24 24\" fill=\"none\" stroke=\"currentColor\" stroke-width=\"2\" stroke-linecap=\"round\" stroke-linejoin=\"round\"><circle cx=\"12\" cy=\"12\" r=\"10\"/><path d=\"M12 16v-4\"/><path d=\"M12 8h.01\"/></svg></span>\n  <div>\n    <p class=\"title\">Note</p>\n    <p>Valgrind and the sanitizer never run in the same process, global time budgets are\n    always respected, and a skipped pass records the reason in\n    <code>stage_results.sanitizer</code>.</p>\n  </div>\n</div>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"performance\">9. Performance at a glance<a class=\"anchor\" href=\"#performance\">#</a></h2>\n\n<p>\n  The engine was profiled with a formal audit. The original design polled the CPU\n  registers after every single instruction — useful for a register panel, but it\n  consumed about <strong>90&nbsp;% of all debugger time</strong>. Visual C will not show\n  register panels, so version&nbsp;2.1 removed that collection entirely.\n</p>\n\n<p>Result on the audit benchmark suite (median of 3 runs, same machine):</p>\n\n<div class=\"table-wrap\">\n<table>\n  <tr><th>Workload</th><th>Before</th><th>After</th><th>Speed-up</th></tr>\n  <tr><td>Finite loop (1,012 instructions)</td><td>19.1 s</td><td>6.1 s</td><td>3.1×</td></tr>\n  <tr><td>Function calls (1,413)</td><td>28.5 s</td><td>8.9 s</td><td>3.2×</td></tr>\n  <tr><td>Heap churn (1,363)</td><td>31.1 s</td><td>12.3 s</td><td>2.5×</td></tr>\n  <tr><td>Nested loops (1,352)</td><td>29.9 s</td><td>13.3 s</td><td>2.2×</td></tr>\n  <tr><td>Recursion (671)</td><td>20.0 s</td><td>10.1 s</td><td>2.0×</td></tr>\n  <tr><td>Simple arithmetic (18)</td><td>3.6 s</td><td>3.8 s</td><td>— (fixed startup cost dominates)</td></tr>\n</table>\n</div>\n\n<div class=\"callout seealso\">\n  <span class=\"co-icon\"><svg width=\"16\" height=\"16\" viewBox=\"0 0 24 24\" fill=\"none\" stroke=\"currentColor\" stroke-width=\"2\" stroke-linecap=\"round\" stroke-linejoin=\"round\"><path d=\"M5 12h14\"/><path d=\"m12 5 7 7-7 7\"/></svg></span>\n  <div>\n    <p class=\"title\">See also</p>\n    <p>Instruction addresses were never taken from registers — they come from the\n    debugger's stop reports — so nothing about the recorded execution changed. The\n    same audit confirmed the remaining big cost is capturing the C-level state\n    photos, which is the core educational feature and stays. Full methodology and\n    numbers: <a href=\"v2.1/performance.md\"><code>docs/v2.1/performance.md</code></a>.</p>\n  </div>\n</div>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"run-it\">10. Running it yourself<a class=\"anchor\" href=\"#run-it\">#</a></h2>\n\n<figure class=\"codeblock\">\n  <figcaption><span class=\"lang\">sh</span><button class=\"copy\" type=\"button\">Copy</button></figcaption>\n<pre><code><span class=\"cm\"># the basics: compile, run, write trace.json, print the trace to stdout</span>\ncargo run -- sample.c\n\n<span class=\"cm\"># save to a file; give the program some arguments</span>\ncargo run -- sample.c --output trace.json --  --verbose 42\n\n<span class=\"cm\"># common knobs</span>\ncargo run -- sample.c --timeout 3 --max-steps 200\ncargo run -- sample.c --trace-mode source          <span class=\"cm\"># cheaper, C-level only</span>\ncargo run -- sample.c --sanitizer-trigger always\ncargo run -- sample.c --gdb-path /usr/bin/gdb-14   <span class=\"cm\"># override tool discovery</span>\n\n<span class=\"cm\"># a failed build still produces a trace with the compiler diagnostics</span>\ncargo run -- broken.c</code></pre>\n</figure>\n\n<div class=\"table-wrap\">\n<table>\n  <tr><th>Exit code</th><th>Meaning</th></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>0</code></td><td>A trace was produced (completed, crashed, timed out, or hit a limit are all \"success\" for the recorder).</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>2</code></td><td>Compilation failed; a partial trace with the diagnostics is still emitted.</td></tr>\n  <tr><td><code>1</code></td><td>Operational error (bad arguments, missing source, missing required tool). No trace.</td></tr>\n</table>\n</div>\n\n<h3>The optional journal</h3>\n<p>\n  With <code>--journal run.jsonl</code> the engine additionally streams every record\n  (configuration, disassembly entries, instruction events, checkpoints, gaps, …) to a\n  line-oriented log as execution proceeds, and finalizes it with a footer record.\n  This is what allows very long runs to keep a complete, durable record even when the\n  JSON is instructed to keep only a bounded index in memory\n  (<code>--journal-only</code>).\n</p>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"limitations\">11. Known limitations<a class=\"anchor\" href=\"#limitations\">#</a></h2>\n\n<ul class=\"tight\">\n  <li>Instruction coverage is <strong>user code only</strong>: program startup and\n      excluded library internals appear as explicit gaps, not recordings.</li>\n  <li>In multi-threaded programs the engine records the <strong>selected\n      thread's</strong> steps; a complete interleaving of all threads is out of scope\n      (the trace marks coverage incomplete and explains why).</li>\n  <li>Children created by <code>fork</code> are not instruction-traced (their\n      allocations may still be recorded).</li>\n  <li>Self-modifying / JIT code is unsupported; the disassembly cache assumes code\n      does not change under the engine.</li>\n  <li>The allocator wrapper sees the program's own allocation calls; memory allocated\n      <em>inside</em> libc or other libraries is invisible to the heap timeline\n      (Valgrind still sees all of it).</li>\n  <li>Per-instruction <strong>CPU register values are not collected</strong> (removed\n      in V2.1 with the feature they served). Old traces that contain them still load.</li>\n  <li>The trace is produced by a development machine, not a security sandbox —\n      see the limits section.</li>\n</ul>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<h2 id=\"glossary\">12. Glossary<a class=\"anchor\" href=\"#glossary\">#</a></h2>\n\n<dl class=\"glossary\">\n  <dt>Trace</dt><dd>The versioned JSON document this engine produces — the complete, replayable record of one program run. Schema version 2.</dd>\n  <dt>Snapshot / checkpoint</dt><dd>A \"state photo\": the source location, call stack, variables, heap contents and output captured at one debugger stop in user code.</dd>\n  <dt>Instruction event</dt><dd>One attempted machine instruction: where it was, where execution went next, and what happened. Attempts are recorded even when they fault.</dd>\n  <dt>Disassembly table</dt><dd>A de-duplicated catalog of instruction definitions (text, bytes, function). Events reference it by ID instead of repeating assembly text.</dd>\n  <dt>GDB / MI2</dt><dd>The GNU debugger, and its machine-oriented command interface (\"MI\") that the engine uses to drive it reliably.</dd>\n  <dt>Inferior</dt><dd>Debugger jargon for the program being debugged.</dd>\n  <dt>Valgrind / memcheck</dt><dd>An independent analysis tool that re-runs the program and detects memory errors and leaks without a crash.</dd>\n  <dt>Sanitizer (ASan/UBSan)</dt><dd>Compiler-instrumented error detection linked into a second build of the program; used here as a reproduction pass.</dd>\n  <dt>DWARF</dt><dd>The debug information format GCC embeds in the binary; it is how addresses map back to source lines, variables and types.</dd>\n  <dt>Heap timeline</dt><dd>The ordered story of <code>allocated</code> / <code>reallocated</code> / <code>freed</code> events reconstructed from the program's own allocator calls.</dd>\n  <dt>Trace gap</dt><dd>An explicit record of an interval that was deliberately or necessarily not observed (startup, skipped library code), with observed boundary addresses.</dd>\n  <dt>Stage result</dt><dd>Per-stage health report (compiler, debugger, Valgrind, sanitizer, allocation tracker): completed, failed, timed out, skipped or cancelled — with a reason.</dd>\n  <dt>Journal</dt><dd>The optional line-by-line log the engine writes while running; enables durable recording and memory-bounded operation.</dd>\n</dl>\n\n<!-- ==================================================================== -->\n<nav class=\"pager\" aria-label=\"Page navigation\">\n  <a class=\"next\" href=\"architecture.md\">\n    <span class=\"dir\">Next →</span>\n    <span class=\"dest\">Engine architecture</span>\n  </a>\n</nav>\n\n<footer class=\"docinfo\">\n  <p>\n    <strong>Document info.</strong> Trace engine version: V2.1 (schema version 2),\n    November 2026. import re
from html.parser import HTMLParser

class Text(HTMLParser):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__(convert_charrefs=True)
        self.parts=[]
        self.skip=0
    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        if tag in ('style','script'): self.skip+=1
    def handle_endtag(self, tag):
        if tag in ('style','script'): self.skip=max(0,self.skip-1)
    def handle_data(self, d):
        if not self.skip: self.parts.append(d)

def text_of(p):
    t=Text(); t.feed(open(p).read())
    s=' '.join(t.parts)
    s=s.replace('¶','#')
    s=re.sub(r'\s+',' ',s)
    return s

Edit 13 — main script before </body>:
```
<script>
(function () {
  var root = document.documentElement;
  var btn = document.getElementById('theme-toggle');
  var ICONS = {
    dark: '<svg width="15" height="15" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="4"/><path d="M12 2v2"/><path d="M12 20v2"/><path d="m4.93 4.93 1.41 1.41"/><path d="m17.66 17.66 1.41 1.41"/><path d="M2 12h2"/><path d="M20 12h2"/><path d="m6.34 17.66-1.41 1.41"/><path d="m19.07 4.93-1.41 1.41"/></svg>',
    light: '<svg width="15" height="15" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M12 3a6 6 0 0 0 9 9 9 9 0 1 1-9-9Z"/></svg>'
  };
  var theme = root.getAttribute('data-theme') === 'light' ? 'light' : 'dark';
  function paint() {
    btn.innerHTML = ICONS[theme];
    btn.setAttribute('aria-label', theme === 'dark' ? 'Switch to light theme' : 'Switch to dark theme');
    btn.title = btn.getAttribute('aria-label');
  }
  btn.addEventListener('click', function () {
    theme = theme === 'dark' ? 'light' : 'dark';
    root.setAttribute('data-theme', theme);
    try { localStorage.setItem('vc-theme', theme); } catch (e) {}
    paint();
  });
  paint();
})();
</script>
</body>
```
