parse_bytes(bytes: &[u8], options: &TraceLoadOptions) -> Result<JournalTrace> {\n    if bytes.len() as u64 > options.max_bytes {\n        return Err(TraceParseError::LimitExceeded {\n            limit: options.max_bytes,\n        });\n    }\n    parse_reader(std::io::Cursor::new(bytes), options)\n}\n\n/// Parse a journal line-by-line from a reader.\n///\n/// Memory stays bounded: one line is buffered at a time (a line may never\n/// exceed `options.max_bytes`), and decoded records are typed (the raw JSON\n/// value of each record is dropped after decoding, not retained).\npub(crate) fn parse_reader(\n    mut reader: impl BufRead,\n    options: &TraceLoadOptions,\n) -> Result<JournalTrace> {\n    let mut records = Vec::new();\n    let mut counts = JournalCounts::default();\n    let {\n                return Err(TraceParseError::JournalRecordLimitExceeded {\n                    limit: options.max_journal_records,\n                });\n            }\n            push_record(record, &mut records, &mut counts, line_count, &mut saw_configuration)?;\n        }\n    }\n\n    Ok(JournalTrace {\n        records,\n        counts,\n        finalized: records.iter().any(|r| matches!(r, JournalRecord::Finalized)),\n        torn_tail,\n        line_count,\n    })\n}\n\n/// Insert one record, enforcing the configuration-first writer invariant and\n/// updating per-kind counts.\nfn push_record(\n    record: JournalRecord,\n    records: &mut Vec<JournalRecord>,\n    counts: &mut JournalCounts,\n    line: usize,\n    saw_configuration: &mut bool,\n) -> Result<()> {\n    if records.is_empty() && !*saw_configuration {\n        // The very first record must be the session configuration.\n        if !matches!(record, JournalRecord::Configuration(_)) JournalRecord::Allocation { .. } => counts.allocations += 1,\n        JournalRecord::Gap(_) => counts.gaps += 1,\n        JournalRecord::Disassembly(_) => counts.disassembly += 1,\n        JournalRecord::Instruction(_) => counts.instructions += 1,\n        JournalRecord::Finalized => {}\n        JournalRecord::Unknown { .. } => counts.unknown += 1,\n    }\n    records.push(record);\n pub fn open(path: impl AsRef<Path>, options: TraceLoadOptions) -> Result<Self> {
    let path = path.as_ref();
    Self::from_path_inner(path, &options).map_err(|e| TraceParseError::Source { path: path.to_path_buf(), source: Box::new(e) })
}
fn from_path_inner(path: &Path, options: &TraceLoadOptions) -> Result<Self> {
    let file = File::open(path).map_err(|e| TraceParseError::Io { source: e })?;
    let declared = file.metadata().map_err(|e| TraceParseError::Io { source: e })?.len();
    if declared > options.max_bytes { return Err(TraceParseError::LimitExceeded { limit: options.max_bytes }); }
    let mut bytes = Vec::new();
    let read_len = (&file).take(options.max_bytes.saturating_add(1)).read_to_end(&mut bytes).map_err(|e| TraceParseError::Io { source: e })?;
    if read_len as u64 > options.max_bytes { return Err(TraceParseError::LimitExceeded { limit: options.max_bytes }); }
    let source = TraceSourceMetadata { path: Some(path.to_path_buf()), byte_len: read_len as u64, format: TraceFormat::Json };
    // NOTE: format here is provisional; corrected after detection below.
    match ingest_bytes(&bytes, options)? {
        Ingested::Trace(trace) => Ok(Self { trace: Arc::new(trace), source }),
        Ingested::Journal(_) => Err(TraceParseError::JournalReconstructionUnsupported),
    }
}

```rust
pub(crate) fn detect_format(text: &str) -> DetectedFormat {
    let mut total = 0usize;
    let mut valid_records = 0usize;
    let mut last_bad: Option<usize> = None;
    let mut any_bad_not_last = false;
    for line in text.lines() {
        let trimmed = line.trim();
        if trimmed.is_empty() { continue; }
        total += 1;
        if journal_record_shape(trimmed) {
            valid_records += 1;
        } else {
            last_bad = Some(total);
        }
    }
    // A bad line is tolerable only as the single torn final line.
    if let Some(idx) = last_bad {
        if idx != total { return DetectedFormat::JsonDocument; } // bad line mid-file
        if valid_records == 0 { return DetectedFormat::JsonDocument; } // no valid record before it
    }
    if valid_records >= 1 { DetectedFormat::Journal } else { DetectedFormat::JsonDocument }
}
```

{
  "content": "# Trace Parser — TP-1: Ingestion, Validation & Canonical Store\n\nTP-1 is the foundational phase of the Trace Parser: the component that\nreceives Stage 1 (`c-trace-engine`) trace outputs, deserializes them with the\nengine's own Serde models, validates their structure, and hands back **one\ncanonical, immutable, shareable owner of the loaded trace** — the\n`TraceStore` — to be shared by every future consumer without re-parsing.\n\nIt is *not* a debugging engine, not a Semantic Engine, and not a GUI layer.\nIt never executes programs, invokes tools, reads live memory, or interprets\nwhat the recorded data *means*. Recorded evidence is preserved verbatim;\nderiving C-language meaning from it is Stage 2's job.\n\nLocation: `src/trace_parser/` inside the existing `c-trace-engine` crate\n(single-crate repository; the models are already in a library target, so no\nnew crate and no refactoring were needed). Public API lives in\n`src/trace_parser/mod.rs`, the error model in `error.rs`, JSON handling in\n`json.rs`, journal handling in `journal.rs`.\n\n---\n\n## Supported inputs\n\n| input | support | details |\n|---|---|---|\n| JSON trace (V2.1 / V2) | full | one `DebugSessionTrace` document, exactly as the engine prints to stdout / `--output`. Schema marker is the integer `2`; a trace **without** the field also loads (the model's serde default is 2 — the documented back-compat contract). Any other version is rejected. |\n| Session journal (JSONL) | records only | `{\"kind\":\"<record>\",\"data\":<value>}` per line, decoded and validated per record. **Full-trace reconstruction from a journal is unsupported** (see below). |\n| Other encodings / versions | rejected | Non-UTF-8 input, schema versions ≠ 2, and content that is neither format are typed errors, never guesses. |\n\nFormat selection is **content-based** (`TraceFormatSelection::Auto` by\ndefault, or forced with `Json` / `Journal`). File names and extensions are\nnever consulted, and malformed JSON is never silently reinterpreted as a\njournal: journal detection requires every complete line to be a JSON object\ncarrying a string `kind` and a `data` member, with at most one torn final\nline and at least one valid record before it.\n\n### Resource limits (defaults in `TraceLoadOptions`)\n\n* `max_bytes` — 512 MiB input cap. File loads check the size before reading;\n  stream loads stop at the cap; over-limit inputs are rejected with a typed\n  error, never truncated into a confusing parse failure.\n* `max_journal_records` — 2,000,000 records.\n* One journal line may never exceed `max_bytes` (bounds per-record buffering).\n\n---\n\n## Public API\n\n```rust\nuse c_trace_engine::trace_parser::{TraceLoadOptions, TraceStore};\n\nlet store = TraceStore::open(\"examples/v21_normal.json\", TraceLoadOptions::default())?;\n\nstore.trace();              // &DebugSessionTrace — the canonical data\nstore.shared();             // Arc<DebugSessionTrace> — cheap handle for future consumers\nstore.execution_status();   // Completed / Crashed / Timeout / StepLimitReached / ...\nstore.execution();          // exit code, signal, stop reason\nstore.session_meta();       // build config + toolchain versions, when recorded\nstore.source();             // path, exact byte length, detected format\n```\n\n* `TraceStore::open(path, options)` — from a file (size pre-checked; errors\n  wrapped in `TraceParseError::Source` naming the path).\n* `TraceStore::from_reader(reader, options)` — from any byte source; same\n  validation, no filesystem access.\n* `TraceStore::from_json_bytes(bytes, options)` — explicit JSON from memory\n  (unit tests, pre-fetched bytes).\n* `TraceStore::from_trace(trace)` — adopt an already-deserialized model\n  (in-process engine output); only the schema-version gate runs.\n* `parse_journal(path | reader | bytes, options)` — validated journal record\n  stream (`JournalTrace`): typed `JournalRecord`s in file order, per-kind\n  counts, `finalized` / `torn_tail` completeness flags.\n\n### Ownership and sharing\n\nThe trace is held in one `Arc<DebugSessionTrace>`. Loading parses exactly\nonce; every read borrows into that structure; `Clone` on the store is one\n`Arc` increment. The original input text is **not** retained — only compact\nprovenance metadata (`TraceSourceMetadata`: path, byte length, format).\nThere are no `&mut` methods, so cross-thread sharing is safe. Future\nconsumers (Query/Replay API, Semantic Engine) will each hold `shared()`\nhandles over the *same* data: one trace, one store, many views.\n\n---\n\n## What the parser deliberately does not do\n\n* No renumbering of events, reassignment of allocation ids, address\n  rewriting, reordering, merging of repeated instructions, or invented\n  defaults. The round-trip tests assert the loaded model is value-identical\n  to what Stage 1 wrote.\n* No fabrication of missing observations. A failed memory read stays\n  `None`/`not_captured`; a truncated trace stays truncated; skipped tool\n  stages stay `Skipped`. Partial traces load as first-class stores.\n* No reconstruction of journal fields that Stage 1 computes at session end\n  (execution outcome/status, compile diagnostics, `heap_state`, allocation\n  lifetimes, crash/Valgrind/sanitizer reports, resource-usage and profiling\n  totals, coverage, `session_meta`, analysis notes, stage results) — those\n  are never journaled, so requesting a `TraceStore` from journal input\n  returns an explicit error that names `parse_journal` as the alternative.\n* No indexing, cross-record referential-integrity validation, or query\n  optimization (TP-2), no specialized consumer views or GUI pagination\n  (TP-3), no semantic interpretation (Stage 2).\n\n---\n\n## Journal details (as implemented by `storage::Journal`)\n\nRecord kinds and payload types:\n\n| kind | payload |\n|---|---|\n| `configuration` | `config::TracingConfig` (always the first record) |\n| `checkpoint` | `models::ExecutionSnapshot` |\n| `allocation` | `{\"observed_at_stop\": u64, \"event\": HeapEvent}` |\n| `gap` | `models::TraceGap` |\n| `disassembly` | `models::DisassembledInstruction` |\n| `instruction` | `models::InstructionEvent` |\n| `finalized` | `true` (terminal control record) |\n\nReader policy:\n\n* Every complete line must decode to a known kind — no silent skipping.\n* A final line **without a trailing newline** is a suspected torn write\n  (append-only, unbuffered writer): accepted only if it fully decodes,\n  otherwise reported via `torn_tail: true` and never interpreted.\n* Blank lines are tolerated; the first record of a non-empty journal must\n  be `configuration`.\n* Unknown record kinds are rejected by default; setting\n  `allow_unknown_journal_records` preserves them verbatim as\n  `JournalRecord::Unknown` (forward compatibility without fabrication).\n\n---\n\n## Known limitations\n\n* **Monolithic JSON memory.** The whole file is read and deserialized at\n  once; peak memory is roughly the input plus the parsed structures. There\n  is no constant-memory or seek-based parsing (that belongs to TP-2/TP-3).\n* **V2-era example files.** The four `examples/v2_*.json` files carry\n  `max_register_snapshot_bytes` in `execution_limits` — a field removed\n  from the models during the V2.1 register rework — and `ExecutionLimits`\n  rejects unknown fields. This is Stage 1's pre-existing model contract\n  (the engine itself never re-loads traces); the parser surfaces it as a\n  typed error naming the field rather than guessing. Schema-version-2\n  traces that use current fields parse fine.\n* **Journal reconstruction** is explicitly unsupported (see above).\n* Deprecated CPU-register fields (`registers`, `initial_registers`) remain\n  parse-only exactly as the models define them; V2.1 traces omit them, and\n  the parser does not reintroduce register processing.\n\n## Testing\n\n`cargo test` covers: unit tests for detection/decoding edge cases\n(`src/trace_parser/*`), and integration tests in `tests/trace_parser.rs`\nagainst **real Stage 1 fixtures** — the six `examples/v21_*.json` traces\n(normal, dual, heap, crash, timeout, skipped-sanitizer) and the two journals\nin `tests/fixtures/journal/` written by real engine runs. Categories:\nnormal ingestion, source/assembly fidelity (80 events over 58 addresses;\n4146 events over 7 — repeats never collapsed), memory/heap fidelity (ids,\norder, hex-exact bytes), partial traces, invalid inputs (empty, malformed,\ntruncated, wrong structure, bad version, bad field type, oversize, missing\nfile, non-UTF-8), journal compatibility, and ownership/repeat access.\n",

# TP-1 Implementation Report — Trace Parser

## A. Repository findings

- **Single crate** (`c-trace-engine`, lib + bin), not a workspace. All trace models already live in a library target, so no refactoring was needed to share them.
- **Source-of-truth models** (`src/models.rs`): `DebugSessionTrace` = `execution_limits`, `execution: ExecutionOutcome`, **flattened** `recording: RecordingData` (disassembly table, instruction events, `source_checkpoints: Vec<usize>`, trace gaps, storage, profiling), `tracing_configuration`, `schema_version: u32` with `#[serde(default = ...)] → 2`, `compiled_successfully` + `compile_errors`, `snapshots`, `heap_events`, `heap_state`, `crash_report`, `valgrind_report`, `execution_status`, `resource_usage`, `sanitizer_report`, `session_meta`, `analysis_notes`, `stage_results`. Deprecated register fields are `Option` + `skip_serializing_if` — parse-only V2 compat.
- **JSON format**: one monolithic `serde_json` document (pretty or compact).
- **Journal** (`src/storage.rs`): append-only JSONL, `{"kind","data"}` per line; kinds `configuration` (`TracingConfig`), `checkpoint`, `allocation` (`{"observed_at_stop","event"}`), `gap`, `disassembly`, `instruction`, `finalized`; refuses overwrite; `storage::recover()` exists but silently drops errors and torn tails — reused the *format*, not the reader.
- **Fixtures**: 6 real V2.1 traces in `examples/v21_*.json`; 4 V2-era `examples/v2_*.json`; C sources in `fixtures/c/`.
- **Assumption deltas vs. the brief**: schema marker is integer `2` (not "2.1"); journal records `TracingConfig` (not `TraceConfig`); journal-only mode exists, so "snapshots == checkpoints" is not a universal invariant — referential checks stay out (TP-2).

## B. Implementation summary

| path | what |
|---|---|
| `src/trace_parser/mod.rs` | `TraceStore` (Arc-owned canonical store), `TraceLoadOptions`, `TraceFormatSelection`/`TraceFormat`, `TraceSourceMetadata`, `parse_journal{,_reader,_bytes}` |
| `src/trace_parser/error.rs` | `TraceParseError` — 13 typed variants, `Source{path}` wrapper, cause chains via `#[source]` |

**Stage 1 untouched**: zero modifications to recorder, trace, gdb, models, CLI, or any other engine file.

## C. Architectural decisions

- **One canonical representation**: `TraceStore` holds `Arc<DebugSessionTrace>`. Loading parses once; every read borrows; `Clone` = one `Arc` increment; no `&mut` surface. `shared()` hands future consumers (Query/Replay, Semantic Engine) handles over the *same* structure — no per-consumer copies, no GUI-shaped data.
- **Input text is not retained** — only compact provenance (`path`, exact byte length, detected format). The parsed representation is authoritative.
- **Module-in-crate** over a new crate: models are already lib-public; a separate crate would have required moving them for no dependency benefit. Parser depends only on `models` + `config` + serde; no recorder, no GUI, no future-engine dependency.
- **Format boundaries are internal** (`json`, `journal` submodules): new sources plug in behind the same gate/dispatch without touching the store.

## D. Input compatibility

- **Works**: all six `examples/v21_*.json` (completed ×4, crashed, timeout, skipped-sanitizer) — value-identical round-trip asserted; journals from real runs fully decode (counts: 29 checkpoints/97 instructions/46 disassembly/2 gaps for `finite_loop`; 40/349/70/5 + 2 allocations for `calloc`); missing `schema_version` loads as 2 (documented serde contract); reader/path/in-memory ingestion all equivalent.
- **Does not work, by design**: schema versions ≠ 2; the four `examples/v2_*.json` — they carry `max_register_snapshot_bytes`, a field removed from `ExecutionLimits` in the V2.1 register rework, and `ExecutionLimits` rejects unknown fields. This is **pre-existing Stage 1 model behavior** (the engine never re-loads traces); the parser surfaces a typed error naming the field rather than guessing. Reported as a finding, not silently "fixed."
- **Journal**: records are fully validated/decoded; *full-trace reconstruction* is explicitly unsupported with an error naming exactly which finalized field categories can never be journaled. No fabrication anywhere.

## E. Validation and error handling

Structural validation = content gates (empty, UTF-8) → format detection → serde type/structure validation (enforces all required fields) → schema-version gate. Partial/incomplete *executions* are never validation failures. Typed errors cover: empty input, size limit (pre-checked for files, take-capped for streams), non-UTF-8, malformed JSON (line/column), unrecognized format, unsupported schema version, malformed journal record (line + reason), unsupported journal kind, record limit, journal reconstruction, missing-configuration-first. No panics on adversarial input; malformed/truncated JSON is never reinterpreted as a journal (detection requires ≥1 valid record before any torn tail; mid-file or doubled bad lines fail detection).

## F. Test evidence

`cargo test` — **160 passed, 0 failed**:
- lib: **112** (86 pre-existing + 26 new parser unit tests: detection edge cases, journal decode policies, limits, error wrappers)
- `tests/v2.rs`: **12** ✓ (Stage 1 regression, unchanged)
- `tests/trace_parser.rs`: **13** ✓ (A–G categories from the brief, against real fixtures)
- integration: **22** ✓ (engine recording suites, ~125 s)
- doc-tests: **1** ✓ (the module example runs against `examples/v21_normal.json`)

`cargo clippy --all-targets`: 0 warnings · `cargo fmt --check`: clean.

Notable fidelity assertions: 80 events over 58 addresses and 4146 events over 7 addresses preserved un-merged with recorded order; heap event order/ids unchanged; hex-exact memory bytes (heap blocks + variables) compared against the original JSON; full-value round-trip equality for five traces; `Arc::ptr_eq` proves single-parse sharing; concurrent readers across 4 threads.

## G. Resource behavior

- Size limit (default 512 MiB) enforced *before* reading for files (metadata), via `take(max+1)` for streams (over-limit detected, not truncated), and by `len()` check for in-memory buffers.
- Journal ingestion streams line-by-line (`BufReader`, 64 KiB buffer): one record buffered at a time; per-line cap = `max_bytes`; record-count cap 2,000,000; each record's raw JSON `Value` is dropped after typed decode (moved, not cloned).
- No quadratic behavior: detection is a single linear scan with early exit for JSON documents; JSON path parses once with zero intermediate `Value` tree.
- Safe conversions throughout (`usize as u64` lossless comparisons, `saturating_add` on limits).

## H. Known limitations

- Monolithic JSON → peak memory ≈ input + parsed structures; no constant-memory/seek parsing (deferred to TP-2/TP-3, as scoped).
- V2-era example files don't deserialize (see D) — existing model contract, documented in `docs/trace-parser.md` and asserted in a test so the behavior is explicit.
- Journal → full-trace reconstruction unsupported (fundamental: fields are never journaled); journal provenance (path/byte length) is not attached to `JournalTrace` (caller knows the source; can be added with TP-2 if wanted).
- Torn-tail detection is content-based: a valid-but-unterminated final line is accepted, an invalid one is reported (`torn_tail`) and dropped — it can't be distinguished from garbage bytes without extra protocol (documented).

## I. TP-2 handoff

- `TraceStore::shared()` → `Arc<DebugSessionTrace>` is the indexing substrate; `trace()`/`recording` slices are already in final recorded order, so indexes (checkpoint-id, instruction-range, source file/line, disassembly, heap, diagnostics) can be built once over the `Arc` and shared the same way.
- `JournalTrace.records` (typed, ordered, with `counts`/`finalized`/`torn_tail`) is the raw material for journal-based reconstruction if a future phase adds a writer-side finalization record — the reader needs no redesign, only new record kinds (and `allow_unknown_journal_records` already tolerates forward extensions).
- `TraceParseError` variants for cross-record integrity failures can extend the existing enum (`InvalidTrace { reason }` is the designated catch-all); `TraceLoadOptions` is the natural home for future validation-depth toggles.
- Nothing in the ownership model needs to change for dual-consumer views: build indexes/views that borrow or `Arc`-clone `shared()`; the store stays the single authority.

1. **`event_id`** = **0-based execution-order index into `instruction_events`** — the engine asserts `event.event_id == position` (contiguity). So event_id IS an index/position, not an opaque id.
2. **`instruction_id`** = **index into `disassembly_table`** (`data.disassembly_table.get(id as usize)`), with an invariant that the disassembly entry's address matches the event's address. It's a 0-based Vec index, NOT an opaque id.
3. **`checkpoint_id`** (on InstructionEvent) = **0-based index into `snapshots`** (`id >= trace.snapshots.len()` → invalid).
4. **`source_checkpoints: Vec<usize>`** = 0-based indices into `snapshots`.
5. **`instruction_count`** = execution-order position counter (== len(instruction_events) when events retained; can exceed when `retain_instruction_events` is false — the guard is `!=` only when non-empty... interesting: `if !events.is_empty() && count != len` → mismatch. When events are empty (not retained), count can be anything).
6. **`instruction_position`** (SnapshotObservation, TraceGap) = position in the instruction-event timeline (compared against `instruction_count`).
7. **`step_index`** = 0-based index of the captured stop — and `source_checkpoints` holds exactly `snapshot.step_index` values (recorder.rs:113), so step_index == position within `snapshots` Vec (0-based), provided snapshots are never dropped. If capped mid-run, later snapshots aren't added, so indices remain contiguous ✓.
8. **`stop_id`** (SnapshotObservation) — GDB stop id. Not a Vec index (GDB's own counter). recorder allocations: `observed_at_stop: stop_id` — journal allocation records reference the GDB stop id, NOT the snapshot index! Important distinction: journal `allocation.observed_at_stop` = stop_id (GDB counter), and `HeapBlockInfo.observed_at_stop` = same.
9. **`sequence`** (HeapEvent) + `allocation_sequence`/`free_sequence` (HeapBlockInfo) = runtime chronological sequence numbers.
10. **`allocation_id`** — engine-assigned stable block identity (0 = untracked); `realloc_from_id` references allocation_id namespace. Addresses are separate ("0x..." strings) — reused addresses get fresh ids (documented in models).

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Trace-model integrity validators for c-trace-engine V2 (audit suite E).

Semantics matched to the PROBED engine schema (not assumed):
- heap_events entries: {pid, allocation_id, event_type(allocated|freed), address,
  size_bytes, source_file, source_line, old_allocation_id, ...}
- variable pointer targets: {kind(null|heap|global|...), allocation_id,
  base_address, offset_bytes, ...}
- register blocks in instruction events are POST-attempt observations:
  event N's rip equals its next_address (for faulted events, address).
  V2.1 traces contain no register blocks (capture removed); E8a/E8b/E8c
  detect this and validate V2.1 address semantics instead.
- valgrind detailed_errors entries may be dicts OR plain strings.
"""
import json, re, sys

def _hx(s):
    try:
        return int(s, 16)
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        return None

def _reg_map(regblock):
    return {v.get("name"): v for v in (regblock or {}).get("values", [])}

def _vg_errors(vr):
    errs = []
    for k in ("detailed_errors", "errors"):
        errs += (vr.get(k) or [])
    return errs

| 2 | No duplication / no reparse | **PASS** | Repeat `trace()` calls return the same pointer; `shared()`/`trace()` point at one allocation; **100 clones → RSS delta 0 KiB** (`Arc::ptr_eq` across clones); 8 concurrent reader threads consistent |
| 3 | Stress ingestion (real trace) | **PASS** | 46.4 MiB / **94,306 instruction events** (timeout+trace-budget terminated, real Stage 1 output): load **903.8 ms** (release build; debug build 8.4 s), peak RSS **206.1 MiB (≈4.4× input)**, steady post-load 157 MiB; 100 clones on the loaded store: 0 KiB |
| 4 | Limits + malformed inputs | **PASS** | Oversize **file** (1 MiB cap): rejected before reading, error names the path, VmHWM stayed ≤3.1 MiB; oversized **reader**: rejected in **1.25 ms** with **192 KiB** RSS delta (no unbounded buffering); truncated 2 MB of real trace → `MalformedJson`; empty/whitespace → `EmptyInput`; non-UTF-8 → `InvalidEncoding`; `schema_version: 3` (mutated real trace) → `UnsupportedSchemaVersion{3}`; journal-shaped input via auto-detect → `JournalReconstructionUnsupported` |
| 5 | JSON vs journal boundary | **PASS** | Same-run comparison: journal 468 records (config 1, checkpoints 40, instructions 349, disassembly 70, allocations 2, gaps 5, finalized) — **counts identical to the JSON trace** (40/349/70/5/2); `TraceStore::open(journal)` refused with the reconstruction error |
| 6 | Reference-semantics audit | **PASS** (see table) | All references catalogued from Stage 1 code paths + `processor::validate` invariants |
| 7 | No Stage 1 regression | **PASS** | Full suite rerun: **160/160 green** (112 lib, 12 v2, 13 parser, 22 integration, 1 doctest); engine source untouched; fresh traces pass the engine's own validator |

## 5. Exact JSON ↔ journal difference

**Journal keeps (per-stop evidence)**: `configuration` (= `tracing_configuration`, incl. `mode`), `checkpoint` records (= `snapshots`, incl. `step_index`/`observation.stop_id`), `instruction` records (= `instruction_events`), `disassembly` records (= `disassembly_table`), `allocation` records (= `heap_events` + `observed_at_stop`), `gap` records (= `trace_gaps`), and the `finalized` control flag.

**Never journaled (computed at session finalize) — these block full reconstruction**: `execution_limits`, `schema_version`, `compiled_successfully`, `compile_errors`, `execution` (outcome/exit/signal), `execution_status`, `heap_state`, `allocation_lifetimes`, `crash_report`, `valgrind_report`, `sanitizer_report`, `resource_usage`, `session_meta`, `analysis_notes`, `stage_results`, and recording subfields `internal_diagnostics`, `instruction_count`, `coverage`, `storage`, `profiling`. Plus one *derived* ambiguity: `source_checkpoints` (index list) is reconstructible only under the assumption "every journaled checkpoint is a source checkpoint" (true in dual mode, not in journal-only/source mixes) — a TP-2 decision, not a TP-1 fabrication target.

## 6. Reference dictionary for TP-2 (verified against engine code)

| field | kind | semantics |
|---|---|---|
| `event_id` | **0-based index** | position in `instruction_events`; engine asserts contiguity (`event_id == position`) — *not* an opaque id despite the name |
| `instruction_id` | **0-based index** | resolved via `disassembly_table.get(id)`; invariant: that entry's `address` == event `address` |
| `checkpoint_id` (`InstructionEvent`) | **0-based index** | into `snapshots` (`id >= snapshots.len()` is invalid) |
| `source_checkpoints[]`, `step_index` | **0-based index** | both index `snapshots`; recorder pushes `snapshot.step_index`; snapshots are never removed, so index == position |
| `stop_id`, `stop_id_before/after`, allocation `observed_at_stop` | **1-based counter** | engine stop counter (`stop_id += 1` per processed GDB stop); execution-order position of *stops* — **different sequence** from events/snapshots; journal allocations join to snapshots via `observation.stop_id` |
| `instruction_position` (snapshot/gap) | **order position** | attempted instruction events preceding the stop; compare against `instruction_count` |
| `instruction_count` | **counter** | total attempted events (== `instruction_events.len()` when events retained; larger when retention off) |
| `allocation_id` | **engine-assigned id** | stable block identity; `0` = untracked; reused addresses get fresh ids; shared namespace across `HeapEvent`, `HeapBlockInfo`, `PointerTarget`, `realloc_from_id` — *never* a Vec index |
| `sequence`, `allocation_sequence`/`free_sequence` | **runtime counter** | chronological order from the C instrumentation runtime |
| `activation_id`, `lexical_scope_id` | engine id / scope key | per-activation counter; `"block:<start>-<end>:<line>"` string |
| `StackFrameInfo.level` | **order position** | frame depth, 0 = innermost |
| all `address`/`points_to`/`base_address`/`next_address` | **recorded address** | `"0x…"` strings from the traced process — never ids or indices |

**TP-2 trap flagged**: `event_id`/`instruction_id` read like opaque ids but are Vec indices; `stop_id` reads like an index but is a 1-based counter over a different sequence. Any index building must use the table above, not the field names.

## Warnings (no action required for TP-2)

1. **`WARNING` — schema-version rejection happens after full deserialization.** The version is a field *inside* the struct, so an incompatible-version file is parsed completely before rejection. Memory stays bounded by `max_bytes` (measured worst case on the mutated 46 MB file: 259.8 MiB peak ≈ 5.6× input, then freed). Correctness holds; a pre-scan shortcut was deliberately not added (false-positive risk > benefit).
2. **`WARNING` — debug-build ingestion is ~9× slower** (8.4 s vs 903.8 ms on 46 MB). Set performance expectations against release builds only.
3. Known pre-existing: `examples/v2_*.json` carry the removed `max_register_snapshot_bytes` field and don't deserialize — Stage 1's own model contract, unchanged by TP-1.

## Unresolved risks

- None blocking. All measurements are from a single machine/session; no dedicated TP-1 benchmark suite exists (correctly deferred to TP-3).

## Recommendation

**PASS — TP-2 can safely begin.** The canonical-store ownership model (single `Arc`, parse-once, zero-cost sharing) is verified under stress; ingestion fidelity is exact on freshly recorded traces; limits and error paths are typed and bounded; the reference dictionary above gives TP-2 everything needed to build indexes without misinterpreting ids, indices, addresses, or positions. No TP-1 code was modified during this audit.

## User

# VISUAL C — TRACE PARSER
## TP-2: Efficient Indexing, Cross-Record Resolution & Raw Execution Queries

### Your role

Act as a senior Rust systems engineer continuing development of the existing Visual C backend.

Your assignment is to implement **TP-2**, the second phase of the Trace Parser.

TP-1 has already been implemented, tested, and audited. You must **extend that existing implementation**, not replace or independently reimplement it.

The Trace Parser is a shared Rust infrastructure component that consumes execution traces produced by the existing `c-trace-engine` V2.1.

Its purpose is to make recorded execution information efficiently accessible to two future consumers:

1. **Stage 2 — Semantic Engine:** Will interpret recorded execution data to build memory objects, relationships, state differences, timelines, and educational diagnostics.
2. **Stage 3 — GUI Query/Replay API:** Will expose raw and semantic information to Visual C's frontend.

The Trace Parser must remain independent of both consumers.

**TP-2's objective is to transform the canonical `TraceStore` created in TP-1 into an efficiently queryable execution-data store, without duplicating the underlying trace or interpreting C program semantics.**

Do not implement TP-3, the Semantic Engine, or the GUI.

# 2. TP-1 acceptance audit findings — authoritative implementation context

The TP-1 acceptance audit reported:

- 160 tests passed.
- Six real V2.1 JSON fixtures successfully ingested.

- Value-identical trace round trips.
- One canonical `Arc`-owned representation.
- No reparsing during repeated access.
- Safe concurrent readers.
- No Stage 1 regressions.

Large-trace test:

These measurements establish a baseline, not guaranteed performance targets.

### Critical limitation

The existing journal format can be decoded, but cannot reconstruct a complete `DebugSessionTrace` because certain finalized fields are never journaled.

Therefore:

**Use complete V2.1 JSON traces as the authoritative input for TP-2 indexing and queries.**

Do not fabricate fields to make journal data equivalent to complete JSON.

Do not modify the journal writer during this phase.

Existing journal decoding must remain functional.

# 3. Mandatory reference-semantics contract

The TP-1 audit examined the actual Stage 1 implementation and established the following reference meanings.

You must verify these against the repository before coding and preserve their semantics.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `event_id` | Zero-based position in `instruction_events`; recorder enforces contiguity |
| `instruction_id` | Zero-based index into `disassembly_table` |
| `checkpoint_id` in instruction events | Zero-based index into `snapshots` |
| `source_checkpoints[]` | Snapshot indices, not independent checkpoint objects |
| `step_index` | Snapshot index |
| `stop_id` | One-based counter of processed GDB stops |
| `stop_id_before` / `stop_id_after` | References to GDB stop-counter positions |
| `observed_at_stop` | GDB stop-counter position associated with an allocation observation |
| `instruction_position` | Execution-order position relative to attempted instruction events |
| `instruction_count` | Total attempted instruction-event count; may exceed retained events |
| `allocation_id` | Engine-assigned stable heap-allocation identity |
| `realloc_from_id` | Allocation identity associated with reallocation |
| `sequence` | Runtime instrumentation sequence counter |
| `activation_id` | Function-activation identity |
| `lexical_scope_id` | Existing lexical-scope identifier |
| `StackFrameInfo.level` | Stack depth, zero being the innermost frame |
| Address fields | Recorded process memory addresses, commonly represented as hexadecimal strings |

Additional established facts:

- Allocation ID `0` means untracked.
- Heap allocation IDs are **not** vector indices.
- Different allocations can reuse the same address.
- Repeated machine instruction addresses represent distinct execution events.
- Instruction IDs reference disassembly records, not individual executions.
- GDB stop counters use a different sequence from instruction-event positions.
- `source_checkpoints` does not necessarily include every snapshot.
- Some trace configurations retain fewer instruction events than were attempted.

### Absolute rule

**Never infer reference semantics from a field's name.**

For example:

```text
event_id        -> vector position
instruction_id  -> disassembly position
checkpoint_id   -> snapshot position
stop_id         -> separate GDB stop counter
allocation_id   -> stable allocation identity
address         -> observed memory location
```

These are fundamentally different concepts.

Do not convert them into a single generic index or assume that they share a numbering system.

---

# 4. TP-2 responsibilities

Implement the following capabilities as extensions of the existing Trace Parser.

### Required

1. Efficient direct access to existing vector-indexed records.
2. Compact indexes for genuinely nontrivial lookups.
3. Checkpoint and execution-stop navigation.
4. Instruction-event and disassembly relationships.
5. Source-location-to-instruction relationships.
6. Heap-allocation and allocation-event lookup.
7. Raw diagnostic and evidence lookup where supported.
8. Cross-record reference validation.
9. Efficient ordered-range queries.
10. Tests and measured query-performance comparisons.

### Not required

- Semantic object identification.
- Pointer target inference.
- Memory relationship graphs.
- State differences.
- Educational diagnostics.
- Reconstructing unrecorded memory.
- Re-running the traced program.
- GUI-specific data models.
- Tauri commands.
- Separate semantic-input and GUI-query facades.
- Advanced query caching.
- Journal format redesign.

Those belong to later phases.

---

# 5. Build indexes only where they provide value

This requirement is particularly important.

Some existing references are already ordinary vector indices.

For example:

```rust
trace.instruction_events.get(event_id)
```

is already constant-time access when `event_id` is a valid vector position.

Creating a hash map that maps every `event_id` back to the same vector position would add memory usage without providing meaningful improvement.

### Indexing policy

For each proposed index:

1. Identify the corresponding lookup operation.
2. Establish the complexity of direct access without the index.
3. Determine whether repeated linear scans are currently required.
4. Choose an efficient representation.
5. Estimate index memory overhead.
6. Avoid the index if direct access is already sufficient.

Prefer:

- Direct vector access for positional identifiers.
- Compact vector-based mappings for dense numeric domains.
- Hash maps for sparse, non-positional identities.
- Ordered position lists for one-to-many relationships.
- Bounded ranges where records are already grouped.
- Borrowed slices or iterators over existing records.

Avoid:

- Duplicate full events inside maps.
- A hash map for every numeric index.
- Redundant copies of source strings for every event.
- Sorting or copying entire event collections on each query.
- Building many rarely used indexes without justification.

**The goal is faster access per unit of additional memory, not the maximum possible number of indexes.**

---

# 6. Index lifetime and ownership

Extend `TraceStore` so that indexes are associated with the same canonical trace.

The desired ownership model is:

```text
TraceStore
|
+-- Canonical DebugSessionTrace
|      |
|      +-- snapshots
|      +-- instruction_events
|      +-- disassembly_table
|      +-- heap_events
|      +-- diagnostics
|      +-- metadata
|
+-- TraceIndexes
       |
       +-- source-location lookup
       +-- stop-to-snapshot lookup
       +-- allocation-event lookup
       +-- instruction relationships
       +-- other justified indexes
```

This is conceptual, not a required Rust structure.

### Requirements

- Do not replace the canonical `Arc<DebugSessionTrace>`.
- Do not require callers to deserialize the trace again.
- Do not duplicate raw records inside indexes.
- Preserve safe, immutable concurrent access.
- Ensure cloned `TraceStore` handles share the same indexes.
- Avoid unnecessary locks during read-only queries.
- Prevent partial or inconsistent index initialization.
- Keep index initialization errors explicit.

### Eager versus lazy indexing

Evaluate both approaches.

**Eager:** Build the justified indexes once when the store is created.

**Lazy:** Build an index group on its first use, then share it across subsequent queries.

Choose based on actual implementation complexity, typical usage, and memory cost.

A thread-safe `OnceLock`-style implementation is acceptable if appropriate.

Do not introduce an elaborate cache-management system merely to support lazy initialization.

If initial TP-2 indexing is eager, measure its additional loading cost.

If lazy, benchmark first-query cost separately from subsequent queries.

### Sharing invariant

Cloning a `TraceStore` must not reconstruct indexes or create an independent full index set per clone.

The raw trace and indexes should belong to a common shareable storage context.

Preserve TP-1's existing `shared()` behavior wherever possible.

---

# 7. Source checkpoint and snapshot access

Provide efficient access to recorded snapshots.

Supported operations should conceptually include:

```rust
get_snapshot(snapshot_index)
get_source_checkpoint(source_checkpoint_position)
get_source_checkpoint_indices()
get_snapshots_in_range(start, end)
```

Adapt the names and signatures to existing models.

### Critical distinction

A source-checkpoint position is not automatically the same thing as a snapshot index.

For example:

```text
source_checkpoints = [0, 4, 9, 15]
```

Then:

```text
source checkpoint #2 -> snapshots[9]
```

Do not return `snapshots[2]`.

### Requirements

- Preserve snapshot ordering.
- Preserve source-checkpoint ordering.
- Treat the index list as the authoritative mapping.
- Support empty source-checkpoint lists.
- Handle invalid positions safely.
- Avoid cloning snapshots for normal queries.
- Do not infer missing source checkpoints.
- Do not assume every snapshot corresponds to a source checkpoint.

The GUI will eventually use these operations to move through actual observed execution states.

---

# 8. Instruction-event access and range queries

Instruction events represent executed machine instructions recorded by Stage 1.

Implement efficient operations conceptually equivalent to:

```rust
get_instruction_event(event_index)
get_instruction_range(start, end)
get_instruction_count()
```

### Requirements

- Direct positional lookup should be constant-time.
- Contiguous ranges should ideally borrow existing slices.
- Preserve original event ordering.
- Preserve repeated instruction addresses.
- Never collapse repeated executions into one event.
- Do not return the entire timeline when only a small range is requested.
- Handle empty ranges.
- Handle invalid or overflowing bounds safely.
- Make range-boundary semantics explicit.

### Attempted versus retained instructions

The trace may contain:

```text
instruction_count > instruction_events.len()
```

because of retention settings or incomplete recording.

Expose these values distinctly.

Do not claim that every attempted instruction has a retained event.

Do not generate synthetic instruction events to fill the difference.

### Design principle

**A recorded instruction execution is identified by its event position, not solely by its machine address.**

This is essential for replaying loops correctly.

---

# 9. Instruction-to-disassembly resolution

Each instruction event may reference an entry in the disassembly table through `instruction_id`.

Provide efficient, typed resolution.

Conceptual operations:

```rust
get_disassembly_entry(instruction_id)
get_disassembly_for_event(event_index)
get_execution_events_for_instruction(instruction_id)
```

### Requirements

- Resolve an instruction event to its actual disassembly entry.
- Verify available ID/address invariants.
- Preserve distinctions between static disassembly entries and dynamic execution events.
- Support repeated execution of one disassembled instruction.
- Return explicit unavailable or invalid-reference results when appropriate.
- Avoid copying disassembly records.

### Reverse lookup

A reverse relationship from a disassembly entry to its executed event positions may be valuable.

Implement this efficiently if it provides a clear query benefit.

Prefer compact lists of event positions rather than copies of events.

For example:

```text
Disassembly entry #17
    -> event positions [31, 44, 57, 70]
```

These are distinct executions of the same static instruction.

### Missing information

A trace may contain incomplete disassembly information.

Do not fabricate assembly text or assume an instruction can be resolved if the recorded data does not support it.

---

# 10. Source-to-assembly relationships

Visual C will display both C code and the corresponding assembly execution.

TP-2 must establish efficient access to recorded source and disassembly mappings.

Conceptual operations:

```rust
get_disassembly_for_source(file, line)
get_executed_events_for_source(file, line)
get_source_for_instruction(instruction_id)
```

These signatures are illustrative.

Use the actual mapping fields provided by Stage 1.

### Important distinction

There are two different questions:

**Question A:** Which disassembled instructions are associated with this source location?

**Question B:** Which recorded execution events executed instructions associated with this source location?

These must not be confused.

For example, a source line can correspond to three static instructions, each executed many times.

The source-to-disassembly lookup may return three entries.

The source-to-execution lookup may return hundreds of instruction events.

### Requirements

- Preserve one-to-many mappings.
- Support repeated visits to the same source line.
- Support multiple instructions per source line.
- Support multiple source locations where the existing representation permits them.
- Preserve execution ordering in dynamic-event results.
- Handle instructions with unavailable source mappings.
- Support source files with identical basenames.
- Avoid guessing that two paths refer to the same file.

Use the actual recorded file identity and mapping rules.

Do not introduce aggressive filename normalization that could merge distinct files.

### Performance

Avoid scanning every instruction event and disassembly entry on every source lookup.

Build compact indexes for the necessary relationships.

Do not duplicate whole instruction-event records.

---

# 11. Execution-stop and checkpoint relationships

The Stage 1 trace records GDB stops using `stop_id`.

This value is not a snapshot vector index.

Implement indexed relationships based on actual recorded evidence.

Useful operations may include:

```rust
get_snapshots_at_stop(stop_id)
get_allocation_events_at_stop(stop_id)
get_instruction_events_related_to_stop(stop_id)
```

Use names that accurately describe the actual relationship.

### Requirements

- Respect the one-based stop-counter semantics.
- Preserve repeated or shared stop associations.
- Distinguish `stop_id_before` and `stop_id_after`.
- Preserve allocation `observed_at_stop`.
- Do not assume every stop has a snapshot.
- Do not assume every snapshot has a uniquely associated instruction.
- Do not treat stop IDs as dense snapshot positions.

### Instruction positions

Snapshots and trace gaps may reference instruction positions.

These positions must be interpreted according to Stage 1's actual recording contract.

Do not assume that an attempted instruction-event position is always an index into the retained event vector.

In particular, retention-disabled or truncated traces may not provide every instruction event needed for direct resolution.

### Missing joins

If a stop, checkpoint, or instruction position cannot be linked using available evidence, return an explicit unresolved/unavailable result.

Do not use the closest timestamp or nearest index as an invented relationship.

---

# 12. Heap allocation and memory-event indexing

Stage 1 records heap allocation events and associated identities.

Provide efficient lookup of those records.

Conceptual operations:

```rust
get_heap_events_for_allocation(allocation_id)
get_heap_block(allocation_id)
get_heap_events_at_stop(stop_id)
```

Adapt these to the actual models.

### Allocation identity

The allocation ID is the authoritative identity.

Memory addresses are not allocation identities.

Consider:

```text
Allocation A:
    id = 12
    address = 0x1000

Allocation A is freed.

Allocation B:
    id = 19
    address = 0x1000
```

These are two different allocations even though the address was reused.

A query for allocation `12` must never accidentally return allocation `19`.

### Requirements

- Index heap events by actual allocation ID.
- Preserve event ordering.
- Handle allocation ID `0` as untracked according to the existing contract.
- Handle `realloc_from_id` without inventing identity equivalence.
- Preserve allocation and free sequence metadata.
- Handle events associated with the same GDB stop.
- Avoid treating hexadecimal addresses as allocation keys.
- Preserve malformed or unavailable data according to validation policy.

### Reallocation

Do not assume `realloc` always preserves the same allocation identity or address.

Use the actual recorded IDs and relationships.

TP-2 may expose the recorded `realloc_from_id` reference but must not build higher-level allocation-lifetime interpretations.

Those belong to Stage 2.

---

# 13. Raw memory and variable observations

TP-2 should make the existing recorded observations accessible without interpreting them.

At minimum, callers should be able to retrieve a checkpoint and inspect its existing variable, stack, heap, and memory data.

Where a narrowly scoped query avoids repeated expensive scans, add an appropriate accessor.

However, **do not build a complete semantic memory model**.

### Requirements

- Preserve raw addresses.
- Preserve recorded sizes.
- Preserve exact bytes.
- Preserve unavailable/read-failure states.
- Preserve variable and frame metadata.
- Avoid copying large byte buffers unnecessarily.
- Return references where Rust ownership permits.

### Important limitation

TP-2 must not provide an API that pretends arbitrary process memory can be read at any checkpoint.

Only recorded memory observations are available.

For example, an address absent from a checkpoint must not be returned as zero-filled memory.

Similarly, a value recorded at checkpoint 10 must not automatically be presented as an observation at checkpoint 11.

The Semantic Engine will later decide how to represent changes and observation gaps.

TP-2 should preserve the original evidence.

---

# 14. Diagnostic and evidence access

Stage 1 already contains raw diagnostic reports from tools such as GDB, Valgrind, and sanitizers.

Make these records available through lightweight, typed accessors.

### Requirements

- Preserve the original diagnostic content.
- Preserve source locations and recorded addresses.
- Preserve optional fields.
- Preserve tool-stage completion statuses.
- Do not duplicate diagnostic reports into another large representation.

Where the existing schema provides stable identifiers or references, support their resolution.

Where no stable ID exists, use documented positional access within the relevant report collection.

Do not invent cross-tool evidence relationships.

### Critical scope distinction

TP-2 can answer:

"Which raw Valgrind findings were recorded?"

TP-2 must not answer:

"Why did this pointer become dangling?"

The second question requires semantic interpretation and belongs to Stage 2.

---

# 15. Cross-record validation

TP-1 handles basic structural validation.

TP-2 must extend validation to meaningful relationships between existing records.

### Validate supported invariants

Examples include:

1. Instruction `event_id` matches its recorded vector position where required.
2. Instruction IDs resolve to valid disassembly entries.
3. Event addresses match their referenced disassembly entries where Stage 1 guarantees that invariant.
4. Snapshot references are within bounds.
5. Source-checkpoint indices reference actual snapshots.
6. Snapshot `step_index` follows the existing recording contract.
7. Stop and instruction-position references follow their documented domains.
8. Allocation references are interpreted according to the actual allocation-ID contract.
9. Existing chronological-order invariants are respected where guaranteed.
10. Referenced diagnostic or evidence records exist where the schema explicitly requires them.

Do not invent invariants that Stage 1 does not guarantee.

### Validation severity

Separate:

**Structural corruption:** A record violates a guaranteed invariant.

**Partial coverage:** The trace does not contain every observation.

**Unavailable evidence:** A relationship cannot be established because information was not recorded.

**Optional absence:** The schema permits a field to be missing.

These situations must not be conflated.

### Valid incomplete traces

The following must remain supportable:

- Crashes.
- Timeouts.
- Step-limit termination.
- Truncated execution coverage explicitly recorded by Stage 1.
- Skipped diagnostic stages.
- Unavailable memory observations.
- Missing source mappings.
- Instruction retention gaps.

Do not reject such traces merely because they lack observations.

### Validation implementation

Choose a clean separation between:

- Existing TP-1 ingestion.
- TP-2 index construction.
- Optional or explicit deep referential validation.

Avoid silently making the TP-1 loader reject previously accepted, legitimately partial traces because of new assumptions.

Document whether deep validation is performed automatically or explicitly requested.

Report violations using typed errors with useful record context.

Preserve existing TP-1 error behavior wherever practical.

---

# 16. Typed query results and errors

Design query methods using idiomatic Rust.

Do not force every method into a single generic return type.

Suitable patterns may include:

```rust
Option<&T>
Result<&T, QueryError>
&[T]
impl Iterator<Item = &T>
```

Choose based on the operation.

### Important distinctions

Clearly distinguish:

- An invalid query argument.
- An out-of-range positional index.
- A valid query with no matching records.
- A reference that is structurally invalid.
- An observation not recorded.
- An unsupported query for the available trace format.

Do not use a successful empty result to conceal data corruption.

Likewise, a valid source line with no executed instructions should not automatically be treated as a malformed trace.

### Efficient ownership

Prefer borrowed references, slices, lightweight positions, and iterators.

Do not clone a large vector merely to return a small range.

Do not expose mutable references to canonical trace data.

---

# 17. Preserve recorded execution order

The Trace Parser's eventual purpose includes time-travel debugging and stepwise execution visualization.

TP-2 must make recorded ordering reliable.

### Required rules

- Instruction events remain ordered by recorded event position.
- Snapshots remain ordered by their original vector positions.
- Source checkpoints preserve their explicit sequence.
- Allocation events preserve their existing recorded order.
- Stop counters remain distinct from event indices.
- Runtime allocation sequence counters remain distinct from GDB stop counters.
- Partial coverage and trace gaps remain visible.

If an index groups events by source line, instruction, allocation, or stop, preserve the original order within that group unless the query explicitly requests another documented ordering.

Do not sort canonical trace arrays in place.

---

# 18. Memory and resource efficiency

TP-1's large-trace audit showed meaningful memory expansion during JSON deserialization.

TP-2 should not substantially worsen this without a justified query-performance benefit.

### Engineering expectations

- Use compact indexes.
- Avoid redundant dense-ID maps.
- Store positions instead of whole records.
- Avoid cloning long source-path strings per instruction event.
- Avoid unnecessary `Arc` allocations for each event.
- Avoid global mutable caches.
- Avoid building enormous nested hash maps by default.
- Keep read-only queries lock-free where feasible.
- Make index construction bounded by actual trace size and configured resource constraints.

### Construction complexity

Aim for linear or near-linear index construction relative to the relevant trace collections.

Avoid accidental quadratic algorithms.

If an index requires sorting, document its complexity and whether it affects the original record order.

### Index memory audit

Measure the additional memory required by index construction.

Report the result separately from the memory required to deserialize the raw trace.

If a proposed index is expensive and offers little improvement over direct access, remove it.

---

# 19. Performance benchmarking

TP-2 must provide measured evidence of improvement.

Do not report guessed or theoretical speedups as measured results.

### Benchmark scenarios

Use representative real V2.1 traces, including:

- A small ordinary trace.
- A finite loop with repeated instruction addresses.
- A source/assembly trace.
- A heap-allocation trace.
- A large instruction-heavy trace, preferably the 94,306-event case if available.

### Compare

For relevant query types, compare:

**Baseline:** A straightforward repeated linear scan of the canonical arrays.

**TP-2:** The new indexed query.

Measure:

1. Initial index-construction time.
2. Direct event lookup latency.
3. Source-location lookup latency.
4. Reverse disassembly-to-event lookup latency.
5. Allocation-event lookup latency.
6. Stop-to-checkpoint lookup latency.
7. Repeated-query throughput.
8. Additional index memory usage.
9. Total store memory usage after indexing.

Only benchmark operations for which a comparison is meaningful.

For example, direct vector indexing is already constant-time and does not require a linear-scan baseline.

### Benchmark methodology

- Prefer optimized/release builds.
- Use a reasonable number of repeated queries.
- Prevent the compiler from optimizing away query work.
- Separate cold index-building costs from warm query costs.
- Use representative successful and unsuccessful lookups.
- Document test hardware and input trace sizes.
- Present actual measured results.
- Do not claim speedups for query categories not tested.

### Acceptance principle

TP-2 does not need to make every query faster.

It needs to make frequently repeated nontrivial lookups significantly more efficient while keeping resource overhead sensible.

# 20. Tests

Add comprehensive tests for the new indexing and query behavior.

Keep all existing tests.

### A. Basic positional access

- First event.
- Last event.
- Out-of-range event.
- Empty range.
- Full range.
- Invalid range bounds.
- First and last snapshots.

### B. Source checkpoint mapping

- Source-checkpoint list with noncontiguous snapshot indices.
- Multiple snapshots without source-checkpoint membership.
- Empty source-checkpoint list.
- Invalid source-checkpoint reference.
- Preservation of original ordering.

### C. Instruction and disassembly

- Multiple events referencing one disassembly entry.
- Repeated instruction addresses.
- Correct event-to-disassembly resolution.
- Reverse disassembly-to-event lookup.
- Unavailable disassembly.
- Invalid instruction reference.

### D. Source mapping

- Multiple machine instructions for one C source line.
- Repeated execution of one C source line.
- Distinct files with identical basenames.
- Source locations without executed events.
- Instruction events without available source mapping.
- Correct static-versus-dynamic lookup distinctions.

### E. Execution stops

- One-based `stop_id`.
- Multiple records associated with a stop.
- Stops without snapshots.
- Snapshot and event positions that do not equal stop IDs.
- Correct allocation observation stop mapping.
- Missing stop relationships.

### F. Heap allocations

- Multiple events with the same allocation ID.
- Multiple allocations reusing the same address.
- Allocation ID zero.
- Reallocation references.
- Allocation and free event ordering.
- No false merging by address.

### G. Partial traces

- Crash traces.
- Timeout traces.
- Instruction retention gaps.
- `instruction_count` greater than retained event count.
- Missing optional source locations.
- Incomplete tool-stage reports.

### H. Referential validation

- Broken snapshot reference.
- Broken disassembly reference.
- Inconsistent event ID.
- Inconsistent instruction address where the invariant is guaranteed.
- Invalid source-checkpoint position.
- Legitimately absent observations.
- Distinction between corruption and partial coverage.

### I. Ownership and concurrency

- Repeated queries do not reparse.
- Store clones share canonical data.
- Store clones share initialized indexes.
- Parallel readers return consistent results.
- No mutation of source arrays.
- No unexpected full-vector copies during queries.

### J. Integration tests

Use the real V2.1 fixtures already in the repository.

Verify raw query results against direct inspection of the corresponding canonical trace arrays.

Where feasible, generate at least one fresh Stage 1 trace for compatibility testing.

],\n  \"heap_events\":  [ { \"event_type\": \"allocated\", \"allocation_id\": 1, \"size_bytes\": 12 }, ... ],\n  \"heap_state\":   [ { \"allocation_id\": 1, \"allocation_type\": \"malloc\", ┌──────────────┐\n  .c sources ───────▶│   compiler   │──▶ program_debug  (+ alloc_tracker.c)\n  BuildConfig ──────▶│  (GCC/SARIF) │──▶ program_asan   (sanitizers)\n pass only)    (caller file:line resolution)\n        └───────────────────┴────────────────────┘\n                            ▼\n                     DebugSessionTrace (JSON)\n```\n\n1. **Build** (`compiler.rs`): every translation unit is compiled with `-g -O0`\n   plus GCC's machine-readable diagnostics (`sarif-stderr` first, with\n   fallbacks for older GCC), linked with a small C runtime -  "content": "# Engine internals\n\nHow `c-trace-engine` observes a program. The guiding rules are:\n\n* **Never fabricate.** Everything in the trace came from a real observation\n  (compiler output, a GDB response, an event line, a tool report).\n* **Unobservable = `null`.** Fields the engine could not learn are absent or\n  `null`, not guessed.\n* **Partial results always survive.** Any stop condition degrades\n  gracefully and the trace records what happened in `analysis_notes`.\n\n## 1. Build & allocation instrumentation (`compiler.rs`, `c_runtime/alloc_tracker.c`)\n\nEach translation unit is compiled with `-g -O0 -fno-omit-frame-pointer` plus\nGCC 16's SARIF diagnostics on stderr (`-fdiagnostics-format=sarif-stderr`);\nolder GCC falls back to `-fdiagnostics-format=json` and then to plain text.\nGCC 16 emits **one SARIF document per translation unit** concatenated on\nstderr, so the parser consumes a *stream* of JSON documents\n(`serde_json::Deserializer::from_str(..).into_iter::<SarifDoc>()`).\n\nThe debug link embeds the C runtime (`alloc_tracker.c`) and redirects the\nprogram's allocator calls with `-Wl,--wrap=malloc --wrap=calloc\n--wrap=realloc --wrap=free`. The wrappers:\n\n* keep a small fixed-size process-local table of live blocks,\n* write **one line per operation** to the file named by\n  `C_TRACE_EVENT_FILE` (a dedicated file, never stdout/stderr, so program\n  output and telemetry cannot interleave or deadlock),\n* use a spinlock, no recursion and no allocation of their own — the tracker\n  must not perturb the allocator it observes,\n* assign per-process allocation ids; when an address is reused by a new\n  block it gets a fresh id, so `address` alone is never an identity,\n* report a **failed realloc** without freeing the original (glibc\n  semantics), and `realloc(p, 0)` as a free.\n\nEvent line format:\n\n```\n<pid> <seq> <kind> <id> <addr-hex> <size> <old_id> <old_addr-hex> <caller-hex> <status>\n```\n\n`kind` ∈ `malloc|calloc|realloc|free`; `status` ∈ `ok|ok_same|ok_moved|new|\nzero|failed|unknown|null`. `caller` is the return address of the allocator\ncall, resolved to `file:line` later by one batched `addr2line` run.\n\n`__wrap_malloc` forwards to `__real_malloc` etc.; this covers the\n*program's own* calls (and direct libc calls that land in the wrapped\nsymbols). Memory allocated inside libraries already linked against the real\nallocator is invisible to the timeline — Valgrind is the independent check\nthat sees everything.\n\n## 2. GDB session (`gdb_mi.rs`)\n\nThe session runs `gdb --nx --quiet --interpreter=mi2 <binary>` and speaks\nMI2 with:\n\n* **Token-matched commands**: every command is prefixed with a monotonically\n  increasing token; the matching result record resolves a oneshot channel.\n  Stream records (`~`, `&`, `@`) captured between command and response are\n  delivered with the response (needed for console-mode results such as\n  `whatis`).\n* **A dedicated pty for the inferior** via `-inferior-tty-set`: program\n  output never enters the MI stream. The master end is read by a tokio task\n  into a capped ring buffer (`max_output_bytes`).\n* **One channel** between reader task and session for async records\n  (`*running`, `*stopped`, `=notify`); the reader fails all pending\n  commands on EOF so a dead GDB never strands a wait.\n\nObserved GDB 18 behaviors the engine adapts to:\n\n* execution commands answer `^running` + async `*stopped` (including for\n  exits: `*stopped,reason=\"exited-normally\"`),\n* a `finish` from the outermost frame returns\n  `^error,msg=\"…finish… not meaningful in the outermost frame.\"`,\n* GDB occasionally reports a `*stopped` **without reason** after failing to\n  insert a temporary breakpoint while unwinding the outermost libc frame\n  (`Cannot insert breakpoint 0. Cannot access memory at address 0x101`).\n  Such stops cannot be finished; the engine continues instead, which lets\n  the imminent exit happen naturally,\n* GDB puts the inferior in its own process group, so killing GDB's group\n  does not kill the inferior — the engine kills both groups.\n\nTermination: every wait is timeout-bounded (per-command 20s, per-step 10s,\nsession wall = `4 × timeout_seconds + 30s`). On limit endings the engine\nkills the process groups (GDB's and the inferior's) and the cgroup subtree\nwhen available.\n\n## 3. Execution loop & snapshots (`trace.rs`)\n\n`run_gdb_phase` breaks at `main`, then:\n\n1. ingest allocation events that accumulated while the inferior ran,\n2. classify the stop: exit → `Completed` (+ exit code from the stop record\n   or `=thread-group-exited`); signal → fatal (`SIGSEGV`, `SIGABRT`, … →\n   `Crashed` + crash report), resource (`SIGXCPU`, `SIGKILL` →\n   `ResourceLimitReached`), benign (`SIGPIPE`, … → continue, bounded by the\n   step budget), no-reason stop → continue (see above),\n3. capture one snapshot:\n   * `-stack-list-frames` for the call stack,\n   * `-stack-list-variables --all-values` + `whatis` per variable for types,\n     own address, value and pointed-to address (`points_to`) — with raw\n     bytes read from the inferior within the per-snapshot budget,\n   * live heap blocks: for each tracked alive block one\n     `-data-read-memory-bytes` bounded by `max_memory_read_bytes` and the\n     remaining snapshot budget (blocks beyond the budget are recorded with\n     `memory_read_error`, not dropped),\n   * program output head (64 KiB cap per snapshot),\n4. step: `-exec-step` in user code; in non-user frames `-exec-finish`\n   (capped chain of 32, then `-exec-continue`).\n\nSnapshots are capped by `max_snapshot_count`; the memory budget is shared\nbetween variables and heap reads so one snapshot can never blow up the\ntrace.\n\n## 4. Heap reconstruction (`allocation_tracker.rs`)\n\n`HeapTimeline` ingests the raw event stream and reconstructs, per process:\n\n* **blocks** — one `BlockState` per allocation with allocation id, address,\n  size, type (`malloc`/`calloc`/`realloc`), realloc chain link\n  (`realloc_from_id`), caller pc, and final status (freed or still alive),\n* **events** — the full ordered history (allocated / reallocated / freed /\n  allocation_failed) with optional human-readable details (double free,\n  `free(NULL)`, failed realloc preserving the original),\n* **live byte counters** per process.\n\nIds are per-process; when a run produced more than one pid the serialized\nids are widened to `(pid << 32) | id` to stay unique across the trace —\nwith a single pid they stay plain (matches the C runtime's view).\n\nThe final `heap_state` lists every reconstructed block. A block's\n`raw_bytes_hex` is the last capture taken **while it was alive**; freed\nblocks keep that historical capture.\n\n## 5. Independent analyses\n\n**Valgrind** (`valgrind.rs`) runs the debug binary (without instrumentation\nwrappers — Valgrind replaces the allocator itself) under memcheck with\n`--xml=file --xml-user-prog-args`-style options, parses the XML with\n`roxmltree` (heap summary, error records with stacks, leak records) and\ncorrelates findings with allocation ids by `(file, line)` pairs resolved by\naddr2line. A Valgrind timeout leaves the partial XML; the engine notes it.\n\n**Sanitizer pass** (`sanitizer.rs`) runs only after a crash: the ASan-built\nbinary executes once with the same arguments and working directory; its\nstderr (`ERROR: AddressSanitizer: …`) is parsed into a structured report and\nthe `SUMMARY:` line is attached to the crash report as `asan_summary`.\nSanitizer runtimes are detected at link time: if libubsan is missing the\nbuild degrades to ASan-only, and if libasan is missing entirely the pass is\ndisabled with a note. Sanitizer and Valgrind children get CPU/file-size\nrlimits but **no address-space cap** — ASan maps terabytes of shadow memory\nand aborts under a small `RLIMIT_AS`.\n\n## 6. Resource controls (`resource_limits.rs`)\n\nLayered enforcement:\n\n1. **Engine clocks** — wall deadline, per-command and per-step timeouts;\n   every path is bounded, verified with real GDB.\n2. **rlimits** — `RLIMIT_CPU` (from `timeout_seconds`), `RLIMIT_FSIZE`,\n   `RLIMIT_NOFILE` on sanitizer/valgrind children. `RLIMIT_NPROC` is\n   deliberately never used: on Linux it is enforced per *real user id*, so\n   a low value breaks every `fork` on the whole desktop session\n   (empirically: `vfork: Resource temporarily unavailable` with 173 user\n   processes).\n3. **cgroup v2** — when a delegated subtree is writable, the inferior pid\n   is moved into it with `pids.max`, `memory.max` and `cpu.max`; on teardown\n   the subtree is killed (`cgroup.kill`). Best effort; its availability is\n   reported in `session_meta.cgroup_enforced`.\n\nThese limits protect the engine and the session — they are **not a\nsecurity sandbox** for hostile binaries.\n",

-}

-## What was blocking (and how it was fixed)
-
-The session began with the end-to-end run hanging. Diagnosed with `ps`/`/proc` inspection and a raw MI-stream echo, three real bugs were found and fixed:
-
-1. **addr2line pipe deadlock** (the actual hang): `ChildStdin::shutdown()` in tokio only flushes — it does **not** close the descriptor, so addr2line blocked in `anon_pipe_read` forever while the engine waited on stdout that would never EOF. Fixed by dropping the stdin handle after writing (true EOF) and wrapping both stages in 30s timeouts (`allocation_tracker.rs`).
-2. **GDB "no-reason" stops**: finishing out of `__libc_start_call_main` fails to unwind (caller pc reads as `0x101`) → "Cannot insert breakpoint 0" → GDB emits `*stopped` with no reason → a second finish aborts the phase. The engine now **continues** past no-reason stops and recovers any aborted execution command with one bounded continue (`trace.rs`). Verified: 12/12 bounded runs + full default runs all complete.
-3. **rlimit mis-targeting**: the inferior's budget (incl. `RLIMIT_AS`) was applied to GDB, Valgrind and the ASan pass. ASan aborted instantly (`ReserveShadowMemoryRange failed… errno: 12`). GDB now runs unrestricted; tool children get CPU/FSIZE/NOFILE only (`resource_limits.rs`).
-
-## Verified behavior
-
-- **Acceptance**: `cargo run -- sample.c` → complete trace, exit 0, in ~5s: 26 snapshots (stepping through `main` → `__wrap_malloc` → `sum_of_three`), heap events (malloc 12 B + free), `heap_state` with raw bytes `0a000000140000001e000000` (10,20,30) and resolved call site `sample.c:30`, pointer own-address vs `points_to`, clean Valgrind report, exit code 0.
-- **Crash path** (`null_deref.c`): `crashed` + SIGSEGV report with backtrace + ASan `SUMMARY: AddressSanitizer: SEGV … in main` attached; Valgrind independently reports `InvalidRead`.
-- **Limits** (`infinite_loop.c`, `many_allocs.c`): partial snapshots preserved, `limits_triggered` includes `max_steps`/`max_snapshot_count`, no orphaned inferior (GDB *and* inferior process groups now killed).
-- **13 fixtures**: realloc chains, `calloc`, `allocation_failed`, leak, use-after-free, uninit, invalid write, big output, multi-TU project (steps across `main.c`/`helper.c`) all behave.
-- **Exit codes**: 0 trace / 2 compile-failed (with precise SARIF line:col diagnostics — found and fixed a `startLine` camelCase bug) / 1 config error.
-
-## Test suites

-- **68 unit tests** green; **12 integration tests** green (19–38s, real gcc/gdb/valgrind, graceful skips with reasons on tool-less machines); `cargo clippy --all-targets` fully clean.

# c-trace-engine

## V2: synchronized source and instruction recording

Dual capture is now the default. Source checkpoints and executed-instruction
attempts come from **one GDB run**, not two executions. Legacy JSON fields are
retained with `schema_version: 2`; see [V2 schema and semantics](docs/v2.md).
New to the engine or want the plain-language version? Start with
**[The Trace Engine](docs/trace-engine.html)** — a visual, self-contained
introduction (pipeline, trace contents, guarantees, limits). For a conceptual
architectural overview (channels, budgets, the stop loop, the trust model),
see [Engine architecture](docs/architecture.md). Building on traces from Rust?
**[Trace Parser (TP-1)](docs/trace-parser.md)** ingests and validates V2/V2.1
traces and journals into one canonical, shareable `TraceStore`.

```sh
cargo run -- sample.c --timeout 20 --output trace.json
cargo run -- sample.c --trace-mode dual --sanitizer-trigger always
cargo run -- sample.c --trace-mode source             # lower-cost capture
cargo run -- sample.c --max-instruction-events 5000 --max-gdb-commands 50000
cargo run -- sample.c --journal run.jsonl --journal-only --output index.json
cargo run -- fixtures/c/globals.c --memory-region '&global_value:4'
```

## TP-2 Design

### Reference semantics (verified in audit)
- `event_id` = 0-based index into `instruction_events` (contiguous)
- `instruction_id` = 0-based index into `disassembly_table` (optional on events)
- `checkpoint_id` (on InstructionEvent) = 0-based index into `snapshots` (optional)
- `source_checkpoints[]` = snapshot indices
- `step_index` = snapshot index (== position since snapshots never removed)
- `stop_id`, `stop_id_before/after`, `observed_at_stop` = 1-based GDB stop counter
- `instruction_position` (snapshot/gap) = attempted-events position (may exceed retained)
- `instruction_count` = total attempted
- `allocation_id` = stable identity, 0=untracked, sparse, not an index
- `realloc_from_id` = allocation identity
- `sequence`/`allocation_sequence`/`free_sequence` = runtime counters
- addresses = hex strings
- `StackFrameInfo.level` = depth

58:             scope: "user_code".into(),

61:             stop_model: "gdb_all_stop".into(),
62:             truncation_reasons: Vec::new(),
63:             limitations: vec![
64:                 "Capture begins at main; startup and excluded-code intervals are gaps.".into(),
65:                 "Memory is exact only at its recorded stopped observation, never inferred from registers.".into(),
66:                 "Lexical DWARF DIE IDs and non-top-frame locals are not collected.".into(),
67:                 "All-stop pauses inferior threads, not external processes sharing memory.".into(),
68:                 "Disassembly assumes unchanged user code; self-modifying/JIT code is unsupported.".into(),
69:             ],
70:         }, ..Default::default() };

73:         data.profiling.enabled = true;

157:     pub async fn disassemble(
158:         &mut self,
159:         session: &mut GdbSession,
160:         stop: &StoppedInfo,
161:     ) -> Result<Option<u64>> {
162:         if !self.config.static_disassembly {
163:             return Ok(None);
164:         }
165:         if self.module_epoch != session.module_epoch() {
166:             self.cache.clear();
167:             self.module_epoch = session.module_epoch();
168:         }
169:         let Some(addr) = stop.frame.as_ref().and_then(|f| f.address.as_ref()) else {
170:             return Ok(None);
171:         };
172:         if let Some(id) = self.cache.get(addr) {
173:             self.data.profiling.disassembly_cache_hits += 1;
174:             return Ok(Some(*id));
175:         }
176:         let start = Instant::now();
177:         // Bounded windows avoid asking GDB for an arbitrarily huge function.
178:         // Start at an observed instruction boundary; cache every native result.
179:         let end = crate::memory::address(addr)
180:             .and_then(|pc| pc.checked_add(128))
181:             .ok_or_else(|| EngineError::Gdb("invalid observed PC".into()))?;
182:         let response = session
183:             .execute(&format!("-data-disassemble -s {addr} -e 0x{end:x} -- 2"))
184:             .await?;
185:         self.data.profiling.disassembly_queries += 1;
186:         self.data.profiling.disassembly_time_us += start.elapsed().as_micros() as u64;
187:         if let Some(message) = response.error_message() {
188:             return Err(EngineError::Gdb(message));
189:         }
190:         let module_identity = format!(
191:             "pid={}:module_epoch={}:{}",
192:             session.inferior_pid.unwrap_or(0),
193:             self.module_epoch,
194:             module_at(session.inferior_pid, addr).unwrap_or_else(|| "unknown_module".into())
195:         );
196:         if let Some(MiValue::List(items)) = response.record.result("asm_insns") {
197:             for item in items {
198:                 let MiListItem::Value(MiValue::Tuple(fields)) = item else {
199:                     continue;
200:                 };
201:                 let Some(address) = field(fields, "address") else {
202:                     continue;
203:                 };
204:                 if self.cache.contains_key(address) {
205:                     continue;
206:                 }
207:                 let instruction_id = self.data.disassembly_table.len() as u64;
208:                 let instruction = DisassembledInstruction {
209:                     instruction_id,
210:                     module_identity: module_identity.clone(),
211:                     address: address.into(),
212:                     bytes: field(fields, "opcodes").map(str::to_owned),
213:                     text: field(fields, "inst").unwrap_or("").into(),
214:                     function: field(fields, "func-name").map(str::to_owned),
215:                 };
216:                 self.reserve(serde_json::to_vec(&instruction)?.len())?;
217:                 self.journal.append("disassembly", &instruction)?;
218:                 self.cache.insert(address.into(), instruction_id);
219:                 self.data.disassembly_table.push(instruction);
220:             }
221:         }
222:         Ok(self.cache.get(addr).copied())
223:     }
