225:     pub async fn selected_memory(&self, session: &mut GdbSession) -> Vec<MemoryObservation> {
226:         let mut budget = self.limits.max_snapshot_memory_bytes;
227:         let mut observations = Vec::new();
228:         for region in &self.config.memory_regions {
229:             let size = region
230:                 .size
231:                 .min(self.limits.max_memory_read_bytes)
232:                 .min(budget);
233:             let address = session
234:                 .evaluate(&format!("(unsigned long)({})", region.address))
235:                 .await
236:                 .ok()
237:                 .and_then(|s| s.parse::<u64>().ok())
238:                 .map(|n| format!("0x{n:x}"));
239:             let result = if size == 0 {
240:                 Err("memory observation budget exhausted".into())
241:             } else if let Some(address) = &address {
242:                 session.read_memory_bytes(address, size as u64).await
243:             } else {
244:                 Err("address expression unavailable at this stop".into())
245:             };
246:             budget = budget.saturating_sub(size);
247:             let (raw_bytes_hex, status, error) = match result {
248:                 Ok(hex) => (
249:                     Some(hex),
250:                     if size < region.size {
251:                         DataValidity::Truncated
252:                     } else {
253:                         DataValidity::Valid
254:                     },
255:                     None,
256:                 ),
257:                 Err(e) => (None, DataValidity::Unreadable, Some(e)),
258:             };
259:             observations.push(MemoryObservation {
260:                 expression: region.address.clone(),
261:                 address,
262:                 requested_bytes: region.size,
263:                 raw_bytes_hex,
264:                 status,
265:                 error,
266:             });
267:         }
268:         observations
269:     }

271:     pub fn event(&mut self, event: InstructionEvent) -> Result<()> {
272:         let start = Instant::now();
273:         let size = serde_json::to_vec(&event)?.len();
274:         if self.config.retain_instruction_events {
275:             self.reserve(size)?;
276:         }
277:         self.journal.append("instruction", &event)?;
278:         self.data.instruction_count += 1;
279:         if self.config.retain_instruction_events {
280:             self.data.instruction_events.push(event);
281:         }
282:         self.data.profiling.journal_time_us += start.elapsed().as_micros() as u64;
283:         Ok(())
284:     }

286:     pub fn finish(mut self) -> RecordingData {
287:         self.data.storage.resident_event_bytes = self.resident;
288:         self.data.storage.bytes_written = self.journal.bytes;
289:         self.data.storage.finalized = self.journal.finalize().is_ok();
290:         if !self.data.storage.finalized {
291:             self.truncate("journal_finalization_failed");
292:         }
293:         self.data
294:     }
295: }

297: fn module_at(pid: Option<u32>, address: &str) -> Option<String> {
298:     let address = crate::memory::address(address)?;
299:     let maps = std::fs::read_to_string(format!("/proc/{}/maps", pid?)).ok()?;
300:     for line in maps.lines() {
301:         let fields: Vec<_> = line.split_whitespace().collect();
302:         let (start, end) = fields.first()?.split_once('-')?;
303:         if address >= u64::from_str_radix(start, 16).ok()?
304:             && address < u64::from_str_radix(end, 16).ok()?
305:         {
306:             return Some(format!(
307:                 "{}:range={}:file_offset={}",
308:                 fields.get(5).copied().unwrap_or("anonymous"),
309:                 fields[0],
310:                 fields[2]
311:             ));
312:         }
313:     }
314:     None
315: }

317: pub fn event_outcome(before: &StoppedInfo, after: &StoppedInfo) -> &'static str {
318:     if after.is_signal() {
319:         // A synchronous fault is attributable only when the stopped PC is the attempted PC.
320:         if matches!(
321:             after.signal_name.as_deref(),
322:             Some("SIGSEGV" | "SIGBUS" | "SIGILL" | "SIGFPE")
323:         ) && before.frame.as_ref().and_then(|f| f.address.as_ref())
324:             == after.frame.as_ref().and_then(|f| f.address.as_ref())
325:         {
326:             "faulted"
327:         } else {
328:             "interrupted"
329:         }
330:     } else if after.reason.as_deref() == Some("end-stepping-range") {
331:         "completed"
332:     } else {
333:         "unknown"
334:     }
335: }

337: pub async fn capture_global(
338:     session: &mut GdbSession,
339:     name: &str,
340:     limits: &ExecutionLimits,
341: ) -> VariableInfo {

343:         name: name.into(),

345:             session

347:                 .get(name)
348:                 .cloned()
349:                 .unwrap_or_else(|| "global".into()),
350:         ),

352:         ..Default::default()
353:     };

355:         Ok(value) => var.value = value,
356:         Err(e) => {
357:             var.read_error = Some(e.to_string());
358:             set_validity(&mut var);
359:             return var;
360:         }
361:     }
362:     let type_key = format!("global:{}:{name}", session.module_epoch());
363:     if let Some(c_type) = session.type_cache.get(&type_key) {
364:         var.c_type = c_type.clone();
365:     } else {
366:         if let Ok(response) = session
367:             .execute(&format!(
368:                 "-interpreter-exec console {}",
369:                 crate::gdb_mi::quote_for_mi(&format!("whatis {name}"))
370:             ))
371:             .await
372:         {
373:             for (_, text) in response.streams {
374:                 if let Some(t) = text.trim().strip_prefix("type = ") {
375:                     var.c_type = t.into();
376:                 }
377:             }
378:         }
379:         if !var.c_type.is_empty() {
380:             session.type_cache.insert(type_key, var.c_type.clone());
381:         }
382:     }
383:     var.address = session
384:         .evaluate(&format!("&({name})"))
385:         .await
386:         .ok()
387:         .and_then(|s| crate::gdb_mi::extract_hex_address(&s));
388:     var.size_bytes = session
389:         .evaluate(&format!("sizeof({name})"))
390:         .await
391:         .ok()
392:         .and_then(|s| s.parse().ok());
393:     if var.c_type.contains('*') {
394:         var.points_to = session
395:             .evaluate(&format!("(unsigned long)({name})"))
396:             .await
397:             .ok()
398:             .and_then(|v| v.parse::<u64>().ok())
399:             .map(|v| format!("0x{v:x}"));

401:     if let (Some(addr), Some(size)) = (&var.address, var.size_bytes) {

407:             Err(e) => var.read_error = Some(e),

409:     }

1: //! TP-1: Trace Parser — ingestion, structural validation, canonical store.
2: //!
3: //! This module is the **Trace Parser** foundation: it receives Stage 1
4: //! (`c-trace-engine`) trace inputs, identifies the input format, deserializes
5: //! the recorded data with the existing Serde models, validates structural
6: //! correctness (schema version, required structures), and hands back one
7: //! canonical, immutable, shareable owner of the loaded trace —
8: //! [`TraceStore`].
9: //!
10: //! It intentionally does **not**: execute programs, invoke tools, infer
11: //! object identities or pointer graphs, reconstruct missing events, or
12: //! expose GUI/Tauri shapes. Recorded evidence is preserved verbatim; deriving
13: //! C-language meaning from it is the future Semantic Engine's job, and
14: //! indexed/query views are future Trace Parser phases (TP-2/TP-3).
15: //!
16: //! # Supported inputs
17: //!
18: //! | input             | support | notes                                     |
19: //! |-------------------|---------|-------------------------------------------|
20: //! | JSON trace file   | full    | schema version `2` (V2 / V2.1); a missing `schema_version` field defaults to 2 per the model's serde contract |
21: //! | Session journal   | records | JSONL journal is validated and decoded per record; full-trace reconstruction is explicitly unsupported (see [`parse_journal`]) |
22: //!
23: //! # Example
24: //!
25: //! ```
26: //! use c_trace_engine::trace_parser::{TraceLoadOptions, TraceStore};
27: //!
28: //! let store = TraceStore::open("examples/v21_normal.json", TraceLoadOptions::default())?;
29: //!
30: //! // The canonical trace: immutable, cheap to share, never re-parsed.
31: //! let trace = store.trace();
32: //! assert_eq!(trace.schema_version, 2);
33: //! assert!(matches!(
34: //!     store.execution_status(),
35: //!     c_trace_engine::models::ExecutionStatus::Completed
36: //! ));
37: //! # Ok::<(), c_trace_engine::trace_parser::TraceParseError>(())
38: //! ```

55: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
56: // Options and format selection
57: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
58: 
59: /// How the parser should decide between the supported input formats.
60: ///
61: /// Selection is always content-based — file names and extensions are never
62: /// consulted — and malformed JSON is never silently reinterpreted as a
63: /// journal ([`json::detect_format`] enforces the signature rules).
64: #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, Default, PartialEq, Eq)]
65: pub enum TraceFormatSelection {
66:     /// Inspect the content: one JSON document, or line-oriented journal.
67:     #[default]
68:     Auto,
69:     /// Require a single JSON `DebugSessionTrace` document.
70:     Json,
71:     /// Require the existing JSONL session journal.
72:     Journal,
73: }
74: 
75: /// The format an input was actually ingested as (reported in
76: /// [`TraceStore::source`]).
77: #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
78: pub enum TraceFormat {
79:     /// One complete JSON document.
80:     Json,
81:     /// Line-oriented JSONL session journal.
82:     Journal,
83: }
84: 
85: /// Ingestion limits and toggles.
86: #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]
87: pub struct TraceLoadOptions {
88:     /// Input-format policy. Default: [`TraceFormatSelection::Auto`].
89:     pub format: TraceFormatSelection,
90:     /// Maximum accepted input size in bytes. A larger input is rejected
91:     /// before parsing (file loads check the size first; stream loads stop
92:     /// at the cap), so no unbounded buffering happens. Default: 512 MiB.
93:     pub max_bytes: u64,
94:     /// Maximum journal record count. Default: 2,000,000.
95:     pub max_journal_records: usize,
96:     /// Accept journal record kinds unknown to this engine version and
97:     /// preserve them verbatim ([`JournalRecord::Unknown`]) instead of
98:     /// rejecting the record. Default: `false` (reject with
99:     /// [`TraceParseError::UnsupportedJournalRecord`]).
100:     pub allow_unknown_journal_records: bool,
101: }
102: 
103: impl Default for TraceLoadOptions {
104:     fn default() -> Self {
105:         Self {
106:             format: TraceFormatSelection::Auto,
107:             max_bytes: 512 * 1024 * 1024,
108:             max_journal_records: 2_000_000,
109:             allow_unknown_journal_records: false,
110:         }
111:     }
112: }

114: /// Compact provenance metadata for an ingested input.
115: ///
116: /// Deliberately *not* a copy of the input: after successful ingestion the
117: /// parsed representation is authoritative, and only this small descriptor is
118: /// retained alongside it.
119: #[derive(Debug, Clone)]
120: pub struct TraceSourceMetadata {
121:     /// Filesystem path when loaded from a file; `None` for reader/slice
122:     /// ingestion and pre-parsed traces.
123:     pub path: Option<PathBuf>,
124:     /// Exact input size in bytes as read (0 for pre-parsed traces).
125:     pub byte_len: u64,
126:     /// The format the input was actually ingested as.
127:     pub format: TraceFormat,
128: }

130: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
131: // Canonical store
132: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
133: 
134: /// The single canonical owner of one successfully ingested Stage 1 trace.
135: ///
136: /// The store wraps the deserialized [`DebugSessionTrace`] in an [`Arc`]: all
137: /// access is immutable, repeated reads never re-parse or copy, and future
138: /// consumers (Query/Replay API, Semantic Engine) can each hold
139: /// [`TraceStore::shared`] handles over the same authoritative data — one
140: /// trace, one store, many views. A trace whose C program crashed, timed out,
141: /// or hit a step limit is still a valid store; those outcomes are recorded
142: /// data (see [`TraceStore::execution_status`]), not ingestion failures.
143: ///
144: /// # Ownership model
145: ///
146: /// * Loading parses once; afterwards the store is a cheap `Clone` handle
147: ///   (one `Arc` increment) plus small provenance metadata.
148: /// * The original input text is not retained — only
149: ///   [`TraceSourceMetadata`] (path, byte length, detected format).
150: /// * There are no `&mut` methods; the trace is immutable from the moment of
151: ///   ingestion, so shared access across threads is safe.
152: #[derive(Debug, Clone)]
153: pub struct TraceStore {
154:     trace: Arc<DebugSessionTrace>,
155:     source: TraceSourceMetadata,
156: }
157: 
158: impl TraceStore {
159:     /// Load and validate a JSON trace from a filesystem path.
160:     ///
161:     /// The file size is checked against `options.max_bytes` before reading.
162:     /// Every failure is wrapped in [`TraceParseError::Source`] naming `path`.
163:     ///
164:     /// Journal input is detected but cannot become a `TraceStore` — full
165:     /// reconstruction from a journal is explicitly unsupported; use
166:     /// [`parse_journal`] for the validated record stream.
167:     pub fn open(path: impl AsRef<Path>, options: TraceLoadOptions) -> Result<Self> {
168:         let path = path.as_ref();
169:         Self::open_inner(path, &options).map_err(|e| TraceParseError::Source {
170:             path: path.to_path_buf(),
171:             source: Box::new(e),
172:         })
173:     }
174: 
175:     fn open_inner(path: &Path, options: &TraceLoadOptions) -> Result<Self> {
176:         let file = File::open(path).map_err(|e| TraceParseError::Io { source: e })?;
177:         let declared_len = file
178:             .metadata()
179:             .map_err(|e| TraceParseError::Io { source: e })?
180:             .len();
181:         if declared_len > options.max_bytes {
182:             return Err(TraceParseError::LimitExceeded {
183:                 limit: options.max_bytes,
184:             });
185:         }
186:         let mut bytes = Vec::new();
187:         // +1 so an over-limit stream is *detected* rather than silently
188:         // truncated into a confusing parse error (also covers files whose
189:         // reported metadata length lies, e.g. some /proc entries).
190:         let read_len = (&file)
191:             .take(options.max_bytes.saturating_add(1))
192:             .read_to_end(&mut bytes)
193:             .map_err(|e| TraceParseError::Io { source: e })?;
194:         if read_len as u64 > options.max_bytes {
195:             return Err(TraceParseError::LimitExceeded {
196:                 limit: options.max_bytes,
197:             });
198:         }
199:         let byte_len = read_len as u64;
200:         let trace = load_trace_document(&bytes, options)?;
201:         Ok(Self {
202:             trace: Arc::new(trace),
203:             source: TraceSourceMetadata {
204:                 path: Some(path.to_path_buf()),
205:                 byte_len,
206:                 format: TraceFormat::Json,
207:             },
208:         })
209:     }
210: 
211:     /// Load a JSON trace from any byte reader (no filesystem access).
212:     ///
213:     /// Reads at most `options.max_bytes + 1` bytes: over-limit inputs are
214:     /// rejected with [`TraceParseError::LimitExceeded`] instead of being
215:     /// buffered unboundedly. Errors carry no path context (there is none).
216:     pub fn from_reader(mut reader: impl Read, options: TraceLoadOptions) -> Result<Self> {
217:         let mut bytes = Vec::new();
218:         let read_len = (&mut reader)
219:             .take(options.max_bytes.saturating_add(1))
220:             .read_to_end(&mut bytes)
221:             .map_err(|e| TraceParseError::Io { source: e })?;
222:         if read_len as u64 > options.max_bytes {
223:             return Err(TraceParseError::LimitExceeded {
224:                 limit: options.max_bytes,
225:             });
226:         }
227:         let byte_len = read_len as u64;
228:         let trace = load_trace_document(&bytes, &options)?;
229:         Ok(Self {
230:             trace: Arc::new(trace),
231:             source: TraceSourceMetadata {
232:                 path: None,
233:                 byte_len,
234:                 format: TraceFormat::Json,
235:             },
236:         })
237:     }
238: 
239:     /// Parse an in-memory JSON trace document.
240:     ///
241:     /// The name is explicit on purpose: the input is always parsed as a JSON
242:     /// document, and `options.format` selection is not consulted
243:     /// (`Auto` detection also never classifies a real trace as a journal,
244:     /// so behavior matches `Auto` for genuine trace files). Convenient for
245:     /// unit tests and pre-fetched bytes.
246:     pub fn from_json_bytes(bytes: &[u8], options: TraceLoadOptions) -> Result<Self> {
247:         if bytes.len() as u64 > options.max_bytes {
248:             return Err(TraceParseError::LimitExceeded {
249:                 limit: options.max_bytes,
250:             });
251:         }
252:         let byte_len = bytes.len() as u64;
253:         let text = gates(bytes)?;
254:         let trace = json::decode_document(text)?;
255:         Ok(Self {
256:             trace: Arc::new(trace),
257:             source: TraceSourceMetadata {
258:                 path: None,
259:                 byte_len,
260:                 format: TraceFormat::Json,
261:             },
262:         })
263:     }
264: 
265:     /// Adopt an already-deserialized trace (e.g. produced in-process by the
266:     /// engine). Only the schema-version gate runs; the model is trusted as
267:     /// Stage 1's own output. No byte length is known, so
268:     /// `TraceSourceMetadata::byte_len` is 0.
269:     pub fn from_trace(trace: DebugSessionTrace) -> Result<Self> {
270:         json::validate_schema_version(&trace)?;
271:         Ok(Self {
272:             trace: Arc::new(trace),
273:             source: TraceSourceMetadata {
274:                 path: None,
275:                 byte_len: 0,
276:                 format: TraceFormat::Json,
277:             },
278:         })
279:     }
280: 
281:     /// The canonical trace. Reads never re-parse, never copy, and never
282:     /// mutate: every call borrows into the same `Arc`-owned structure.
283:     pub fn trace(&self) -> &DebugSessionTrace {
284:         &self.trace
285:     }
286: 
287:     /// Cheap shareable handle to the canonical trace for future consumers.
288:     /// Sharing never requires reparsing; the callers all see one structure.
289:     pub fn shared(&self) -> Arc<DebugSessionTrace> {
290:         Arc::clone(&self.trace)
291:     }
292: 
293:     /// Provenance metadata of the ingested input.
294:     pub fn source(&self) -> &TraceSourceMetadata {

296:     }
297:

300:     /// Partial-trace statuses are data, not errors.

303:     }
304: 
305:     /// Program-level outcome details (exit code, signal, stop address,

310: 
311:     /// Session metadata (build config, toolchain versions, program args)

318: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
319: // Journal ingestion
320: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
321: 
322: /// Load and validate a session journal from a filesystem path.
323: ///
324: /// Returns the validated record stream ([`JournalTrace`]) — never a
325: /// `DebugSessionTrace`. See [`TraceParseError::JournalReconstructionUnsupported`]
326: /// for why full reconstruction is out of scope. Failures are wrapped in
327: /// [`TraceParseError::Source`] naming `path`.
328: pub fn parse_journal(path: impl AsRef<Path>, options: TraceLoadOptions) -> Result<JournalTrace> {
329:     let path = path.as_ref();
330:     parse_journal_inner(path, &options).map_err(|e| TraceParseError::Source {
331:         path: path.to_path_buf(),
332:         source: Box::new(e),
333:     })
334: }
335: 
336: fn parse_journal_inner(path: &Path, options: &TraceLoadOptions) -> Result<JournalTrace> {
337:     let file = File::open(path).map_err(|e| TraceParseError::Io { source: e })?;
338:     let declared_len = file
339:         .metadata()
340:         .map_err(|e| TraceParseError::Io { source: e })?
341:         .len();
342:     if declared_len > options.max_bytes {
343:         return Err(TraceParseError::LimitExceeded {
344:             limit: options.max_bytes,
345:         });
346:     }
347:     let reader = std::io::BufReader::with_capacity(64 * 1024, file);
348:     journal::parse_reader(reader, options)
349: }
350: 
351: /// Parse a session journal from an in-memory buffer.
352: ///
353: /// Like [`TraceStore::from_json_bytes`], the name is explicit: the input is
354: /// always parsed as a journal, `options.format` is not consulted.
355: pub fn parse_journal_bytes(bytes: &[u8], options: TraceLoadOptions) -> Result<JournalTrace> {
356:     journal::parse_bytes(bytes, &options)
357: }
358: /// Parse a session journal from a line-oriented reader (no filesystem access).
359: pub fn parse_journal_reader(
360:     reader: impl std::io::BufRead,
361:     options: TraceLoadOptions,
362: ) -> Result<JournalTrace> {
363:     journal::parse_reader(reader, &options)
364: }
365: 
366: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
367: // Ingestion dispatch
368: // ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
369: 
370: /// Load a JSON trace document, honoring the format-selection policy.
371: ///
372: /// Journal-shaped input can never become a `TraceStore` (full reconstruction
373: /// from a journal is unsupported), so it is rejected up front — without
374: /// wasting effort decoding records that would be discarded.
375: fn load_trace_document(bytes: &[u8], options: &TraceLoadOptions) -> Result<DebugSessionTrace> {
376:     let text = gates(bytes)?;
377:     match options.format {
378:         TraceFormatSelection::Json => json::decode_document(text),
379:         TraceFormatSelection::Journal | TraceFormatSelection::Auto => {
380:             if options.format == TraceFormatSelection::Auto
381:                 && json::detect_format(text) == json::DetectedFormat::JsonDocument
382:             {
383:                 return json::decode_document(text);
384:             }
385:             Err(TraceParseError::JournalReconstructionUnsupported)
386:         }
387:     }
388: }
389: 
390: /// Input gates shared by every entry point: reject empty input and non-UTF-8
391: /// encodings before any format dispatch happens.
392: fn gates(bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<&str> {
393:     if bytes.iter().all(|&b| b.is_ascii_whitespace()) {
394:         return Err(TraceParseError::EmptyInput);
395:     }
396:     std::str::from_utf8(bytes).map_err(|e| TraceParseError::InvalidEncoding { source: e })
397: }

1: //! JSON trace document ingestion and input-format detection.
2: //!
3: //! The parser deliberately does not re-serialize, normalize, or "repair" the
4: //! trace: `DebugSessionTrace` is deserialized directly from the input bytes,
5: //! so what Stage 1 recorded is exactly what the [`TraceStore`](super::TraceStore)
6: //! exposes. No event renumbering, no address rewriting, no invented defaults.

8: use crate::models::DebugSessionTrace;
9: 
10: use super::error::{Result, TraceParseError};
11: 
12: /// The one schema version this engine family currently emits and accepts.
13: /// The serialized marker is the integer `2` — V2 and V2.1 share it.
14: pub(crate) const SUPPORTED_SCHEMA_VERSION: u32 = 2;
15: 
16: /// Human-readable summary used in error messages.
17: pub(crate) const SUPPORTED_SCHEMA_VERSION_LABEL: &str = "2 (V2 / V2.1 traces)";
18: 
19: /// Deserialize one complete JSON trace document, then gate its schema version.
20: pub(crate) fn decode_document(text: &str) -> Result<DebugSessionTrace> {
21:     let trace: DebugSessionTrace =
22:         serde_json::from_str(text).map_err(|e| TraceParseError::MalformedJson {
23:             line: e.line(),
24:             column: e.column(),
25:             message: e.to_string(),
26:         })?;
27:     validate_schema_version(&trace)?;
28:     Ok(trace)
29: }
30: 
31: /// Schema-version gate.
32: ///
33: /// A *missing* `schema_version` field is not an error: `DebugSessionTrace`
34: /// declares `#[serde(default = ...)]` returning 2, which is the engine's
35: /// documented compatibility contract for legacy V2 traces (they omit the
36: /// field and still parse). Anything other than 2 is rejected explicitly —
37: /// an incompatible version is never silently interpreted as the current one.
38: pub(crate) fn validate_schema_version(trace: &DebugSessionTrace) -> Result<()> {
39:     if trace.schema_version != SUPPORTED_SCHEMA_VERSION {
40:         return Err(TraceParseError::UnsupportedSchemaVersion {
41:             found: trace.schema_version,
42:             supported: SUPPORTED_SCHEMA_VERSION_LABEL,
43:         });
44:     }
45:     Ok(())
46: }
47: 
48: /// The input kind decided by content inspection (never by file name).
49: #[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
50: pub(crate) enum DetectedFormat {
51:     /// One complete JSON document — the trace file Stage 1 prints to stdout
52:     /// and writes to `--output`.
53:     JsonDocument,
54:     /// Line-oriented `{"kind":...,"data":...}` JSONL session journal.
55:     Journal,
56: }
57: 
58: /// Decide whether `text` is a JSON trace document or a JSONL journal.
59: ///
60: /// Policy (documented in `docs/trace-parser.md`):
61: /// * journal-shaped means every complete line parses as a JSON object
62: ///   carrying a string `kind` member and a `data` member;
63: /// * a journal may end with ONE torn (incomplete) final line — writes are
64: ///   append-only, so a crashed session leaves exactly that — but only when
65: ///   at least one valid record precedes it. Malformed JSON is therefore
66: ///   never reinterpreted as a journal;
67: /// * anything else is attempted as a JSON document (and a failure there is
68: ///   reported as `MalformedJson`, the honest diagnosis).
69: pub(crate) fn detect_format(text: &str) -> DetectedFormat {
70:     let mut total = 0usize;
71:     let mut valid_records = 0usize;
72:     let mut bad_first: Option<usize> = None;
73:     let mut bad_last: Option<usize> = None;
74: 
75:     for line in text.lines() {
76:         let trimmed = line.trim();
77:         if trimmed.is_empty() {
78:             continue;
79:         }
80:         total += 1;
81:         if journal_record_shape(trimmed) {
82:             valid_records += 1;
83:         } else {
84:             if bad_first.is_none() {
85:                 bad_first = Some(total);
86:             }
87:             bad_last = Some(total);
88:         }
89:     }
90: 
91:     // A bad line is tolerable only as the single torn final line, and only
92:     // when at least one valid record precedes it. A bad line mid-file, two
93:     // bad lines at the end, or a bad line with no valid record before it
94:     // (truncated compact or pretty JSON) is treated as a JSON document
95:     // attempt — malformed JSON is never reinterpreted as a journal.
96:     if let (Some(first), Some(last)) = (bad_first, bad_last) {
97:         if first != last || last != total || valid_records == 0 {
98:             return DetectedFormat::JsonDocument;
99:         }
100:     }
101:     if valid_records >= 1 {
102:         DetectedFormat::Journal
103:     } else {
104:         DetectedFormat::JsonDocument
105:     }
106: }
107: 
108: /// Cheap shape check for one journal line. No typed decoding happens here;
109: /// the journal parser re-validates every line with full error context.
110: fn journal_record_shape(line: &str) -> bool {
111:     let Ok(value) = serde_json::from_str::<serde_json::Value>(line) else {
112:         return false;
113:     };
114:     let Some(obj) = value.as_object() else {
115:         return false;
116:     };
117:     obj.get("kind").is_some_and(|k| k.is_string()) && obj.contains_key("data")
118: }

**Index inventory** (each justified, per the policy):
| Lookup | Baseline | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| `event_id`/`instruction_id`/snapshot index → record | O(1) vector access | **no index** (policy: direct access) |
| source-checkpoint position → snapshot | O(1) (`source_checkpoints[pos]`) | **no index** |

| source (file,line) → static instruction ids / dynamic event positions | O(E) scan | **one shared map + 2 CSR arrays** |
| instruction id → source locations (reverse of above) | O(E·D) | **small CSR over source keys** |
| allocation id → heap events / heap_state / lifetime | O(H) scan | **HashMap of positions** |
| stop → snapshot | O(S) scan | **zero-memory binary search** (verified strictly-increasing) |
| stop / checkpoint → events | O(E) scan | **zero-memory binary search** (verified non-decreasing `stop_id_before` / `checkpoint_id`) |
| stop → heap events | O(H) scan | **derived** from `snapshot.observation.heap_event_count` boundaries (recorded evidence) |

  "newString": "/// Errors returned by TP-2 indexed queries on a [`TraceStore`](super::TraceStore).\n///\n/// Distinct from [`TraceParseError`]: ingestion succeeded, and these describe\n/// *query* outcomes. The variants separate the situations the TP-2 contract\n/// requires callers to tell apart:\n///\n/// * an invalid query argument (`InvalidRange`),\n/// * an out-of-range positional index (`OutOfRange`),\n/// * a reference that cannot resolve in the recorded data\n///   (`InvalidReference`),\n/// * a relationship the trace simply does not record (`Unavailable`),\n/// * a recorded ordering invariant the index relies on being violated —\n///   detected corruption, surfaced instead of concealed\n///   (`OrderingViolation`).\n///\n/// A *successful but empty* result (empty slice, empty iterator, `None`) is\n/// never returned to conceal corruption: it always means \"valid query, no\n/// such records were recorded\".\n#[derive(Debug, Error, Clone, PartialEq, Eq)]\npub enum QueryError {\n    /// A positional index is beyond the recorded records.\n    #[error(\"{collection} index {index} is out of range (recorded len {len})\")]\n    OutOfRange {\n        /// Which canonical collection was addressed.\n        collection: &'static str,\n        /// The rejected index.\n        index: usize,\n        /// How many records were actually recorded.\n        len: usize,\n    },\n\n    /// A range argument is malformed for the addressed collection: `start`\n    /// must be `<= end` and `end` must be `<= len`. Ranges are half-open and\n    /// are never silently clamped.\n    #[error(\"invalid {collection} range {start}..{end} (recorded len {len})\")]\n    InvalidRange {\n        /// Which canonical collection was addressed.\n        collection: &'static str,\n        /// Range start as given.\n        start: usize,\n        /// Range end as given.\n        end: usize,\n        /// How many records were actually recorded.\n        len: usize,\n    },\n\n    /// A cross-record reference (stored in a record) does not resolve within\n    /// the collection it names. This is\n    /// *unavailable data*, not corruption: partial traces legitimately lack\n    /// observations (retention gaps, missing mappings, dropped snapshots).\n    #[error(\"the trace does not record {what}\")]\n    Unavailable {\n        /// What evidence is absent, phrased as recorded-data language.\n        what: &'static str,\n    },\n\n    /// A recorded ordering the index build verified (and the reference\n    /// dictionary guarantees for engine-written traces) does not hold. Binary search details:
- snapshot_at_stop: `trace.snapshots.partition_point(|s| s.observation.stop_id < stop_id)` → idx; check snapshots[idx].stop_id == stop_id → Some else None.
- events_at_stop: lo = partition_point(|e| e.stop_id_before < stop), hi = partition_point(|e| e.stop_id_before <= stop) → &[lo..hi].
- events_at_checkpoint: lo = partition_point(|e| ck(e) < k as i64), hi = partition_point(|e| ck(e) <= k as i64). k as i64 — usize as i64 fine.
- heap_events_at_stop(stop): snapshot_at_stop(stop)? → cur_count = snapshot.observation.heap_event_count; prev_count = if snapshot.step_index > 0 { snapshots[step_index-1].observation.heap_event_count } else { 0 } → &heap_events[prev..cur]. Edge: if ordering facts say heap_counts_sorted false → OrderingViolation. Also snapshot observation set... note: cur snapshot's count ≥ prev's (verified). Return slice.

Careful — events_at_stop when events empty: partition_point on empty → 0,0 → empty slice ✓.

Range checks:
- snapshot(index): index < len else OutOfRange.
- snapshots_in_range(Range): start <= end <= len else InvalidRange (start>end) / OutOfRange? Distinguish: start > end → InvalidRange; end > len → OutOfRange... my InvalidRange error includes len; simpler: if start > end || end > len → InvalidRange. Document. Also handle RangeTo/RangeFrom? Only Range<usize> for simplicity + document. Hmm — GUI pagination would like Range bounds... keep Range<usize>.
- instruction_range same.

For `disassembly_for_event(index)`: event = instruction_event(index)?; event.instruction_id → Some(id) → disassembly_entry(id) (which errors InvalidReference if OOR); None → Err(Unavailable { what: "the event recorded no disassembly entry reference" }).

`event_source(index)`: instruction_event(index)?; Ok(&event.source).

    Interrupted,
    /// Program ran to completion.
    Completed,
    /// Program died from a fatal signal.
    Crashed,
    /// Wall-clock timeout hit; partial trace preserved.
    Timeout,
    /// Step/snapshot limit hit; partial trace preserved.

    /// Kernel-enforced resource limit killed the run.
    ResourceLimitReached,
    /// GDB itself failed (missing, inoperable, protocol error).
    DebuggerFailure,
    /// Execution failed for another reason.

    /// Compilation failed; nothing was executed.

6:pub fn validate(trace: &DebugSessionTrace) -> Result<(), String> {
pub fn validate(trace: &DebugSessionTrace) -> Result<(), String> {
    let data = &trace.recording;
    for (position, event) in data.instruction_events.iter().enumerate() {
        if event.event_id != position as u64 {
            return Err("noncontiguous instruction IDs".into());
        }
        if let Some(id) = event.instruction_id {
            let instruction = data
                .disassembly_table
                .get(id as usize)
                .ok_or("invalid disassembly reference")?;
            if instruction.address != event.address {
                return Err("instruction address/reference mismatch".into());
            }
        }
        if event
            .checkpoint_id
            .is_some_and(|id| id >= trace.snapshots.len())
        {
            return Err("invalid checkpoint reference".into());
        }
    }
    if !data.instruction_events.is_empty()
        && data.instruction_count != data.instruction_events.len() as u64
    {
        return Err("instruction count mismatch".into());
    }
    for id in &data.source_checkpoints {
        let checkpoint = trace
            .snapshots
            .get(*id)
            .ok_or("invalid source checkpoint")?;
        if checkpoint.observation.instruction_position > data.instruction_count {
            return Err("checkpoint beyond timeline".into());
        }
    }
    Ok(())
}

Now — one subtlety in `heap_events_at_stop`: it uses `snapshot.step_index.checked_sub(1)`. For the first snapshot step_index 0 → previous count = 0. Good.

For test H mutation of stop ids (OrderingViolation): mutate snapshots[0].observation.stop_id = 5 and snapshots[1].observation.stop_id = 5 (equal) → not strictly increasing → snapshot_at_stop returns OrderingViolation; also validate_deep reports SNAPSHOT_STOP_ORDER. But engine validator doesn't check stop order — good, my code catches it.

Also in test H: STOP_AFTER_NOT_NEXT — mutate one event's stop_id_after = stop_id_before + 7 → validate_deep finding STOP_AFTER_NOT_NEXT corruption; trace remains indexable (queries don't use stop_id_after).

One more design consideration — `events_at_stop` uses `stop_id_before` only. stop_id_after doesn't matter.

Let me also confirm `TraceStore::from_trace` doesn't reject schema-2 traces from examples — it validates schema version only. Good.

## User

# VISUAL C — TRACE PARSER
## TP-2: Efficient Indexing, Cross-Record Resolution & Raw Execution Queries

### Your role

Act as a senior Rust systems engineer continuing development of the existing Visual C backend.

Your assignment is to implement **TP-2**, the second phase of the Trace Parser.

TP-1 has already been implemented, tested, and audited. You must **extend that existing implementation**, not replace or independently reimplement it.

The Trace Parser is a shared Rust infrastructure component that consumes execution traces produced by the existing `c-trace-engine` V2.1.

Its purpose is to make recorded execution information efficiently accessible to two future consumers:

1. **Stage 2 — Semantic Engine:** Will interpret recorded execution data to build memory objects, relationships, state differences, timelines, and educational diagnostics.
2. **Stage 3 — GUI Query/Replay API:** Will expose raw and semantic information to Visual C's frontend.

The Trace Parser must remain independent of both consumers.

**TP-2's objective is to transform the canonical `TraceStore` created in TP-1 into an efficiently queryable execution-data store, without duplicating the underlying trace or interpreting C program semantics.**

Do not implement TP-3, the Semantic Engine, or the GUI.

---

# 1. Existing architecture — preserve it

TP-1 established the following architecture:

```text
             c-trace-engine V2.1
                       |
                       v
               Raw JSON Trace
                       |
                       v
              TRACE PARSER
                       |
        +-----------------------------+
        |                             |
        | TP-1: TraceStore            |
        |                             |
        | - Format detection          |
        | - Deserialization          |
        | - Structural validation     |
        | - Canonical trace ownership |
        | - Schema compatibility      |
        | - Typed ingestion errors    |
        |                             |
        +-----------------------------+
                       |
                       v
        +-----------------------------+
        |                             |
        | TP-2: Indexed Access        |
        |                             |
        | - Compact indexes           |
        | - Raw queries               |
        | - Reference resolution      |
        | - Deep validation           |
        | - Efficient range access    |
        |                             |
        +-----------------------------+
                       |
                       v
         Shared Trace Access Foundation
                  /          \
                 /            \
                v              v
          Raw consumers     Semantic Engine
```

The existing `TraceStore` owns an `Arc<DebugSessionTrace>`.

This canonical representation is already verified to preserve recorded information without duplicating the trace.

Continue using this model.

Do not create a second full representation of `DebugSessionTrace`.

Do not duplicate arrays of instruction events, snapshots, disassembly records, heap events, or raw memory bytes merely to support queries.

Indexes must reference the canonical data.

### Existing code

Inspect and extend the actual implementation, particularly:

- `src/trace_parser/mod.rs`
- `src/trace_parser/json.rs`
- `src/trace_parser/journal.rs`
- `src/trace_parser/error.rs`
- `src/models.rs`
- `src/storage.rs`
- `docs/trace-parser.md`
- Existing unit and integration tests.

The repository currently contains one Rust crate, `c-trace-engine`, with library and binary targets.

Do not introduce another crate unless an actual architectural necessity is demonstrated.

Preserve the TP-1 public API and existing Stage 1 functionality.

---

# 2. TP-1 acceptance audit findings — authoritative implementation context

The TP-1 acceptance audit reported:

- 160 tests passed.
- Six real V2.1 JSON fixtures successfully ingested.
- Fresh Stage 1 traces loaded successfully.
- Value-identical trace round trips.
- One canonical `Arc`-owned representation.
- No reparsing during repeated access.
- Safe concurrent readers.
- No Stage 1 regressions.
- Structured error handling and bounded ingestion.

Large-trace test:

- Input size: 46.4 MiB.
- Instruction events: 94,306.
- Release ingestion time: approximately 904 ms.
- Peak RSS: approximately 206 MiB.
- Steady RSS: approximately 157 MiB.

These measurements establish a baseline, not guaranteed performance targets.

The TP-2 implementation must prioritize efficient queries while keeping additional memory overhead reasonable.

### Critical limitation

The existing journal format can be decoded, but cannot reconstruct a complete `DebugSessionTrace` because certain finalized fields are never journaled.

Therefore:

**Use complete V2.1 JSON traces as the authoritative input for TP-2 indexing and queries.**

Do not fabricate fields to make journal data equivalent to complete JSON.

Do not modify the journal writer during this phase.

Existing journal decoding must remain functional.

---

# 3. Mandatory reference-semantics contract

The TP-1 audit examined the actual Stage 1 implementation and established the following reference meanings.

You must verify these against the repository before coding and preserve their semantics.

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `event_id` | Zero-based position in `instruction_events`; recorder enforces contiguity |
| `instruction_id` | Zero-based index into `disassembly_table` |
| `checkpoint_id` in instruction events | Zero-based index into `snapshots` |
| `source_checkpoints[]` | Snapshot indices, not independent checkpoint objects |
| `step_index` | Snapshot index |
| `stop_id` | One-based counter of processed GDB stops |
| `stop_id_before` / `stop_id_after` | References to GDB stop-counter positions |
| `observed_at_stop` | GDB stop-counter position associated with an allocation observation |
| `instruction_position` | Execution-order position relative to attempted instruction events |
| `instruction_count` | Total attempted instruction-event count; may exceed retained events |
| `allocation_id` | Engine-assigned stable heap-allocation identity |
| `realloc_from_id` | Allocation identity associated with reallocation |
| `sequence` | Runtime instrumentation sequence counter |
| `activation_id` | Function-activation identity |
| `lexical_scope_id` | Existing lexical-scope identifier |
| `StackFrameInfo.level` | Stack depth, zero being the innermost frame |
| Address fields | Recorded process memory addresses, commonly represented as hexadecimal strings |

Additional established facts:

- Allocation ID `0` means untracked.
- Heap allocation IDs are **not** vector indices.
- Different allocations can reuse the same address.
- Repeated machine instruction addresses represent distinct execution events.
- Instruction IDs reference disassembly records, not individual executions.
- GDB stop counters use a different sequence from instruction-event positions.
- `source_checkpoints` does not necessarily include every snapshot.
- Some trace configurations retain fewer instruction events than were attempted.

### Absolute rule

**Never infer reference semantics from a field's name.**

For example:

```text
event_id        -> vector position
instruction_id  -> disassembly position
checkpoint_id   -> snapshot position
stop_id         -> separate GDB stop counter
allocation_id   -> stable allocation identity
address         -> observed memory location
```

These are fundamentally different concepts.

Do not convert them into a single generic index or assume that they share a numbering system.

---

# 4. TP-2 responsibilities

Implement the following capabilities as extensions of the existing Trace Parser.

### Required

1. Efficient direct access to existing vector-indexed records.
2. Compact indexes for genuinely nontrivial lookups.
3. Checkpoint and execution-stop navigation.
4. Instruction-event and disassembly relationships.
5. Source-location-to-instruction relationships.
6. Heap-allocation and allocation-event lookup.
7. Raw diagnostic and evidence lookup where supported.
8. Cross-record reference validation.
9. Efficient ordered-range queries.
10. Tests and measured query-performance comparisons.

### Not required

- Semantic object identification.
- Pointer target inference.
- Memory relationship graphs.
- State differences.
- Educational diagnostics.
- Reconstructing unrecorded memory.
- Re-running the traced program.
- GUI-specific data models.
- Tauri commands.
- Separate semantic-input and GUI-query facades.
- Advanced query caching.
- Journal format redesign.

Those belong to later phases.

---

# 5. Build indexes only where they provide value

This requirement is particularly important.

Some existing references are already ordinary vector indices.

For example:

```rust
trace.instruction_events.get(event_id)
```

is already constant-time access when `event_id` is a valid vector position.

Creating a hash map that maps every `event_id` back to the same vector position would add memory usage without providing meaningful improvement.

### Indexing policy

For each proposed index:

1. Identify the corresponding lookup operation.
2. Establish the complexity of direct access without the index.
3. Determine whether repeated linear scans are currently required.
4. Choose an efficient representation.
5. Estimate index memory overhead.
6. Avoid the index if direct access is already sufficient.

Prefer:

- Direct vector access for positional identifiers.
- Compact vector-based mappings for dense numeric domains.
- Hash maps for sparse, non-positional identities.
- Ordered position lists for one-to-many relationships.
- Bounded ranges where records are already grouped.
- Borrowed slices or iterators over existing records.

Avoid:

- Duplicate full events inside maps.
- A hash map for every numeric index.
- Redundant copies of source strings for every event.
- Sorting or copying entire event collections on each query.
- Building many rarely used indexes without justification.

**The goal is faster access per unit of additional memory, not the maximum possible number of indexes.**

---

# 6. Index lifetime and ownership

Extend `TraceStore` so that indexes are associated with the same canonical trace.

The desired ownership model is:

```text
TraceStore
|
+-- Canonical DebugSessionTrace
|      |
|      +-- snapshots
|      +-- instruction_events
|      +-- disassembly_table
|      +-- heap_events
|      +-- diagnostics
|      +-- metadata
|
+-- TraceIndexes
       |
       +-- source-location lookup
       +-- stop-to-snapshot lookup
       +-- allocation-event lookup
       +-- instruction relationships
       +-- other justified indexes
```

This is conceptual, not a required Rust structure.

### Requirements

- Do not replace the canonical `Arc<DebugSessionTrace>`.
- Do not require callers to deserialize the trace again.
- Do not duplicate raw records inside indexes.
- Preserve safe, immutable concurrent access.
- Ensure cloned `TraceStore` handles share the same indexes.
- Avoid unnecessary locks during read-only queries.
- Prevent partial or inconsistent index initialization.
- Keep index initialization errors explicit.

### Eager versus lazy indexing

Evaluate both approaches.

**Eager:** Build the justified indexes once when the store is created.

**Lazy:** Build an index group on its first use, then share it across subsequent queries.

Choose based on actual implementation complexity, typical usage, and memory cost.

A thread-safe `OnceLock`-style implementation is acceptable if appropriate.

Do not introduce an elaborate cache-management system merely to support lazy initialization.

If initial TP-2 indexing is eager, measure its additional loading cost.

If lazy, benchmark first-query cost separately from subsequent queries.

### Sharing invariant

Cloning a `TraceStore` must not reconstruct indexes or create an independent full index set per clone.

The raw trace and indexes should belong to a common shareable storage context.

Preserve TP-1's existing `shared()` behavior wherever possible.

---

# 7. Source checkpoint and snapshot access

Provide efficient access to recorded snapshots.

Supported operations should conceptually include:

```rust
get_snapshot(snapshot_index)
get_source_checkpoint(source_checkpoint_position)
get_source_checkpoint_indices()
get_snapshots_in_range(start, end)
```

Adapt the names and signatures to existing models.

### Critical distinction

A source-checkpoint position is not automatically the same thing as a snapshot index.

For example:

```text
source_checkpoints = [0, 4, 9, 15]
```

Then:

```text
source checkpoint #2 -> snapshots[9]
```

Do not return `snapshots[2]`.

### Requirements

- Preserve snapshot ordering.
- Preserve source-checkpoint ordering.
- Treat the index list as the authoritative mapping.
- Support empty source-checkpoint lists.
- Handle invalid positions safely.
- Avoid cloning snapshots for normal queries.
- Do not infer missing source checkpoints.
- Do not assume every snapshot corresponds to a source checkpoint.

The GUI will eventually use these operations to move through actual observed execution states.

---

# 8. Instruction-event access and range queries

Instruction events represent executed machine instructions recorded by Stage 1.

Implement efficient operations conceptually equivalent to:

```rust
get_instruction_event(event_index)
get_instruction_range(start, end)
get_instruction_count()
```

### Requirements

- Direct positional lookup should be constant-time.
- Contiguous ranges should ideally borrow existing slices.
- Preserve original event ordering.
- Preserve repeated instruction addresses.
- Never collapse repeated executions into one event.
- Do not return the entire timeline when only a small range is requested.
- Handle empty ranges.
- Handle invalid or overflowing bounds safely.
- Make range-boundary semantics explicit.

### Attempted versus retained instructions

The trace may contain:

```text
instruction_count > instruction_events.len()
```

because of retention settings or incomplete recording.

Expose these values distinctly.

Do not claim that every attempted instruction has a retained event.

Do not generate synthetic instruction events to fill the difference.

### Design principle

**A recorded instruction execution is identified by its event position, not solely by its machine address.**

This is essential for replaying loops correctly.

---

# 9. Instruction-to-disassembly resolution

Each instruction event may reference an entry in the disassembly table through `instruction_id`.

Provide efficient, typed resolution.

Conceptual operations:

```rust
get_disassembly_entry(instruction_id)
get_disassembly_for_event(event_index)
get_execution_events_for_instruction(instruction_id)
```

### Requirements

- Resolve an instruction event to its actual disassembly entry.
- Verify available ID/address invariants.
- Preserve distinctions between static disassembly entries and dynamic execution events.
- Support repeated execution of one disassembled instruction.
- Return explicit unavailable or invalid-reference results when appropriate.
- Avoid copying disassembly records.

### Reverse lookup

A reverse relationship from a disassembly entry to its executed event positions may be valuable.

Implement this efficiently if it provides a clear query benefit.

Prefer compact lists of event positions rather than copies of events.

For example:

```text
Disassembly entry #17
    -> event positions [31, 44, 57, 70]
```

These are distinct executions of the same static instruction.

### Missing information

A trace may contain incomplete disassembly information.

Do not fabricate assembly text or assume an instruction can be resolved if the recorded data does not support it.

---

# 10. Source-to-assembly relationships

Visual C will display both C code and the corresponding assembly execution.

TP-2 must establish efficient access to recorded source and disassembly mappings.

Conceptual operations:

```rust
get_disassembly_for_source(file, line)
get_executed_events_for_source(file, line)
get_source_for_instruction(instruction_id)
```

These signatures are illustrative.

Use the actual mapping fields provided by Stage 1.

### Important distinction

There are two different questions:

**Question A:** Which disassembled instructions are associated with this source location?

**Question B:** Which recorded execution events executed instructions associated with this source location?

These must not be confused.

For example, a source line can correspond to three static instructions, each executed many times.

The source-to-disassembly lookup may return three entries.

The source-to-execution lookup may return hundreds of instruction events.

### Requirements

- Preserve one-to-many mappings.
- Support repeated visits to the same source line.
- Support multiple instructions per source line.
- Support multiple source locations where the existing representation permits them.
- Preserve execution ordering in dynamic-event results.
- Handle instructions with unavailable source mappings.
- Support source files with identical basenames.
- Avoid guessing that two paths refer to the same file.

Use the actual recorded file identity and mapping rules.

Do not introduce aggressive filename normalization that could merge distinct files.

### Performance

Avoid scanning every instruction event and disassembly entry on every source lookup.

Build compact indexes for the necessary relationships.

Do not duplicate whole instruction-event records.

---

# 11. Execution-stop and checkpoint relationships

The Stage 1 trace records GDB stops using `stop_id`.

This value is not a snapshot vector index.

Implement indexed relationships based on actual recorded evidence.

Useful operations may include:

```rust
get_snapshots_at_stop(stop_id)
get_allocation_events_at_stop(stop_id)
get_instruction_events_related_to_stop(stop_id)
```

Use names that accurately describe the actual relationship.

### Requirements

- Respect the one-based stop-counter semantics.
- Preserve repeated or shared stop associations.
- Distinguish `stop_id_before` and `stop_id_after`.
- Preserve allocation `observed_at_stop`.
- Do not assume every stop has a snapshot.
- Do not assume every snapshot has a uniquely associated instruction.
- Do not treat stop IDs as dense snapshot positions.

### Instruction positions

Snapshots and trace gaps may reference instruction positions.

These positions must be interpreted according to Stage 1's actual recording contract.

Do not assume that an attempted instruction-event position is always an index into the retained event vector.

In particular, retention-disabled or truncated traces may not provide every instruction event needed for direct resolution.

### Missing joins

If a stop, checkpoint, or instruction position cannot be linked using available evidence, return an explicit unresolved/unavailable result.

Do not use the closest timestamp or nearest index as an invented relationship.

---

# 12. Heap allocation and memory-event indexing

Stage 1 records heap allocation events and associated identities.

Provide efficient lookup of those records.

Conceptual operations:

```rust
get_heap_events_for_allocation(allocation_id)
get_heap_block(allocation_id)
get_heap_events_at_stop(stop_id)
```

Adapt these to the actual models.

### Allocation identity

The allocation ID is the authoritative identity.

Memory addresses are not allocation identities.

Consider:

```text
Allocation A:
    id = 12
    address = 0x1000

Allocation A is freed.

Allocation B:
    id = 19
    address = 0x1000
```

These are two different allocations even though the address was reused.

A query for allocation `12` must never accidentally return allocation `19`.

### Requirements

- Index heap events by actual allocation ID.
- Preserve event ordering.
- Handle allocation ID `0` as untracked according to the existing contract.
- Handle `realloc_from_id` without inventing identity equivalence.
- Preserve allocation and free sequence metadata.
- Handle events associated with the same GDB stop.
- Avoid treating hexadecimal addresses as allocation keys.
- Preserve malformed or unavailable data according to validation policy.

### Reallocation

Do not assume `realloc` always preserves the same allocation identity or address.

Use the actual recorded IDs and relationships.

TP-2 may expose the recorded `realloc_from_id` reference but must not build higher-level allocation-lifetime interpretations.

Those belong to Stage 2.

---

# 13. Raw memory and variable observations

TP-2 should make the existing recorded observations accessible without interpreting them.

At minimum, callers should be able to retrieve a checkpoint and inspect its existing variable, stack, heap, and memory data.

Where a narrowly scoped query avoids repeated expensive scans, add an appropriate accessor.

However, **do not build a complete semantic memory model**.

### Requirements

- Preserve raw addresses.
- Preserve recorded sizes.
- Preserve exact bytes.
- Preserve unavailable/read-failure states.
- Preserve variable and frame metadata.
- Avoid copying large byte buffers unnecessarily.
- Return references where Rust ownership permits.

### Important limitation

TP-2 must not provide an API that pretends arbitrary process memory can be read at any checkpoint.

Only recorded memory observations are available.

For example, an address absent from a checkpoint must not be returned as zero-filled memory.

Similarly, a value recorded at checkpoint 10 must not automatically be presented as an observation at checkpoint 11.

The Semantic Engine will later decide how to represent changes and observation gaps.

TP-2 should preserve the original evidence.

---

# 14. Diagnostic and evidence access

Stage 1 already contains raw diagnostic reports from tools such as GDB, Valgrind, and sanitizers.

Make these records available through lightweight, typed accessors.

### Requirements

- Preserve the original diagnostic content.
- Preserve source locations and recorded addresses.
- Preserve optional fields.
- Preserve tool-stage completion statuses.
- Do not duplicate diagnostic reports into another large representation.

Where the existing schema provides stable identifiers or references, support their resolution.

Where no stable ID exists, use documented positional access within the relevant report collection.

Do not invent cross-tool evidence relationships.

### Critical scope distinction

TP-2 can answer:

"Which raw Valgrind findings were recorded?"

TP-2 must not answer:

"Why did this pointer become dangling?"

The second question requires semantic interpretation and belongs to Stage 2.

---

# 15. Cross-record validation

TP-1 handles basic structural validation.

TP-2 must extend validation to meaningful relationships between existing records.

### Validate supported invariants

Examples include:

1. Instruction `event_id` matches its recorded vector position where required.
2. Instruction IDs resolve to valid disassembly entries.
3. Event addresses match their referenced disassembly entries where Stage 1 guarantees that invariant.
4. Snapshot references are within bounds.
5. Source-checkpoint indices reference actual snapshots.
6. Snapshot `step_index` follows the existing recording contract.
7. Stop and instruction-position references follow their documented domains.
8. Allocation references are interpreted according to the actual allocation-ID contract.
9. Existing chronological-order invariants are respected where guaranteed.
10. Referenced diagnostic or evidence records exist where the schema explicitly requires them.

Do not invent invariants that Stage 1 does not guarantee.

### Validation severity

Separate:

**Structural corruption:** A record violates a guaranteed invariant.

**Partial coverage:** The trace does not contain every observation.

**Unavailable evidence:** A relationship cannot be established because information was not recorded.

**Optional absence:** The schema permits a field to be missing.

These situations must not be conflated.

### Valid incomplete traces

The following must remain supportable:

- Crashes.
- Timeouts.
- Step-limit termination.
- Truncated execution coverage explicitly recorded by Stage 1.
- Skipped diagnostic stages.
- Unavailable memory observations.
- Missing source mappings.
- Instruction retention gaps.

Do not reject such traces merely because they lack observations.

### Validation implementation

Choose a clean separation between:

- Existing TP-1 ingestion.
- TP-2 index construction.
- Optional or explicit deep referential validation.

Avoid silently making the TP-1 loader reject previously accepted, legitimately partial traces because of new assumptions.

Document whether deep validation is performed automatically or explicitly requested.

Report violations using typed errors with useful record context.

Preserve existing TP-1 error behavior wherever practical.

---

# 16. Typed query results and errors

Design query methods using idiomatic Rust.

Do not force every method into a single generic return type.

Suitable patterns may include:

```rust
Option<&T>
Result<&T, QueryError>
&[T]
impl Iterator<Item = &T>
```

Choose based on the operation.

### Important distinctions

Clearly distinguish:

- An invalid query argument.
- An out-of-range positional index.
- A valid query with no matching records.
- A reference that is structurally invalid.
- An observation not recorded.
- An unsupported query for the available trace format.

Do not use a successful empty result to conceal data corruption.

Likewise, a valid source line with no executed instructions should not automatically be treated as a malformed trace.

### Efficient ownership

Prefer borrowed references, slices, lightweight positions, and iterators.

Do not clone a large vector merely to return a small range.

Do not expose mutable references to canonical trace data.

---

# 17. Preserve recorded execution order

The Trace Parser's eventual purpose includes time-travel debugging and stepwise execution visualization.

TP-2 must make recorded ordering reliable.

### Required rules

- Instruction events remain ordered by recorded event position.
- Snapshots remain ordered by their original vector positions.
- Source checkpoints preserve their explicit sequence.
- Allocation events preserve their existing recorded order.
- Stop counters remain distinct from event indices.
- Runtime allocation sequence counters remain distinct from GDB stop counters.
- Partial coverage and trace gaps remain visible.

If an index groups events by source line, instruction, allocation, or stop, preserve the original order within that group unless the query explicitly requests another documented ordering.

Do not sort canonical trace arrays in place.

---

# 18. Memory and resource efficiency

TP-1's large-trace audit showed meaningful memory expansion during JSON deserialization.

TP-2 should not substantially worsen this without a justified query-performance benefit.

### Engineering expectations

- Use compact indexes.
- Avoid redundant dense-ID maps.
- Store positions instead of whole records.
- Avoid cloning long source-path strings per instruction event.
- Avoid unnecessary `Arc` allocations for each event.
- Avoid global mutable caches.
- Avoid building enormous nested hash maps by default.
- Keep read-only queries lock-free where feasible.
- Make index construction bounded by actual trace size and configured resource constraints.

### Construction complexity

Aim for linear or near-linear index construction relative to the relevant trace collections.

Avoid accidental quadratic algorithms.

If an index requires sorting, document its complexity and whether it affects the original record order.

### Index memory audit

Measure the additional memory required by index construction.

Report the result separately from the memory required to deserialize the raw trace.

If a proposed index is expensive and offers little improvement over direct access, remove it.

---

# 19. Performance benchmarking

TP-2 must provide measured evidence of improvement.

Do not report guessed or theoretical speedups as measured results.

### Benchmark scenarios

Use representative real V2.1 traces, including:

- A small ordinary trace.
- A finite loop with repeated instruction addresses.
- A source/assembly trace.
- A heap-allocation trace.
- A large instruction-heavy trace, preferably the 94,306-event case if available.

### Compare

For relevant query types, compare:

**Baseline:** A straightforward repeated linear scan of the canonical arrays.

**TP-2:** The new indexed query.

Measure:

1. Initial index-construction time.
2. Direct event lookup latency.
3. Source-location lookup latency.
4. Reverse disassembly-to-event lookup latency.
5. Allocation-event lookup latency.
6. Stop-to-checkpoint lookup latency.
7. Repeated-query throughput.
8. Additional index memory usage.
9. Total store memory usage after indexing.

Only benchmark operations for which a comparison is meaningful.

For example, direct vector indexing is already constant-time and does not require a linear-scan baseline.

### Benchmark methodology

- Prefer optimized/release builds.
- Use a reasonable number of repeated queries.
- Prevent the compiler from optimizing away query work.
- Separate cold index-building costs from warm query costs.
- Use representative successful and unsuccessful lookups.
- Document test hardware and input trace sizes.
- Present actual measured results.
- Do not claim speedups for query categories not tested.

### Acceptance principle

TP-2 does not need to make every query faster.

It needs to make frequently repeated nontrivial lookups significantly more efficient while keeping resource overhead sensible.

---

# 20. Tests

Add comprehensive tests for the new indexing and query behavior.

Keep all existing tests.

### A. Basic positional access

- First event.
- Last event.
- Out-of-range event.
- Empty range.
- Full range.
- Invalid range bounds.
- First and last snapshots.

### B. Source checkpoint mapping

- Source-checkpoint list with noncontiguous snapshot indices.
- Multiple snapshots without source-checkpoint membership.
- Empty source-checkpoint list.
- Invalid source-checkpoint reference.
- Preservation of original ordering.

### C. Instruction and disassembly

- Multiple events referencing one disassembly entry.
- Repeated instruction addresses.
- Correct event-to-disassembly resolution.
- Reverse disassembly-to-event lookup.
- Unavailable disassembly.
- Invalid instruction reference.

### D. Source mapping

- Multiple machine instructions for one C source line.
- Repeated execution of one C source line.
- Distinct files with identical basenames.
- Source locations without executed events.
- Instruction events without available source mapping.
- Correct static-versus-dynamic lookup distinctions.

### E. Execution stops

- One-based `stop_id`.
- Multiple records associated with a stop.
- Stops without snapshots.
- Snapshot and event positions that do not equal stop IDs.
- Correct allocation observation stop mapping.
- Missing stop relationships.

### F. Heap allocations

- Multiple events with the same allocation ID.
- Multiple allocations reusing the same address.
- Allocation ID zero.
- Reallocation references.
- Allocation and free event ordering.
- No false merging by address.

### G. Partial traces

- Crash traces.
- Timeout traces.
- Instruction retention gaps.
- `instruction_count` greater than retained event count.
- Missing optional source locations.
- Incomplete tool-stage reports.

### H. Referential validation

- Broken snapshot reference.
- Broken disassembly reference.
- Inconsistent event ID.
- Inconsistent instruction address where the invariant is guaranteed.
- Invalid source-checkpoint position.
- Legitimately absent observations.
- Distinction between corruption and partial coverage.

### I. Ownership and concurrency

- Repeated queries do not reparse.
- Store clones share canonical data.
- Store clones share initialized indexes.
- Parallel readers return consistent results.
- No mutation of source arrays.
- No unexpected full-vector copies during queries.

### J. Integration tests

Use the real V2.1 fixtures already in the repository.

Verify raw query results against direct inspection of the corresponding canonical trace arrays.

Where feasible, generate at least one fresh Stage 1 trace for compatibility testing.

# 21. Public API design

Create a coherent typed API that future components can extend.

The following is a conceptual example only:

```rust
let store = TraceStore::open(
    "trace.json",
    TraceLoadOptions::default(),
)?;

// Direct positional access
let snapshot = store.snapshot(12)?;
let event = store.instruction_event(30)?;

// Recorded range
let events = store.instruction_range(30..80)?;

// Cross-record resolution
let disassembly = store.disassembly_for_event(30)?;

// Source relationship
let instructions = store.instructions_for_source(
    "main.c",
    15,
)?;

// Allocation relationship
let allocations = store.heap_events_for_allocation(7)?;
```

Adapt the actual signatures to the existing Rust types.

Do not implement these exact names mechanically.

Choose a consistent naming convention and document it.

### Required API properties

- Typed.
- Read-only.
- Efficient.
- Predictable ordering.
- Explicit reference semantics.
- Reasonable error handling.
- No unnecessary cloning.
- No dependency on Tauri.
- No dependency on future semantic models.

### Forward compatibility

TP-3 will later add two specialized consumer interfaces:

```rust
// Future interfaces — do not implement in TP-2.

store.raw()
store.semantic_input()
```

TP-2 should produce the reusable query primitives that both future interfaces will rely on.

Do not design TP-2 around specific GUI panels or semantic processing algorithms.

---

# 22. Explicit scope exclusions

Do not implement any of the following:

### Stage 2 — Semantic Engine

- Stable C object registry.
- Stack/heap object interpretation.
- Pointer graph.
- Aliasing analysis.
- Dangling pointer detection.
- Memory layout inference.
- State difference generation.
- Semantic event timeline.
- Educational bug explanations.

### Stage 3 — GUI Query/Replay API

- Tauri IPC commands.
- Frontend transport.
- GUI pagination payloads.
- Replay session controllers.
- Visualization-specific JSON.
- Panel-specific query adapters.

### TP-3 — Consumer interfaces and advanced optimization

- Separate raw/semantic access facades.
- Specialized semantic observation structures.
- Advanced lazy loading.
- Cache eviction policies.
- Database-backed trace storage.
- Journal-to-complete-trace reconstruction.
- Persistent index files.

TP-2 may use simple lazy index initialization if justified.

Do not extend beyond the requested indexing and query layer.

# 24. Acceptance criteria

TP-2 is complete when all of the following are satisfied:

1. Existing TP-1 ingestion and ownership remain intact.
2. The canonical trace is not duplicated.
3. Useful indexes are built over existing records.
4. Redundant indexes are avoided.
5. Positional queries are efficient.
6. Source checkpoint mappings are correct.
7. Instruction events resolve to recorded disassembly entries.
8. Source-location queries distinguish static instructions from dynamic executions.
9. Repeated instruction execution remains distinct.
10. GDB stop counters are never mistaken for snapshot indices.
11. Heap allocation IDs are never mistaken for addresses or array positions.
12. Available cross-record references can be resolved efficiently.
13. Invalid references can be detected without rejecting legitimately partial traces.
14. Query results preserve recorded ordering.
15. Query methods avoid unnecessary large allocations.
16. Shared access is safe across threads.
17. Index-building costs and memory overhead are measured.
18. Indexed query performance is compared with linear scans where meaningful.
19. Existing Stage 1 and TP-1 tests continue passing.
20. Documentation and tests describe the actual implemented behavior.

Do not declare TP-2 complete based on compilation alone.
